scope.title: Verified Part I - Microstructural Foundations for Financial Markets

nodes.title: Principle of Agent Actions
nodes.statement: The admissible actions of any agent are constrained only by available resources and market legislation.
proofBridge: prin:agent-actions documented as a guiding principle in Foundations/Economics.lean.

motivationContexts.text: In what follows, we will present an approach that relaxes some of the ideal assumptions within the field. In our pursuit, we will stick only to three principles.

Let us first remark that an agent is any entity capable of carrying out actions within a market. As such, an agent may be a single person, an institution, or a coalition of people. On that note, a market is any collection of agents wishing to exchange items under a common set of rules. Finally, by items or resources, we mean, in a very broad sense, any physical object, service, or claim attributable to an agent.

The first principle states that any agent is constrained only by available resources and legislation. The former concerns both the resources available from external sources as well as internal sources, such as, e.g., savings. A central component within the forthcoming theory is that we will make no assumptions regarding the rationality of the agents within the market. Any agent within the market is free to take any admissible action they desire, regardless of whether the action can be seen as optimal or not.

Moreover, one could argue that the above implicitly defines utility for the agent; one can always model observed actions as maximizing some unobserved utility, but we do not assume this; we treat actions as primitives and model them statistically. However, even so, the point is that utility is, in practice, never known to others. In fact, we would argue that even the agent themselves may not be explicitly aware of their utility as a stable measure of value of one item against all others.

nodes.title: Principle of Finitism
nodes.statement: Over any finite interval of time, there are \begin{enumerate}[(i)] \item a finite number of agents that act within the market, and \item a finite number of actions that each agent can carry out. \end{enumerate}
proofBridge: prin:finitism documented as a guiding principle in Foundations/Economics.lean.

motivationContexts.text: On these grounds, we should like to avoid the discussion of utility altogether, as utility is not directly observable and hard to falsify without strong auxiliary assumptions; the ulterior motives for one's actions may be suboptimal given some states and information, while optimal given others. Instead, we opt to leverage statistical analysis of orders, providing data-driven models for actions, hence omitting any claim as to whether or not they are optimal, rational, or provide sufficient utility for the respective agents.

Nonetheless, we shall use the word utility from time to time, but one should not think of utility in the strict sense of, e.g., von Neumann and Morgenstern, (von1947theory), but rather in the literal sense of being useful or beneficial.

The second principle is that the market is, in a certain sense, finite. In particular, over any finite interval of time, the number of agents that actually act must be finite. The point is operational rather than metaphysical: any realized market over a finite time window can only involve finitely many instantiated agents or decision systems. Likewise, each such agent can realize only finitely many actions during that finite interval.

The second requirement is that each agent can carry out at most a finite number of actions in any finite interval. Note that the principle does not say that the number of potential actions of an agent is restricted. Instead, it states that the number of actions that are carried out in practice must be finite. To exemplify, consider an agent who is thirsty and wishes to drink some water. Potentially, they could choose to drink any fraction of the water available to them (even all of it), but they cannot dissect the process of drinking into an infinite number of realized steps over a finite interval of time.

nodes.title: Principle of Clearing
nodes.statement: A market is said to be cleared if and only if no admissible exchange remains that the involved agents are jointly willing to carry out.
proofBridge: prin:clearing documented as a guiding principle in Foundations/Economics.lean.

motivationContexts.text: The second principle is that the market is, in a certain sense, finite. In particular, over any finite interval of time, the number of agents that actually act must be finite. The point is operational rather than metaphysical: any realized market over a finite time window can only involve finitely many instantiated agents or decision systems. Likewise, each such agent can realize only finitely many actions during that finite interval.

The second requirement is that each agent can carry out at most a finite number of actions in any finite interval. Note that the principle does not say that the number of potential actions of an agent is restricted. Instead, it states that the number of actions that are carried out in practice must be finite. To exemplify, consider an agent who is thirsty and wishes to drink some water. Potentially, they could choose to drink any fraction of the water available to them (even all of it), but they cannot dissect the process of drinking into an infinite number of realized steps over a finite interval of time.

The final principle simply states that the market is cleared whenever no admissible exchange remains that the relevant agents are willing to undertake. Note that the grounds of the clearing can be very superficial. For instance, suppose that two agents within the market are hostile towards one another, but each has an item that the other wants. Then the market may be cleared, as they do not want to trade with one another directly. Only if a third agent chooses to act as an intermediary between the two would an exchange happen, but whether or not a third party chooses to do so is not guaranteed. We remark that prin:clearing is, for all practical purposes, a definition of what it means for the market to be cleared.

nodes.title: Disjoint Union

references.formatted: Lee, J. Introduction to topological manifolds. Springer Science & Business Media, 2010.

nodes.statement: Let $(X_\alpha)_{\alpha \in A}$ be a family of sets over a non-empty set $A$. The set \begin{align*} \bigsqcup_{\alpha \in A} X_\alpha = \bigcup_{\alpha \in A} X_\alpha \times \{\alpha\} = \bigcup_{\alpha \in A} \{(x,\alpha) \mid x \in X_\alpha \} \end{align*} is called the disjoint union of $(X_\alpha)_{\alpha \in A}$.
proofBridge: defn:disjoint-union Lean-native dependent-sum definition.

motivationContexts.text: Before describing markets, we must first describe orders. An order is an agent's willingness to buy or sell a given amount of an asset at a prespecified price. Depending on the type of market, it may also include information about the agent, the time the order was submitted, or other features.
There are several approaches to the problem. However, to describe the market, it is desirable to distinguish between buy and sell orders. For our purposes, we shall leverage the disjoint union.

Disjoint unions allow us to consider several potentially unrelated sets as a whole, while retaining information about which set the element originally came from. Heuristically, from a financial market perspective, we typically have two types of orders: buy orders and sell orders. Although they are seemingly different, we would like to consider them as a common instance of an order in the market without forgetting which type of order they originally were.

Using disjoint unions, one can restrict the admissible actions over a range of scenarios as seen from Examples exmp:adm-static,exmp:agent-adm-static, exmp:adm-dyn, and exmp:agent-adm-dyn. However, as is shown in Examples exmp:agent-adm-static and exmp:agent-adm-dyn, choosing the sets on which one takes the set product and disjoint union depends highly on the application.

nodes.title: Admissible Orders in a Static Market
nodes.statement: Consider a simple static market, in which each order can be represented by $(p, q)$ where $p \in \mathbb{R}$ is the price\footnote{Classically, one often assumes prices to be positive, but in the power market prices may very well be negative. Moreover, in most, if not all, real markets the potential prices are discrete and elements in the set $\Delta_p \mathbb{Z} = \{\Delta_p \cdot z \mid z \in \mathbb{Z}\}$ for some $\Delta_p > 0$ known as the tick-size} and $q \in [0,\infty)$ is the quantity\footnote{Like the prices, actual orders must have their quantity discretized. That is, the quantity must be an element of $\Delta_q \mathbb{N}_0 =\{\Delta_q \cdot n \mid n \in \mathbb{N}_0\}$ for some $\Delta_q > 0$ known as the lot-size.}. Each order can be classified as a buy or sell order, such that $((p,q), \kappa)$ is an order with intent $\kappa \in \{\mathrm{buy},~\mathrm{sell}\}$. As such, the space of admissible orders may be given by \begin{align*} \bigsqcup_{\kappa \in \{\mathrm{buy},~\mathrm{sell}\}} \mathbb{R}\times [0,\infty). \end{align*} However, in this example, there is no difference between using disjoint unions or the product space \begin{align*} \mathbb{R}\times [0,\infty) \times \{\mathrm{buy},~\mathrm{sell}\}. \end{align*} Indeed, one defines the map \begin{align*} ((p,q), \kappa) \mapsto (p,q,\kappa), \end{align*} which is easily shown to be an isomorphism. In the present example, one may view the disjoint union as a nuisance, but, as we shall later see, it has advantages.

nodes.title: Agent Based Admissible Orders in a Static Market
nodes.statement: We now consider a slight modification of Example \ref{exmp:adm-static}, where one considers a set of agents, $A$, who can engage with the market. Suppose that the admissible orders of each agent are limited in price and quantity based on direction. For instance, retail investors are often limited, if not inhibited, from short-selling assets - the practice of borrowing an asset to sell it, while agreeing to buy the asset back at a later time - due to their limited funds and inability to put forth margins. However, institutional investors backed by companies with large funds can often take larger short-selling positions, as they are capable of posting the required margin. Such a scenario may be covered by letting $P_{\kappa, a}\subseteq \mathbb{R}$ and $Q_{\kappa, a}\subseteq [0,\infty)$ be the sets of potential admissible prices and quantities for agent $a\in A$ when taking positions in direction $\kappa \in \{\mathrm{buy},~\mathrm{sell}\}$. Therefore, each order can be seen as an element in the space \begin{align*} \bigsqcup_{(\kappa, a) \in \{\mathrm{buy},~\mathrm{sell}\}\times A} P_{\kappa, a} \times Q_{\kappa, a}. \end{align*} In addition, note that the mapping \begin{align} ((p,q), \kappa, a) \mapsto (p,q,\kappa, a) \end{align} is generally no longer a bijection, although it is still injective. In particular, if it is not a bijection, then \begin{align*} \bigsqcup_{(\kappa, a) \in \{\mathrm{buy},~\mathrm{sell}\}\times A} P_{\kappa, a} \times Q_{\kappa, a} \subset \mathbb{R}\times [0,\infty) \times \{\mathrm{buy},~\mathrm{sell}\}\times A, \end{align*} where the strict inclusion is meant under the map \eqref{eq:agent-adm-static-inj}.

nodes.title: Admissible Orders in a Dynamic Market
nodes.statement: We now extend Example \ref{exmp:adm-static} to the dynamic setting. Here each order includes the time at which it was submitted. There are three choices; the order is given by $((p,q),(\kappa, t))$, $((p,q,t),\kappa)$, or $(p,q,\kappa,t)$, where $p \in \mathbb{R}$ is the price, $q \in [0,\infty)$ is the quantity, $t\in [0,\infty)$ is the time of submission and $\kappa \in \{\mathrm{buy},~\mathrm{sell}\}$. In the case with no restrictions, one has that \begin{align*} \bigsqcup_{(\kappa, t) \in \{\mathrm{buy},~\mathrm{sell}\}\times [0,\infty) } \mathbb{R}\times [0,\infty) &\cong \bigsqcup_{\kappa \in \{\mathrm{buy},~\mathrm{sell}\}} \mathbb{R}\times [0,\infty)\times [0,\infty)\\ &\cong \mathbb{R}\times [0,\infty)\times [0,\infty)\times \{\mathrm{buy},~\mathrm{sell}\}. \end{align*}

nodes.title: Agent-Based Admissible Orders in a Dynamic Market
nodes.statement: We now extend Example \ref{exmp:agent-adm-static} to the dynamic case. Once again, let $A$ be the set of agents within the market, and let $P_{\kappa, a, t}$ and $Q_{\kappa, a, t}$ be the set of prices and quantities that are admissible for agent $a \in A$ at time $t \in [0,\infty)$ in direction $\kappa \in \{\mathrm{buy},~\mathrm{sell}\}$. The orders can be seen as an element in \begin{align*} \bigsqcup_{(\kappa, a, t) \in \{\mathrm{buy},~\mathrm{sell}\}\times A\times [0,\infty) } P_{\kappa, a, t}\times Q_{\kappa, a, t}. \end{align*} Again, it generally holds that \begin{align*} ((p,q),\kappa, a, t) \mapsto (p,q,\kappa,a,t), \end{align*} or similar maps are injective. In particular, one has that in general \begin{align} &\bigsqcup_{(\kappa, a, t) \in \{\mathrm{buy},~\mathrm{sell}\}\times A\times [0,\infty) } P_{\kappa, a, t}\times Q_{\kappa, a, t} \\ &\subset \bigsqcup_{(\kappa, a) \in \{\mathrm{buy},~\mathrm{sell}\}\times A} P_{\kappa, a}\times Q_{\kappa, a} \times [0,\infty)\\ &\subset \mathbb{R}\times[0,\infty) \times \{\mathrm{buy},~\mathrm{sell}\} \times A \times [0,\infty), \end{align} where \begin{align*} P_{\kappa, a} \equiv \bigcup_{t\in [0,\infty)}P_{\kappa, a, t} \quad \quad Q_{\kappa, a}\equiv \bigcup_{t\in [0,\infty)}Q_{\kappa, a, t}. \end{align*} In general, the set in \eqref{eq:agent-adm-dyn-1} restricts the trading possibilities of each agent in each direction at each time, whereas \eqref{eq:agent-adm-dyn-2} does not have time-varying bounds for each agent and direction in general. These examples are relevant if, say, an agent has already engaged in a short-selling position, and hence cannot engage in further short-selling due to their limitations on margin. Finally, \eqref{eq:agent-adm-dyn-3} is the unrestricted case in Example \ref{exmp:adm-dyn}.
proofBridge: exmp:agent-adm-dyn agent/time-restricted dynamic admissible orders.

nodes.title: Proposition: disjoint isomorphism
nodes.statement: Let $(X_\alpha)_{\alpha \in A}$ be a family of sets which satisfy that \begin{align*} X_\alpha \cap X_{\alpha^\prime} = \emptyset, \end{align*} for all $\alpha, \alpha^\prime \in A: \alpha \neq \alpha^\prime$. Then \begin{align*} \bigcup_{\alpha \in A} X_\alpha \cong \bigsqcup_{\alpha \in A} X_\alpha. \end{align*}

thesisProof.text: We must show that there exists an isomorphism between the sets $\bigcup_{\alpha \in A} X_\alpha$ and $\bigsqcup_{\alpha \in A} X_\alpha$. Let $\iota : \bigsqcup_{\alpha \in A} X_\alpha \to \bigcup_{\alpha \in A} X_\alpha$ be the mapping defined by \begin{align*} \iota(x,\alpha) = x. \end{align*} We now proceed to show that $\iota$ is bijective. To verify the claim, note that we must show that $\iota$ is injective and surjective. For injectivity, note that we must show \begin{align} \iota(x,\alpha) = \iota(x^\prime, \alpha^\prime) \implies (x, \alpha) = (x^\prime, \alpha^\prime), \end{align} but the argument is straightforward; if $x = \iota(x,\alpha) = \iota(x^\prime, \alpha^\prime) = x^\prime$, then clearly $x = x^\prime$. Moreover, since the sets are assumed disjoint, notice that $x = x^\prime$ must immediately imply that $\alpha = \alpha^\prime$. Hence, $\iota$ is injective. Now, $\iota$ is clearly surjective. Therefore, it is bijective and hence an isomorphism between the disjoint union and regular union, when the components are disjoint.

nodes.title: Proposition: disjoint product
nodes.statement: Let $(X_\alpha)_{\alpha \in A}$ be a family of sets, then \begin{align*} \bigsqcup_{\alpha \in A} X_\alpha \subseteq\bigcup_{\alpha \in A} X_\alpha \times A. \end{align*} In particular, \begin{align*} \bigsqcup_{\alpha \in A} X_\alpha = \bigcup_{\alpha \in A} X_\alpha \times A \iff \forall \alpha, \alpha^\prime \in A: X_\alpha = X_{\alpha^\prime} . \end{align*}

thesisProof.text: Notice that by definition \begin{align*} (x,\alpha) \in X_{\alpha} \times \{\alpha\} \implies (x,\alpha) \in \bigcup_{\alpha^\prime \in A} X_{\alpha^\prime} \times A, \end{align*} since $x \in X_\alpha \subseteq X$ and $\alpha \in A$. Therefore, the above shows that in general \begin{align*} \bigsqcup_{\alpha \in A} X_\alpha = \bigcup_{\alpha \in A} X_\alpha \times \{\alpha\} \subseteq \bigcup_{\alpha \in A} X_\alpha \times A. \end{align*} If $X_\alpha = X_{\alpha^\prime}$ for all $\alpha,\alpha^\prime \in A$, then \begin{align*} \bigcup_{\alpha \in A} X_\alpha \times A &= \bigcup_{\alpha \in A} \bigcup_{\alpha^\prime \in A} X_\alpha \times \{\alpha^\prime\}\\ &= \bigcup_{\alpha^\prime \in A} X_{\alpha^\prime} \times \{\alpha^\prime\} = \bigsqcup_{\alpha^\prime \in A} X_{\alpha^\prime}, \end{align*} proving the reverse inclusion and hence equality. Conversely, assume that \begin{align*} \bigsqcup_{\alpha \in A} X_\alpha = \bigcup_{\alpha \in A} X_\alpha \times A. \end{align*} Fix $\alpha,\alpha^\prime \in A$ and let $x \in X_\alpha$. Then $(x,\alpha^\prime)$ belongs to the right-hand side and therefore, by the assumed equality, also to the left-hand side. Hence $(x,\alpha^\prime) \in X_{\alpha^\prime} \times \{\alpha^\prime\}$, which implies $x \in X_{\alpha^\prime}$. Thus $X_\alpha \subseteq X_{\alpha^\prime}$. By symmetry, $X_{\alpha^\prime} \subseteq X_\alpha$, and therefore $X_\alpha = X_{\alpha^\prime}$.

nodes.title: Disjoint Union Partial Ordering
nodes.statement: Let $(X_\alpha, \preceq_\alpha)_{\alpha \in A}$ be a family of partially ordered sets. Let $X = \sqcup_{\alpha \in A} X_\alpha$ and define the relation $\preceq$ on $X$ by \begin{align*} (x,\alpha) \preceq (x^\prime, \alpha^\prime) \iff (\alpha = \alpha^\prime) \land x \preceq_\alpha x^\prime. \end{align*} Then, $(X,\preceq)$ is a partially ordered set.

thesisProof.text: We must show that for all $(x,\alpha),(x^\prime,\alpha^\prime),(x^\ast,\alpha^\ast)\in X$ we have \begin{enumerate} \item $(x,\alpha) \preceq (x, \alpha)$. \label{eq:disjoint-partial-order-1} \item $(x,\alpha) \preceq (x^\prime, \alpha^\prime)$ and $(x^\prime,\alpha^\prime) \preceq (x, \alpha)$ then $(x,\alpha) = (x^\prime, \alpha^\prime)$. \label{eq:disjoint-partial-order-2} \item $(x,\alpha) \preceq (x^\prime, \alpha^\prime)$ and $(x^\prime, \alpha^\prime) \preceq (x^\ast, \alpha^\ast)$ then $(x,\alpha)\preceq (x^\ast, \alpha^\ast)$. \label{eq:disjoint-partial-order-3} \end{enumerate} but these follow trivially; since \begin{enumerate}[-] \item For \eqref{eq:disjoint-partial-order-1} note that $(x,\alpha) \preceq (x, \alpha) \iff (\alpha = \alpha) \land x \preceq_\alpha x$, which is tautological as $\preceq_\alpha$ is a partial order. \item Likewise, for \eqref{eq:disjoint-partial-order-2}, note that $((x,\alpha) \preceq (x^\prime, \alpha^\prime)) \land ((x^\prime,\alpha^\prime) \preceq (x, \alpha))$ holds, if and only if, $(\alpha^\prime =\alpha) \land (x \preceq_\alpha x^\prime) \land (x^\prime \preceq_\alpha x)$. However, as $\preceq_\alpha$ is a partial order, this is equivalent to $(\alpha = \alpha^\prime) \land (x = x^\prime)$. \item Finally, for $\eqref{eq:disjoint-partial-order-3}$, note that $(x,\alpha) \preceq (x^\prime, \alpha^\prime)$ and $(x^\prime, \alpha^\prime)\preceq (x^\ast, \alpha^\ast)$ if, and only if, $\alpha = \alpha^\prime$ and $\alpha^\prime= \alpha^\ast$. But then $\alpha = \alpha^\prime = \alpha^\ast$. Hence, by the transitivity of $\preceq_\alpha$, it holds that $x \preceq_\alpha x^\prime$ and $x^\prime \preceq_\alpha x^\ast$ implies $x \preceq_\alpha x^\ast$. However, then clearly, $(\alpha = \alpha^\ast) \land (x \preceq_{\alpha} x^\ast)$ as desired. \end{enumerate}

nodes.title: Partial Order on a Static Market
nodes.statement: Let us consider the setting of Example \ref{exmp:adm-static}. Now, define \begin{align*} (p,q) \preceq_{\mathrm{buy}} (p^\prime, q^\prime) \iff (p > p^\prime) \lor ((p = p^\prime) \land (q \geq q^\prime)), \end{align*} which states that a buy order is $better'' if the price per unit is greater, or equal and volume is provided. Similarly, \begin{align*} (p,q) \preceq_{\mathrm{sell}} (p^\prime, q^\prime) \iff (p < p^\prime) \lor ((p = p^\prime) \land (q \geq q^\prime)), \end{align*} that is, a sell order is $better'' if the price per unit is smaller or price per unit is equal but more volume is provided. Note that the orders do not imply the order is smaller in a numeric sense to another order, but rather that it one order is prioritized over another. In particular, the order on the left-hand side has priority over the one the right-hand side in both cases. The resulting ordering on the disjoint union allows us to compare orders of the same type, but buy and sell orders are, once again, incomparable.

nodes.title: Lexicographic Order on a Disjoint Union
nodes.statement: Let $(A, \leq)$ be a totally ordered set and let $(X_\alpha, \preceq_\alpha)_{\alpha \in A}$ be a family of totally ordered sets. Let $X = \sqcup_{\alpha \in A} X_\alpha$ and define the relation $\preceq$ on $X$ by \begin{align*} (x,\alpha) \preceq (x^\prime, \alpha^\prime) \iff (\alpha < \alpha^\prime) \lor (\alpha = \alpha^\prime \land x \preceq_\alpha x^\prime). \end{align*} Then, $(X,\preceq)$ is a totally ordered set.

thesisProof.text: We must show for all $(x,\alpha),(x^\prime,\alpha^\prime), (x^\ast, \alpha^\ast)$ that \begin{enumerate} \item $(x,\alpha) \preceq (x,\alpha)$. \label{property:disjoint-total-order-1} \item $(x,\alpha) \preceq (x^\prime,\alpha^\prime)$ and $(x^\prime, \alpha^\prime) \preceq (x^\ast, \alpha^\ast)$ implies $(x,\alpha) \preceq (x^\ast, \alpha^\ast)$. \label{property:disjoint-total-order-2} \item $(x,\alpha) \preceq (x^\prime ,\alpha^\prime )$ and $(x^\prime ,\alpha^\prime ) \preceq (x,\alpha)$ implies $(x,\alpha) =(x^\prime,\alpha^\prime)$. \label{property:disjoint-total-order-3} \item $(x,\alpha) \preceq (x^\prime, \alpha^\prime)$ or $(x^\prime, \alpha^\prime) \preceq (x,\alpha)$. \label{property:disjoint-total-order-4} \end{enumerate} Note that \eqref{property:disjoint-total-order-1} is $(x,\alpha) \preceq (x,\alpha)$ if, and only if, $(\alpha < \alpha) \lor ((\alpha =\alpha) \land (x \preceq_\alpha x))$ which holds if, and only if, $x \preceq_\alpha x$. However, since each $\preceq_\alpha$ is a total order the property follows. For transitivity and antisymmetry, \eqref{property:disjoint-total-order-2} and \eqref{property:disjoint-total-order-3}, note that the properties follows, mutatis mutandis, from the arguments in Proposition \ref{prop:disjoint-partial-order}, which we omit for brevity. Finally, we must show that $(x,\alpha) \preceq (x^\prime, \alpha^\prime)$ or $(x^\prime, \alpha^\prime) \preceq (x,\alpha)$. To do so, notice that \begin{align*} &((x,\alpha) \preceq (x^\prime, \alpha^\prime) )\lor ((x^\prime, \alpha^\prime) \preceq (x,\alpha))\iff\\ &(\alpha < \alpha^\prime) \lor (\alpha^\prime < \alpha) \lor ((\alpha = \alpha^\prime) \land ((x \preceq_\alpha x^\prime) \lor (x^\prime \preceq_\alpha x)), \end{align*} but notice that there are three distinct cases $\alpha < \alpha^\prime$, $\alpha^\prime < \alpha$, or $(\alpha =\alpha^\prime)$ and $(x \preceq_\alpha x^\prime) \lor (x^\prime \preceq_\alpha x)$. However, as $\leq$ is total on $A$ we have either of the three cases, and since $\preceq_\alpha$ is total, the third statement is likewise true conditional on $\alpha =\alpha^\prime$.

nodes.title: Strict Lexicographic Order on a Disjoint Union
nodes.statement: Let $(A, <)$ be a strict totally ordered set and let $(X_\alpha, \prec_\alpha)_{\alpha \in A}$ be a family of strictly totally ordered sets. Let $X = \sqcup_{\alpha \in A} X_\alpha$ and define the order $\prec$ on $X$ by \begin{align*} (x_\alpha,\alpha) \prec (x_{\alpha^\prime}^\prime, \alpha^\prime) \iff (\alpha < \alpha^\prime) \lor (\alpha = \alpha^\prime \land x_\alpha \prec_\alpha x_{\alpha^\prime}^\prime). \end{align*} Then, $(X,\prec)$ is a strict totally ordered set.

nodes.title: Total Order for Static Market
nodes.statement: We continue from Examples \ref{exmp:adm-static} and \ref{exmp:partial-order-static-market} in which we considered the orders as elements of the set \begin{align*} O = \bigsqcup_{\kappa \in \{\mathrm{buy},~\mathrm{sell}\}} \mathbb{R}\times [0,\infty), \end{align*} where we endowed the buy and sell orders with the two orderings defined by \begin{align*} (p,q) \preceq_{\mathrm{buy}} (p^\prime, q^\prime) \iff (p > p^\prime) \lor ((p = p^\prime) \land (q \geq q^\prime)) \end{align*} and \begin{align*} (p,q) \preceq_{\mathrm{sell}} (p^\prime, q^\prime) \iff (p < p^\prime) \lor ((p = p^\prime) \land (q \geq q^\prime)). \end{align*} Now, endow the set $\{\mathrm{buy}, ~\mathrm{sell}\}$ with the arbitrary order $\leq$ defined by \begin{align*} \kappa \leq \kappa^\prime \iff \kappa = \kappa^\prime \lor (\kappa = \mathrm{buy} \land \kappa^\prime = \mathrm{sell}). \end{align*} Since, $\leq, \preceq_{\mathrm{buy}}$, and $\preceq_{\mathrm{sell}}$ are all total orders, we have that the lexicographic order defined by \begin{align*} (o, \kappa) \preceq (o^\prime, \kappa^\prime) \iff \kappa < \kappa^\prime \lor (\kappa = \kappa^\prime \land o \preceq_\kappa o^\prime), \end{align*} is total, where $(o,\kappa) =((p,q),\kappa)\in O$ and $(o^\prime, \kappa^\prime)=((p,q),\kappa^\prime) \in O$.

nodes.title: Total Order for Dynamic Market
nodes.statement: We continue from Examples \ref{exmp:adm-dyn} in which we considered the orders as elements of the set \begin{align*} O = \bigsqcup_{\kappa \in \{\mathrm{buy},~\mathrm{sell}\}} \mathbb{R}\times [0,\infty) \times [0,\infty), \end{align*} where the component of each $o = ((p,q,t), \kappa) \in O$ represents the price, $p \in \mathbb{R}$, quantity, $q \in [0,\infty)$, time of submission, $t \in [0,\infty)$, and direction $\kappa \in \{\mathrm{buy},\mathrm{sell}\}$. Now, define the orders \begin{align*} &(p,q,t) \preceq_{\mathrm{buy}} (p^\prime, q^\prime, t^\prime) \iff\\ &(p > p^\prime) \lor ((p = p^\prime) \land (t < t^\prime)) \lor ((p = p^\prime) \land (t = t^\prime) \land (q \geq q^\prime)), \end{align*} which states that the buy order $(p,q,t)$ is $better'' than another buy order $(p^\prime, q^\prime, t^\prime)$ if either the price is greater, or prices are equal and the time of submission for the first order is smaller than that of the latter order, or if they are moreover submitted at the same time, then whoever wishes to purchase the most is preferred. Similarly, we define \begin{align*} &(p,q, t) \preceq_{\mathrm{sell}} (p^\prime, q^\prime,t^\prime) \iff \\ &(p < p^\prime) \lor ((p = p^\prime) \land (t < t^\prime)) \lor ((p = p^\prime) \land (t = t^\prime) \land (q \geq q^\prime)), \end{align*} where sell orders are ranked increasingly according to price. That is, the $best'' sell order is the one with the smallest price, but otherwise it is constructed analogously to the buy ordering. Now, endow the set $\{\mathrm{buy}, ~\mathrm{sell}\}$ with the arbitrary order $\leq$ defined by \begin{align*} \kappa \leq \kappa^\prime \iff \kappa = \kappa^\prime \lor (\kappa = \mathrm{buy} \land \kappa^\prime = \mathrm{sell}). \end{align*} Since, $\leq, \preceq_{\mathrm{buy}}$, and $\preceq_{\mathrm{sell}}$ are all total orders, we have that the product ordering defined by \begin{align*} (o, \kappa) \preceq (o^\prime, \kappa^\prime) \iff \kappa < \kappa^\prime \lor (\kappa = \kappa^\prime \land o \preceq_\kappa o^\prime), \end{align*} is total, where $(o,\kappa),(o^\prime, \kappa^\prime) \in O$.

nodes.title: Completing Order for Agent Based Admissible Orders in a Static Market
nodes.statement: We continue from Examples \ref{exmp:agent-adm-static} in which we considered the orders as elements of the set \begin{align*} O = \bigsqcup_{(\kappa, a) \in \{\mathrm{buy},~\mathrm{sell}\}\times A} P_{\kappa, a} \times Q_{\kappa, a}, \end{align*} where $A$ is the set of agents in the market, and $P_{\kappa,a}\subseteq\mathbb{R}$ is the set of permissible prices in direction $\kappa\in\{\mathrm{buy},~\mathrm{sell}\}$ for agent $a\in A$, and similarly $Q_{\kappa,a}\subseteq [0,\infty)$ is the set of permissible quantities in direction $\kappa\in\{\mathrm{buy},~\mathrm{sell}\}$ for agent $a\in A$. Notice that attempting to follow the analogous construction as in Example \ref{exmp:total-order-static-market} is not satisfactory; endowing $\{\mathrm{buy},~\mathrm{sell}\}\times A$ with a total order has the adverse consequence of favoring certain agents in the market. To rectify this, one may consider the equivalence relation $\sim$ on $O$ defined by \begin{align*} ((p,q),\kappa, a) \sim ((p^\prime,q^\prime), \kappa^\prime, a^\prime) \iff ((p,q),\kappa) = ((p^\prime,q^\prime), \kappa^\prime), \end{align*} which states that two orders are equivalent if their price, quantity, and direction coincide, regardless of the agent that submitted the order. In particular, it is natural for the market to consider the quotient space \begin{align*} O_{\sim} = \{[((p,q),\kappa,a)]_{\sim} \mid ((p,q), \kappa, a) \in O\}, \end{align*} where \begin{align*} [((p,q),\kappa,a)]_{\sim} = \{((p^\ast, q^\ast), \kappa^\ast, a^\ast) \in O \mid ((p^\ast, q^\ast), \kappa^\ast, a^\ast)\sim ((p,q),\kappa,a)\}. \end{align*} However, the map \begin{align*} [((p,q),\kappa,a)]_{\sim} \mapsto ((p,q),\kappa) \end{align*} is bijective. Therefore, one can conclude that \begin{align*} O_{\sim} \cong \bigsqcup_{\kappa \in \{\mathrm{buy},~\mathrm{sell}\}} \left(\bigcup_{a \in A} P_{\kappa, a} \times Q_{\kappa, a}\right) \subseteq \bigsqcup_{\kappa \in \{\mathrm{buy},~\mathrm{sell}\}} \mathbb{R}\times [0,\infty). \end{align*} Moreover, one can hence utilize the equivalent ordering from Example \ref{exmp:total-order-static-market}, resulting in a total ordering. Notice also that from an economic point of view, one can interpret the equivalence class as the perspective of the market on orders. That is, the market is \textit{indifferent} to which agent submitted the order. It is worth remarking that there may be situations where a total order on $O$ \textit{makes} sense, i.e., some actors in the market are favored, in which case one constructs an order analogously to Example \ref{exmp:partial-order-static-market}.

nodes.title: Disjoint Union Metric
nodes.statement: Let $(X_\alpha, d_\alpha)_{\alpha \in A}$ be a family of metric spaces and $X = \sqcup_{\alpha \in A} X_\alpha$. Define the mapping $d:X\times X\to [0,\infty]$ by \begin{align} d((x,\alpha), (x^\prime, \alpha^\prime)) = \begin{cases} d_\alpha(x,x^\prime) & \alpha = \alpha^\prime\\ \infty & \alpha \neq \alpha^\prime. \end{cases} \end{align} We call $d$ the disjoint union metric induced by $(d_\alpha)_{\alpha\in A}$, or simply the disjoint union metric if the metrics $(d_\alpha)_{\alpha\in A}$ are clear from context. Moreover, we refer to $(X,d)$ as the disjoint union metric space.

nodes.title: Proposition: disjoint union metrization
nodes.statement: Let $(X_\alpha, d_\alpha)_{\alpha \in A}$ be a family of metric spaces. Then, the disjoint union metric space $(X,d)$ is a metric space.

thesisProof.text: We must show that the mapping $d:X\times X \to [0,\infty]$ satisfies the three criteria for all $(x,\alpha),(x^\prime, \alpha^\prime),(x^\ast, \alpha^\ast) \in X = \bigsqcup_{\alpha \in A} X_\alpha$: \begin{enumerate}[(i)] \item $d((x,\alpha), (x^\prime, \alpha^\prime)) = 0$ if, and only if, $(x,\alpha) = (x^\prime, \alpha^\prime)$.\label{eq:disjoint-union-metrization-1} \item $d((x,\alpha), (x^\prime, \alpha^\prime)) = d((x^\prime, \alpha^\prime), (x,\alpha))$. \label{eq:disjoint-union-metrization-2} \item $d((x,\alpha), (x^\prime, \alpha^\prime)) \leq d((x,\alpha), (x^\ast, \alpha^\ast)) + d((x^\ast, \alpha^\ast), (x^\prime, \alpha^\prime))$. \label{eq:disjoint-union-metrization-3} \end{enumerate} The criteria \eqref{eq:disjoint-union-metrization-1} and \eqref{eq:disjoint-union-metrization-2} are trivial. For \eqref{eq:disjoint-union-metrization-3}, notice that the claim is trivially true if $\alpha \neq \alpha^\prime$, since the right-hand side of the inequality will be infinite; $\alpha^\ast$ cannot both be equal to $\alpha$ and $\alpha^\prime$. Hence, we can assume without loss of generality that $\alpha = \alpha^\prime$. Again, if $\alpha^\ast \neq \alpha = \alpha^\prime$ the claim is trivial, so we only need to consider $\alpha^\ast = \alpha = \alpha^\prime$, but then it reduces to the standard triangle inequality for $d_\alpha$, which, by assumption, is a metric.

nodes.title: Proposition: disjoint union metric properties
nodes.statement: Let $(X_\alpha, d_\alpha)_{\alpha \in A}$ be a family of metric spaces over an index set $A$. Let $(X,d)$ be the corresponding disjoint union metric space. Then, \begin{enumerate}[(i)] \item If $A$ is countable and $(X_\alpha, d_\alpha)_{\alpha \in A}$ are all separable metric spaces, then $(X,d)$ is separable, \item If $(X_\alpha, d_\alpha)_{\alpha \in A}$ are all complete metric spaces, then $(X,d)$ is complete. \end{enumerate}

thesisProof.text: First, we show \eqref{property:disjoint-metric-1}. We must show that there is a countable and dense subset $U \subseteq X$. Now, by assumption each $(X_\alpha, d_\alpha)$ is separable. Then, by definition, there exists a countable and dense subset, say $U_\alpha$, for which \begin{align*} \forall x_\alpha \in X_\alpha \forall \varepsilon> 0\exists u_\alpha \in U_\alpha : d_\alpha(x_\alpha, u_\alpha) < \varepsilon. \end{align*} As an ansatz, we claim that \begin{align*} U = \bigsqcup_{\alpha \in A} U_\alpha, \end{align*} is both countable and dense in $(X,d)$. First, note that \begin{align*} U = \bigcup_{\alpha \in A} (U_\alpha \times \{\alpha\}) \end{align*} However, for each $\alpha \in A$, the set $U_\alpha \times \{\alpha\}$ is countable, as it naturally bijects with $U_\alpha$ which is assumed countable. Moreover, $\bigcup_{\alpha \in A} U_\alpha \times \{\alpha\}$ is a countable union of countable sets and therefore countable. Therefore, $U$ is indeed countable. To show that $U$ is dense in $X$, we must show that for every $\varepsilon > 0 $ and $x \in X$ there exists a $u\in U$ such that $d(x,u) < \varepsilon$. To this end, let $\varepsilon > 0$ and $x\in X$ be given. Notice that $x = (x_\alpha, \alpha)$ for some $\alpha \in A$ and $x_{\alpha} \in X_\alpha$. Now, since $U_\alpha$ is dense in $X_\alpha$, there exists an element $u_\alpha \in U_\alpha$ such that $d_\alpha(x_\alpha, u_\alpha) < \varepsilon$. However, define $u = (u_\alpha, \alpha)$ and notice that $u \in U$ and $d(x,u) = d_\alpha(x_\alpha,u_\alpha) < \varepsilon$ as desired. Next, we must show that any Cauchy sequence in $(X,d)$ converges in $X$. To this end, recall that a sequence $(x_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}} \subseteq X$ is said to be Cauchy if \begin{align*} \forall \varepsilon > 0 \exists N \in \mathbb{N}: m,n\geq N \implies d(x_n, x_m) < \varepsilon. \end{align*} However, notice that $x = (x_\alpha, \alpha)$ for each $x \in X$ and so the Cauchy sequence, $(x_n)_{n\in \mathbb{N}}$ admits the representation \begin{align*} x_n = (x_{\alpha_n, n}, \alpha_n). \end{align*} Moreover, since the sequence is Cauchy, observe that for any finite $\varepsilon > 0$ there is an $N \in \mathbb{N}$ such that for $n,m \geq N$ one has $d(x_n, x_m) < \varepsilon$. However, $d(x_n, x_m) < \varepsilon <\infty$ implies $\alpha_n = \alpha_m$ and so set $\alpha = \alpha_N$ for $n,m \geq N$. Now, notice that $d(x_n, x_m) = d_\alpha (x_{\alpha, n}, x_{\alpha,m})$ implying that the sequence $(x_{\alpha, n})_{n = N}^\infty$ is Cauchy in $X_\alpha$. By assumption, $(X_\alpha, d_\alpha)$ was complete, and so the sequence $(x_{\alpha, n})_{n = N}^\infty$ has a limit, say, $x_\alpha \in X_\alpha$. However, then $x = (x_\alpha, \alpha) \in X$ and clearly $(x_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ converges to $x$.

nodes.title: Pasting Lemma for Disjoint Unions

references.formatted: Lee, J. Introduction to topological manifolds. Springer Science & Business Media, 2010.

nodes.statement: Let $(X_\alpha, d_\alpha)_{\alpha \in A}$ be a family of metric spaces and $(Y,d^\ast)$ be a metric space. Moreover, let $(X,d)$ be the disjoint union metric space and let $f:X \to Y$ be a function. Then, $f$ is continuous if, and only if, the maps \begin{align*} f\restriction_{X_\alpha}&: X_\alpha \to Y\\ x &\mapsto f(x,\alpha) \end{align*} are continuous for each $\alpha \in A$.

thesisProof.text: First, notice that if $f$ is continuous, then for every $(x_0,\alpha_0) \in X$ and $\varepsilon > 0$ there exists a $\delta > 0$ such that \begin{align} d((x,\alpha),(x_0, \alpha_0)) < \delta \implies d^\ast(f(x, \alpha), f(x_0, \alpha_0)) < \varepsilon. \end{align} Now, without loss of generality let $\delta < \infty$ and notice that \begin{align*} d((x,\alpha),(x_0, \alpha_0)) < \delta \iff \alpha = \alpha_0, \end{align*} which implies that \begin{align}\label{eq:finite-delta-collapses-disjoint-metric} d((x,\alpha),(x_0, \alpha_0)) < \delta \iff d_\alpha(x,x_0) < \delta. \end{align} Now, to show that $f\restriction_{X_\alpha}$ is continuous, we must show for every $\varepsilon >0$ and $x_0 \in X_\alpha$ there exists an $\delta > 0$ such that \begin{align*} d_\alpha(x,x_0) < \delta \implies d^\ast(f\restriction_{X_\alpha}(x), f\restriction_{X_\alpha}(x_0)) = d^\ast(f(x,\alpha),f(x_0,\alpha)) < \varepsilon. \end{align*} However, the claim follows by invoking \eqref{eq:finite-delta-collapses-disjoint-metric} and the continuity of $f$. The other case is analogous.

nodes.statement: Let $(E, \Sigma)$ be a measurable space and $(X_\alpha, d_\alpha)_{\alpha \in A}$ be a countable family of metric spaces for which $(\mathcal{B}(X_\alpha))_{\alpha \in A}$ denotes the corresponding Borel $\sigma$-algebras induced by $(d_\alpha)_{\alpha \in A}$. Moreover, let $(X,d)$ be the disjoint union metric space and let $\mathcal{B}(X)$ denote the Borel $\sigma$-algebra on $X$ induced by $d$. Then, $f: X \to E$ is measurable if, and only if, \begin{align*} f\restriction_{X_\alpha} &: X_\alpha \to E\\ x &\mapsto f(x,\alpha) \end{align*} is measurable for each $\alpha \in A$.

thesisProof.text: For each $\alpha \in A$, define the canonical injection \begin{align*} \iota_\alpha : X_\alpha \to X,\qquad x \mapsto (x,\alpha). \end{align*} By construction, $\iota_\alpha$ is an isometry from $(X_\alpha,d_\alpha)$ onto the subset $X_\alpha \times \{\alpha\} \subseteq X$. Moreover, each set $X_\alpha \times \{\alpha\}$ is both open and closed in $X$: it is open because every point $(x,\alpha)$ has a ball of radius, say, $1/2$ contained in $X_\alpha \times \{\alpha\}$, and it is closed because its complement is the union of the other open components. If $f$ is measurable, then for every $B \in \Sigma$ and every $\alpha \in A$, \begin{align*} (f\restriction_{X_\alpha})^{-1}(B) = \iota_\alpha^{-1}(f^{-1}(B)) \in \mathcal{B}(X_\alpha), \end{align*} since $\iota_\alpha$ is continuous. Conversely, assume that each $f\restriction_{X_\alpha}$ is measurable. Let $B \in \Sigma$. Then \begin{align*} f^{-1}(B) &= \left\{(x,\alpha) \in \bigsqcup_{\alpha\in A}X_\alpha ~\middle|~ f(x,\alpha) \in B \right\}\\ &= \bigcup_{\alpha \in A} \iota_\alpha\big((f\restriction_{X_\alpha})^{-1}(B)\big). \end{align*} Each set $(f\restriction_{X_\alpha})^{-1}(B)$ belongs to $\mathcal{B}(X_\alpha)$ by assumption, and $\iota_\alpha$ is a homeomorphism onto the Borel set $X_\alpha \times \{\alpha\}$. Hence each image \begin{align*} \iota_\alpha\big((f\restriction_{X_\alpha})^{-1}(B)\big) \end{align*} is Borel in $X$. Since the family is countable, the union is Borel as well. Therefore, $f^{-1}(B) \in \mathcal{B}(X)$ for every $B \in \Sigma$, proving that $f$ is measurable.

nodes.title: Hausdorff distance on Finite Sets
nodes.statement: Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space. Then $(\mathscr{F}(X), d_H)$ is a metric space.

thesisProof.text: Since $\mathscr{F}(X) \subseteq \wp(X)$ it follows by Proposition \ref{prop:hausdorff-distance} that $(\mathscr{F}(X), d_H)$ is a pseudometric space. By Corollary \ref{cor:pseudometric-metric-relation} it suffices to show that for all $\xi, \eta \in \mathscr{F}(X)$ it holds that \begin{align*} d_H(\xi, \eta) = 0 \implies \xi = \eta. \end{align*} First, note that the claim is trivial if either $\xi$ or $\eta$ is the empty set, following Remark \ref{rem:hausdorff-convention}. Therefore, suppose that $\xi$ and $\eta$ are non-empty. Now, notice that since the sets are finite, the infimum coincides with the minimum and similarly the supremum coincides with the maximum, but clearly \begin{align*} \max_{x \in \xi} \min_{x^\prime \in \eta} d(x,x^\prime) = 0 \iff \xi \subseteq \eta. \end{align*} However, notice that $d_H(\xi, \eta) =0$ if, and only if, $\max_{x \in \xi} \min_{x^\prime \in \eta} d(x,x^\prime) = 0$ and $\max_{x^\prime \in \eta} \min_{x\in \xi} d(x,x^\prime) = 0$, which holds if, and only if, $\xi \subseteq \eta$ and $\eta \subseteq \xi$ respectively, and so it follows that $\xi = \eta$.

nodes.title: Finite Sets inherit Separability
nodes.statement: Let $(X,d)$ be a separable metric space. Then, $(\mathscr{F}(X), d_H)$ is separable.

thesisProof.text: We must show that there exists a countable and dense subset of $\mathscr{F}(X)$. We construct one explicitly. First, note that since $X$ is separable, there is a countable and dense set $U \subseteq X$. Now, we claim that $\mathscr{F}(U)$ is countable and dense in $\mathscr{F}(X)$. The countability follows immediately from Proposition \ref{prop:countable-finite-sets}. Therefore, it suffices to show that $\mathscr{F}(U)$ is dense in $\mathscr{F}(X)$. Now, let $\xi \in \mathscr{F}(X)$ and assume without loss of generality that $\xi \neq \emptyset$; if $\xi = \emptyset$ then $\xi \in \mathscr{F}(U)$. Now, we must show that for any $\varepsilon >0$ there exists a $\upsilon \in \mathscr{F}(U)$ such that \begin{align*} d_H(\upsilon, \xi) < \varepsilon. \end{align*} However, as the underlying space $X$ is separable it holds that \begin{align}\label{eq:separable-finite-bound} \forall x \in X\exists u_x \in U: d(x,u_x) < \varepsilon. \end{align} In particular, $x \in \xi\subseteq X$, we can find an element $u_x \in U$ such that \ref{eq:separable-finite-bound} holds. Let $\upsilon$ denote the union of each of these elements. Then by construction, we have that \begin{align*} \forall x \in \xi \exists u \in \upsilon: d(x,u) < \varepsilon, \end{align*} and analogously \begin{align*} \forall u \in \upsilon \exists x \in \xi: d(x,u) < \varepsilon. \end{align*} But, then clearly both $\max_{x\in\xi}\min_{u \in \upsilon} d(x,u) < \varepsilon$ and $\max_{u\in\upsilon}\min_{x \in \xi} d(x,u) < \varepsilon$, and hence \begin{align*} d_H(\xi,\upsilon) = \max\left(\max_{x\in\xi}\min_{u \in \upsilon} d(x,u), \max_{u\in\upsilon}\min_{x \in \xi} d(x,u)\right) < \varepsilon \end{align*} as desired.

nodes.title: Proposition: finite set cauchy
nodes.statement: Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space. Then, if $(x_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}} \subseteq X$ is a Cauchy sequence, the sequence $(\xi_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}} \subseteq \mathscr{F}(X)$ defined by \begin{align*} \xi_{n} = \bigcup_{i = 1}^n \{x_i\} \end{align*} is a Cauchy sequence in $(\mathscr{F}(X), d_H)$.

thesisProof.text: We must show that for any $\varepsilon > 0$ there exists an $N \in \mathbb{N}$ such that \begin{align*} n,m\geq N \implies d_H(\xi_n, \xi_m) < \varepsilon. \end{align*} Now, without loss of generality, assume that $n \leq m$. Then, one easily verifies that \begin{align*} d_H(\xi_n, \xi_m) = \max_{x \in \xi_{m}} \min_{x^\prime \in \xi_n} d(x,x^\prime) \end{align*} since $\xi_n \subseteq \xi_m$. In particular, we know that the maximum must be found over $(x_k)_{k=n+1}^m$. In particular, it holds that \begin{align*} d_H(\xi_n, \xi_m) =\max_{k\in\{n+1,\dots,m\}} \min_{i\leq n} d(x_k,x_i) \leq \max_{k \in \{n+1,\dots,m\}} d(x_k, x_n). \end{align*} Now, we leverage that $(x_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ is a Cauchy sequence. For any given $\varepsilon>0$ there exists an $N \in \mathbb{N}$ such that whenever $n,m\geq N$ it holds that $d(x_n, x_m) < \varepsilon$. In particular, it holds for $n \geq N$ that $\sup_{m > n} d(x_m, x_n) < \varepsilon$ but \begin{align*} d_H(\xi_n, \xi_m) \leq \max_{k \in \{n+1,\dots,m\}} d(x_k, x_n) \leq \sup_{m > n} d(x_m, x_n) < \varepsilon, \end{align*} as desired.

nodes.title: Proposition: isolative finite sets complete
nodes.statement: Let $(X,d)$ be an isolative metric space. Then, any Cauchy sequence $(x_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}} \subseteq X$ is eventually constant. In particular, $(X,d)$ is complete.

thesisProof.text: First, let $(x_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ be a Cauchy sequence. Now, suppose that $B>0$ is the isolation bound, such that $d(x,x^\prime) < B \iff x = x^\prime$. In particular note, that if one takes $\varepsilon < B$, then by the Cauchy property, there exists an $N \in \mathbb{N}$ such that \begin{align*} \forall n ,m \geq N: d(x_n,x_m) < \varepsilon < B, \end{align*} but since $d(x_n,x_m) < B$ implies that $x_n = x_m$, it follows that $x_n \equiv x_N$ for all $n \geq N$, which constitutes the limit. Hence, any Cauchy sequence is eventually constant, and so $(X,d)$ is complete.

nodes.title: Lemma: helpful distinct
nodes.statement: Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space and let $(\mathscr{D}(X), d^\ast_H)$ be the set of distinct finite sets with metric $d^\ast_H$ defined in Theorem \ref{thm:distinct-properties}. Then, for every $\xi,\eta \in \mathscr{D}(X)$ \begin{align*} d^\ast_H(\xi, \eta) < 1 \implies |\xi| = |\eta| \end{align*} Moreover, if $\xi, \eta \neq \emptyset$, then \begin{align*} d^\ast_H(\xi, \eta) < 1 \implies \forall (n,x) \in \xi \exists x^\prime \in X: (d(x,x^\prime) < 1) \land (n, x^\prime) \in \eta. \end{align*}

thesisProof.text: For the first property, note that if either $\xi$ or $\eta$ is the empty set, then $d^\ast_H(\xi, \eta) < 1$ immediately implies $\xi = \eta = \emptyset$ as it is otherwise infinitely far from other elements by definition. Therefore, it suffices to show the properties for $\xi \neq \emptyset$ and $\eta \neq \emptyset$. Now, it follows that \begin{align}\label{eq:bound-distinct-1} d^\ast_H(\xi, \eta) < 1 \implies \max_{(n,x)\in \xi}\min_{(n^\prime,x^\prime)\in \eta} d^\ast((n,x), (n^\prime, x^\prime)) =\max_{(n,x)\in \xi}\min_{(n^\prime,x^\prime)\in \eta} d(x,x^\prime) + |n-n^\prime| < 1 \end{align} if, and only if, \begin{align}\label{eq:dinstinct-conseq-1} \forall (n,x)\in \xi \exists(n^\prime, x^\prime) \in \eta : (d(x,x^\prime) < 1) \land(n = n^\prime), \end{align} since $|n - n^\prime| < 1$ if, and only if, $n = n^\prime$. Similarly, \begin{align}\label{eq:bound-distinct-2} \max_{(n^\prime,x^\prime)\in \eta}\min_{(n,x)\in \xi} d^\ast((n,x), (n^\prime, x^\prime)) =\max_{(n^\prime,x^\prime)\in \eta}\min_{(n,x)\in \xi} d(x,x^\prime) + |n-n^\prime| < 1 \end{align} if, and only if, \begin{align}\label{eq:dinstinct-conseq-2} \forall (n^\prime, x^\prime)\in \eta \exists(n,x) \in \xi : (d(x,x^\prime) < 1) \land(n = n^\prime). \end{align} However, note that by definition, when $d^\ast_H(\xi,\eta)<1$ then both \eqref{eq:bound-distinct-1} and \eqref{eq:bound-distinct-2} hold, and so there is a one-to-one correspondence between $\xi$ and $\eta$, which implies $|\xi| = |\eta|$. Moreover, \eqref{eq:dinstinct-conseq-1} and \eqref{eq:dinstinct-conseq-2} immediately imply the second property.

nodes.title: Theorem: distinct properties
nodes.statement: Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space and endow $\mathbb{N}$ with the Euclidean distance. Let, $(\mathbb{N} \times X, d^\ast)$, where $d^\ast:(\mathbb{N}\times X) \times (\mathbb{N}\times X) \to [0, \infty]$ is defined by \begin{align*} d^\ast((n,x),(n^\prime, x^\prime)) = d(x,x^\prime) + |n-n^\prime|. \end{align*} Let $\mathscr{D}(X) \subseteq \mathscr{F}(\mathbb{N}\times X)$ be endowed with the Hausdorff distance $d^\ast_H : \mathscr{D}(X) \times \mathscr{D}(X) \to [0,\infty]$. It holds that \begin{enumerate}[(i)] \item if $(X,d)$ is separable, then so is $(\mathscr{D}(X), d^\ast_H)$. \item if $(X,d)$ is complete, then so is $(\mathscr{D}(X), d^\ast_H)$. \end{enumerate}

motivationContexts.text: In the previous sections, we showed how disjoint unions can encode market information into its elements and how one can metricize the set of finite sets to produce complete and separable spaces, provided the underlying set is complete and separable. In this section, we combine the results and propose a structure to represent markets. It is worth remarking that the market could be represented by a distinct finite set or a finite set, but these sets are, generally, cumbersome to work within, as most operations carried out during trading or on exchanges can be described algorithmically. Therefore, it is convenient to enumerate each order within the market.

Note, that the construction of the market is independent from the orders at the present stage. Therefore, the forthcoming theory is presented for arbitrary non-empty sets, but one should, in general, think of the sets as being disjoint unions containing the relevant information.

The intuition behind introducing tuples is that we can collect all the orders within a market into a tuple, which defines the market uniquely up to permutations of the domain. Now, it is often convenient to specify the length of the tuple.

Let mT(X) be a tuple representing the market; each entry of the tuple, m(i) where i \1, ,(m)\, corresponds to an order in the set X, which can be thought of as a representative for the admissible orders, as seen in the former section.

nodes.title: Sorted Tuples
nodes.statement: Let $(X,\preceq)$ be a partially ordered set. A tuple $\bm{x} \in \mathscr{T}(X)$ is sorted with respect to $\preceq$ if \begin{align*} \forall i,j \in \mathrm{domain}(\bm{x}): i \leq j \implies \neg(\bm{x}(j) \prec \bm{x}(i)). \end{align*} Moreover, the set of tuples that are sorted with respect to $\preceq$ is denoted by $\mathscr{S}(X, \preceq)$.

motivationContexts.text: Let mT(X) be a tuple representing the market; each entry of the tuple, m(i) where i \1, ,(m)\, corresponds to an order in the set X, which can be thought of as a representative for the admissible orders, as seen in the former section.

In this sense, tuples may seem like an over-parametrization of the problem; if markets stay the same regardless of permutations of the domain, then, really, the market ought to be represented by a tuple modulo the permutation of orders, which is related to the set of distinct finite sets from the former section. However, the indexing is convenient for many theoretical results, as we will later show. Moreover, the indexing is natural when the market is sorted, as is often the case in standardized markets.

However, since the set is only partially ordered, there may be elements which are incomparable. For instance, in a standardized market where each order is represented by its price, quantity, and direction, one encounters the issue of whether to rank buy orders above sell orders or vice versa. Of course, one can choose an arbitrary order on the set to remedy the problem.

The problem is more grave than it seems; consider a standardized market where each order is represented by its price, quantity, direction, and whichever agent submitted it. One could, in principle, encounter situations where two different agents submitted the same price and quantity in the same direction. However, the two cannot be ordered, as it would be unfair to rank one agent over another. Still, as long as all orders before and after can be ranked accordingly, it is arbitrary who comes first.

nodes.title: Proposition: totally ordered tuple sorted iff monotone
nodes.statement: Let $(X,\preceq)$ be a totally ordered set. Then any tuple $\bm{x} \in \mathscr{T}(X)$ is sorted with respect to $\preceq$ if, and only if, \begin{align*} \forall i,j \in \mathrm{domain}(\bm{x}): i \leq j \implies \bm{x}(i) \preceq \bm{x}(j). \end{align*}

thesisProof.text:
Suppose first that $ m{x}$ is sorted. Then, by definition,  egin{align*} i \leq j \implies 
eg( m{x}(j) \prec  m{x}(i)). \end{align*} Since the order is total, for any $a,b \in X$ we have  egin{align*} 
eg(b \prec a) \iff a \preceq b. \end{align*} Therefore,  egin{align*} i \leq j \implies  m{x}(i) \preceq  m{x}(j). \end{align*} Conversely, if  egin{align*} i \leq j \implies  m{x}(i) \preceq  m{x}(j), \end{align*} then certainly  egin{align*} i \leq j \implies 
eg( m{x}(j) \prec  m{x}(i)), \end{align*} so $ m{x}$ is sorted.

nodes.title: Theorem: permutation exists
nodes.statement: Let $(X,\preceq)$ be a partially ordered set. Then, for any tuple in $\mathscr{T}(X)$ there exists a sorting permutation.

thesisProof.text: First, since $(X,\preceq)$ is partially ordered set, note that $(\mathrm{image}(\bm{x}), \preceq)$ is partially ordered. Now, by Theorem \ref{thm:szpilrajn}, the order extends to a total order, $\preceq^\ast$, on $\mathrm{image}(\bm{x})$. Now, since the order is total, define recursively \begin{align*} \pi_1 &= \min\{ j \in \mathrm{domain}(\bm{x}) \mid \bm{x}(j) = \min_{\preceq^\ast} \mathrm{image}(\bm{x})\} \\ I_1 &= \mathrm{domain}(\bm{x}) \backslash\{\pi_1\} \end{align*} and for $k > 1$ \begin{align*} \pi_k &= \min \{j \in I_{k-1} \mid \bm{x}(j) = \min_{\preceq^\ast} \{\bm{x}(m) \mid m \in I_{k-1}\}\}\\ I_k&=\mathrm{domain}(\bm{x})\backslash \{\pi_1, \dots, \pi_k\} \end{align*} where the minimum is taken with respect to the ordering $\preceq^\ast$. Consequently, we define $\bm{\pi}:\mathrm{domain}(\bm{x}) \to \mathrm{domain}(\bm{x})$ by \begin{align*} \bm{\pi}(i) = \pi_i, \end{align*} However, by construction, $\bm{x} \circ \bm{\pi} \in \mathscr{S}(X,\preceq)$, as the total order agrees with the partial order on all comparable elements. Therefore, $\bm{\pi} \in \mathscr{P}_{\bm{x}}$.

Any function $\varsigma:\mathscr{T}(X)\to \mathscr{S}(X,\preceq)$ which satisfies that for any $\bm{x} \in \mathscr{T}(X)$, there exists a bijective map $\bm{\pi}:\mathrm{domain}(\bm{x}) \to \mathrm{domain}(\bm{x})$ such that \begin{align} \varsigma(\bm{x}) = \bm{x} \circ \bm{\pi} \end{align} is called a sorting rule.
proofBridge: defn:sorting-map sorting rule.

motivationContexts.text: A somewhat natural question is whether or not a sorting permutation exists in the first place. Fortunately, the result is positive.
Now, we will require at least one function that sorts any potential market in the order of execution; one can think of such a function as the execution rule for the market or exchange.
Of course, Theorem thm:permutation-exists immediately guarantees that at least one such rule exists.

It is worth noticing that the problem is, as shown, not whether an execution rule exists for a market with a partial order, but rather that there may be several similar rules, from which one has to choose. However, if the market already specifies how all orders are compared explicitly, one does not need to choose the rule in any way, as seen from the following Corollary.

nodes.title: Corollary: unique sorting map total order
nodes.statement: Let $(X,\preceq)$ be a totally ordered set. Then, there exists a unique function $\varsigma:\mathscr{T}(X) \to \mathscr{S}(X,\preceq)$.

thesisProof.text: Existence follows from Corollary \ref{thm:sorting-exists}. To prove uniqueness, let $\varsigma,\varsigma^\prime:\mathscr{T}(X)\to \mathscr{S}(X,\preceq)$ be sorting maps and fix $\bm{x}\in\mathscr{T}(X)$. Set \begin{align*} \bm{y} = \varsigma(\bm{x}) \qquad \text{and} \qquad \bm{y}^\prime = \varsigma^\prime(\bm{x}). \end{align*} Both $\bm{y}$ and $\bm{y}^\prime$ are sorted tuples obtained from $\bm{x}$ by permutations, so they have the same length and the same entries, counted with multiplicity. Suppose for contradiction that $\bm{y} \neq \bm{y}^\prime$. Then there exists a smallest index $k \in \mathrm{domain}(\bm{x})$ such that \begin{align*} \bm{y}(k) \neq \bm{y}^\prime(k). \end{align*} By totality, either $\bm{y}(k) \prec \bm{y}^\prime(k)$ or $\bm{y}^\prime(k) \prec \bm{y}(k)$. Swapping the roles of $\bm{y}$ and $\bm{y}^\prime$ if necessary, we may assume that \begin{align*} \bm{y}(k) \prec \bm{y}^\prime(k). \end{align*} Since $\bm{y}$ and $\bm{y}^\prime$ contain the same entries with the same multiplicities, there exists an index $m > k$ such that \begin{align*} \bm{y}^\prime(m) = \bm{y}(k). \end{align*} However, $\bm{y}^\prime$ is sorted, so $k < m$ implies \begin{align*} \bm{y}^\prime(k) \preceq \bm{y}^\prime(m) = \bm{y}(k), \end{align*} contradicting $\bm{y}(k) \prec \bm{y}^\prime(k)$. Hence $\bm{y} = \bm{y}^\prime$. Since $\bm{x}$ was arbitrary, the sorting map is unique. Now, notice that for $\bm{x}\in \mathscr{S}(X,\preceq)$ that the identity results in a sorted tuple, and by the uniqueness of the sorting map, it must coincide with the identity of $\mathscr{S}(X,\preceq)$, implying that the sorting map is idempotent on $\mathscr{S}(X,\preceq)$.

nodes.title: Uniqueness and Idempotency
nodes.statement: Let $(X,\preceq)$ be a totally ordered set, and let $\mathscr{T}(X)$ and $\mathscr{S}(X,\preceq)$ be the set of tuples and sorted tuples respectively. Then, \begin{enumerate}[(i)] \item The sorting map is unique. \item The sorting map is idempotent, that is $\varsigma \circ \varsigma = \varsigma$. \end{enumerate}
proofBridge: cor:unique-and-idempotent-sort uniqueness and idempotency.

motivationContexts.text: While partial orders are leveraged in practice, it is not unreasonable to assume that the exchange has an underlying total order, which breaks ties. Even if the ties are broken randomly, then there is, in a sense, a local total order, as they are placed into the market based on the random tie break.

Note, that applying a sorting map results in a sorted tuple by definition, since :T(X) S(X,). However, that property alone is insufficient; for instance, the mapping x e, where x is an arbitrary tuple and e is the empty tuple, will always result in a sorted tuple, as the empty tuple is sorted by definition. However, eq:sort-permute guarantees that sorting a tuple is the result of permuting the tuple, and hence the domain and image of the original tuple are preserved, albeit the pairing changes. We visualize the application of a sorting map in Figure fig:sorted-tuple.

The economic rationale for eq:sort-unique is that if orders are sorted within the market, then there can be no ambiguity as to which order takes priority on being executed. The idempotency states that sorting a market that is already sorted does nothing.

nodes.title: Index comparability relation
nodes.statement: Let $(X,\preceq)$ be a partially ordered set and let $\bm{x}\in\mathscr{T}(X)$. We define the relation $\overset{\bm{x}}{\leftrightsquigarrow}$ on $\mathrm{domain}(\bm{x})$ by \begin{align*} i \overset{\bm{x}}{\leftrightsquigarrow} j \iff (\bm{x}(i)\preceq \bm{x}(j))\ \lor\ (\bm{x}(j)\preceq \bm{x}(i)). \end{align*}
proofBridge: defn:index-comparable index comparability relation.

motivationContexts.text: The economic rationale for eq:sort-unique is that if orders are sorted within the market, then there can be no ambiguity as to which order takes priority on being executed. The idempotency states that sorting a market that is already sorted does nothing.

We will take the result presented in Corollary cor:unique-and-idempotent-sort as the characterizing properties of a well-defined sorting map even in the case of a partial order. Therefore, we now turn our attention to constructing a sorting map for a partially ordered set. Our overall strategy is to leverage the domain of the tuple to encode an implicit ordering, when the partial order does not specify one. In particular, we will use the fact that the domain of a tuple is a subset of N, which is totally ordered by the usual order.

The index comparability relation allows us to determine whether two elements of the tuple are immediately comparable. In particular, if i x j, then x(i) and x(j) are comparable, whereas if i x j, then x(i) and x(j) are incomparable. However, comparability need not be transitive: it may happen that i x j and j x k, but i x k. In this case, x(i) and x(k) are incomparable, even though both are comparable to x(j). This indicates that indices can be linked through chains of comparability and should therefore be treated as belonging to the same comparability component. To capture this formally, we extend x by taking its reflexive transitive closure; we call the resulting relation the comparability relation.

Informally, the reflexive transitive closure of a relation is constructed by repeated composing the relation with itself, exploring all of its possible paths and collecting all the pairs that can be reached by following the relation. In particular, if R is a relation on X, then R^n captures all the pairs that can be reached by following n steps of the relation, and the transitive closure R captures all the pairs that can be reached by following any number of steps of the relation. Note, that we have the following property of the transitive closure.

def IndexComparable [Preorder X] (x : Tuple X)

lean.informal: two tuple indices are immediately comparable when their entries are comparable in the ambient preorder.

lean.signature:
theorem indexComparable_refl [Preorder X] (x : Tuple X)

lean.informal: immediate comparability is reflexive.

lean.signature:
theorem indexComparable_symm [Preorder X] (x : Tuple X)
    {i j : Fin x.length} :
    IndexComparable x i j → IndexComparable x j i := by
lean.informal: immediate comparability is symmetric.

nodes.title: Reflexive Transitive Closure
nodes.statement: Let $X$ be a set and let $R \subseteq X \times X$ be a relation on $X$. Then, the transitive closure of $R$ is the relation $\overline{R} \subseteq X \times X$ defined by \begin{align*} \overline{R} = \Delta \cup \bigcup_{n\in\mathbb{N}} R^n, \end{align*} where $R^1 = R$ and $R^{n+1} = R^n \circ R$ for $n \in \mathbb{N}$, and $\Delta = \{(x,x) \mid x \in X\}$ is the diagonal relation on $X$.
proofBridge: defn:reflexive-transitive-closure reflexive transitive closure.

nodes.statement: Let $(X,\preceq)$ be a partially ordered set, $\bm{x}\in\mathscr{T}(X)$, and $\overset{\bm{x}}{\leftrightsquigarrow}$ be as in Definition \ref{defn:index-comparable}. The connectivity relation $\overset{\bm{x}}{\sim}$ on $\mathrm{domain}(\bm{x})$ is the reflexive transitive closure of $\overset{\bm{x}}{\leftrightsquigarrow}$.

motivationContexts.text: Informally, the reflexive transitive closure of a relation is constructed by repeated composing the relation with itself, exploring all of its possible paths and collecting all the pairs that can be reached by following the relation. In particular, if R is a relation on X, then R^n captures all the pairs that can be reached by following n steps of the relation, and the transitive closure R captures all the pairs that can be reached by following any number of steps of the relation. Note, that we have the following property of the transitive closure.

The proposition states, that if there are only |X| elements in the set, then one only needs to explore paths of length at most |X| to capture all the pairs that can be reached by following the relation. In particular, if there is a path of length greater than |X|, then there must be a cycle in the path, which implies that there is a shorter path that captures the same pair.

The advantage is that connectivity is transitive, so if i x j and j x k, then i x k, which means that x(i) and x(k) are connected, even if they are not directly comparable. In particular, if i x j, then there exists a chain of indices i = i_1, , i_n = j such that i_k x i_k+1 for all k < n. This means that x(i) and x(j) are connected through a chain of comparable elements, even if they are not directly comparable, which yields the following result.

Next, we can use the connectivity relation to define connected segments of the tuple, which are segments of the tuple where all elements are connected to all other elements in the section. First, recall that the cardinality of the quotient of an equivalence relation must be bounded above by the cardinality of the original set; as we group'' elements using an equivalence relation, we cannot have more groups than elements. Therefore, the number of equivalence classes of the connectivity relation is bounded above by the length of the tuple. Moreover, we can enumerate the equivalence classes in the order of first appearance within the tuple, which allows us to define the connected segments of the tuple.

nodes.title: Proposition: sim equivalence
nodes.statement: Let $(X,\preceq)$ be a partially ordered set and let $\bm{x}\in\mathscr{T}(X)$. Then $\overset{\bm{x}}{\sim}$ is an equivalence relation on $\mathrm{domain}(\bm{x})$.

thesisProof.text: First, we show that $\overset{\bm{x}}{\sim}$ is reflexive. For any $i \in \mathrm{domain}(\bm{x})$, we have $(i,i) \in \Delta$, and since $\Delta = \{(i,i) : i \in \mathrm{domain}(\bm{x})\}$ is trivially a subset of the reflixive closure, it follows that $i \overset{\bm{x}}{\sim} i$. Next, we show that $\overset{\bm{x}}{\sim}$ is symmetric. Suppose $i \overset{\bm{x}}{\sim} j$. Then, there exists a sequence of indices $i = i_1, i_2, \dots, i_n = j$ such that $i_k \overset{\bm{x}}{\leftrightsquigarrow} i_{k+1}$ for all $k < n$. Since $\overset{\bm{x}}{\leftrightsquigarrow}$ is symmetric, we have $i_{k+1} \overset{\bm{x}}{\leftrightsquigarrow} i_k$ for all $k < n$. Therefore, the sequence $j = i_n, i_{n-1}, \dots, i_1 = i$ shows that $j \overset{\bm{x}}{\sim} i$. Finally, we show that $\overset{\bm{x}}{\sim}$ is transitive. Suppose $i \overset{\bm{x}}{\sim} j$ and $j \overset{\bm{x}}{\sim} k$. Then, there exist sequences of indices $i = i_1, i_2, \dots, i_m = j$ and $j = j_1, j_2, \dots, j_p = k$ such that $i_k \overset{\bm{x}}{\leftrightsquigarrow} i_{k+1}$ for all $k < m$ and $j_l \overset{\bm{x}}{\leftrightsquigarrow} j_{l+1}$ for all $l < p$. Concatenating these sequences gives us a sequence of indices from $i$ to $k$, showing that $i \overset{\bm{x}}{\sim} k$.

nodes.title: Connected segments of a tuple
nodes.statement: Let $(X,\preceq)$ be a partially ordered set and let $\bm{x}\in\mathscr{T}(X)$. Let $\mathrm{domain}(\bm{x})/\overset{\bm{x}}{\sim}$ be the set of equivalence classes of $\overset{\bm{x}}{\sim}$ and let $\kappa$ be the cardinality of $\mathrm{domain}(\bm{x})/\overset{\bm{x}}{\sim}$. Let $(C_k)_{k\le \kappa}$ be an enumeration of the equivalence classes ordered by first appearance: \begin{align*} C_k \leq C_{k^\prime} \iff \min C_k \leq \min C_{k^\prime}. \end{align*} For each $k\leq \kappa$, define a subset of the tuple graph $\Gamma(\bm{x})\subseteq \mathbb{N}\times X$ by \begin{align*} K_k = \{(i,\bm{x}(i))\in \Gamma(\bm{x}) : i\in C_k\}. \end{align*} We call $(K_k)_{k\le \kappa}$ the connected segments of $\bm{x}$ and set \begin{align*} \mathcal{K}(\bm{x}) = \{K_k : k\leq \kappa\}. \end{align*}

nodes.title: Partition and mutual incomparability

nodes.title: Injectivity of arrival index
nodes.statement: Let $(X,\preceq)$ be a partially ordered set and let $\bm{x}\in\mathscr{T}(X)$. Then the map $\tau:\mathcal{K}(\bm{x})\to\mathbb{N}$ is injective.

thesisProof.text: We must show, that $\tau(K) = \tau(K^\prime)$ implies $K = K^\prime$. Suppose $\tau(K) = \tau(K^\prime)$ for some $K, K^\prime \in \mathcal{K}(\bm{x})$. Then, by definition of $\tau$, there exists an index $i = \tau(K) = \tau(K^\prime)$ such that $(i,\bm{x}(i))\in K$ and $(i,\bm{x}(i))\in K^\prime$. However, by Proposition \ref{prop:segments-partition-incomp}, the segments form a partition of the graph of $\bm{x}$, which means that $K$ and $K^\prime$ cannot have any elements in common unless they are the same segment. Therefore, we must have $K = K^\prime$, as desired.

nodes.title: Lemma: distinct finite set natural projection injective
nodes.statement: Let $X$ be a set and let $\Pi_{\mathbb{N}} : \mathbb{N} \times X \to \mathbb{N}$ denote the projection onto $\mathbb{N}$. Then, for any $\xi \in \mathscr{D}(X)$, the restriction of $\Pi_{\mathbb{N}}$ to $\xi$ is injective.

thesisProof.text: Recall that by definition we have \begin{align*} \mathscr{D}(X) = \{\xi \in \mathscr{F}(\mathbb{N} \times X) \mid \forall n \in \mathbb{N}: |\{n\} \times X \cap \xi| \leq 1\}, \end{align*} which means that for any $n \in \mathbb{N}$, there is at most one element of $\xi$ whose first coordinate is $n$. Therefore, if $(n,x)$ and $(n,y)$ are both in $\xi$, then we must have $x = y$, and hence the restriction of $\Pi_{\mathbb{N}}$ to $\xi$ is injective.

nodes.title: Sorting Map for Distinct Finite Sets
nodes.statement: Let $(X,\preceq)$ be a partially ordered set and let $\prec$ denote its strict part. Extend $\prec$ to a strict partial order on $\mathbb{N} \times X$ by defining \begin{align*} (n, x) \prec (m,y) \iff x \prec y \end{align*} Moreover, let $\mathscr{D}(X)$ be the set of distinct finite sets. Let $\varsigma^\ast : \mathscr{D}(X) \to \mathscr{T}(\mathbb{N} \times X)$ be defined recursively as follows: First, we define $\varsigma^\ast(\emptyset) = \bm{e}$, otherwise set $\xi^{(1)} = \xi$ and for $n \in \{1, \dots, |\xi|\}$ define \begin{align*} M^{(n)} &= \{(i,x) \in \xi^{(n)} \mid \not\exists (j,y) \in \xi^{(n)}: (j,y) \prec (i,x)\} \end{align*} and \begin{align*} \varsigma^\ast(\xi)(n) &= \argmin_{(i,x) \in M^{(n)}} i, \end{align*} with \begin{align*} \xi^{(n+1)} = \xi^{(n)} \backslash \{\varsigma^\ast(\xi)(n)\}. \end{align*} We call $\varsigma^\ast$ the sorting map for distinct finite sets. Likewise, let $\Pi_X$ and $\Pi_{\mathbb{N}}$ be the projections onto $X$ and $\mathbb{N}$ respectively, then we define the mapping $\varsigma:\mathscr{D}(X) \to \mathscr{S}(X, \preceq)$ by \begin{align*} \varsigma(\xi)(n) = \Pi_X(\varsigma^\ast(\xi)(n)), \end{align*} and likewise, we define the mapping $\pi:\mathscr{D}(X) \to \mathscr{T}(\mathbb{N})$ by \begin{align*} \pi(\xi)(n) = \Pi_{\mathbb{N}}(\varsigma^\ast(\xi)(n)). \end{align*}

nodes.title: Minimum Sorting Rule for Tuples
nodes.statement: Let $(X, \preceq)$ be a partially ordered set and let $\bm{x} \in \mathscr{T}(X)$ be a tuple. Then, we define the mapping $\varsigma_{\mathrm{min}}:\mathscr{T}(X) \to \mathscr{S}(X,\preceq)$ by \begin{align*} \varsigma_{\mathrm{min}}(\bm{x}) = \begin{cases} \bm{e} & \ell(\bm{x}) = 0\\ \bigoplus_{i = 1}^{|\mathcal{K}(\bm{x})|} \varsigma(K_i) & \ell(\bm{x}) > 0, \end{cases} \end{align*} where $K_i$ is the $i^{\mathrm{th}}$ segment in the total order of $\mathcal{K}(\bm{x})$. We call $\varsigma_{\mathrm{min}}$ the minimum sorting map for tuples.

motivationContexts.text: Next, we require the following definition for the construction of the sorting map; we have split into connected segments, but these are a priory not tuples, but rather subsets of the graph of the tuple. Therefore, we need to extract the tuples from the segments. First, we require the following auxiliary result.

Note, that the above suggests we could sort a tuple simply by applying the sorting map for distinct finite sets to the graph of the tuple, which is indeed true for a general sorting rule. However, it would not work in a well-defined way, c.f. Corollary cor:unique-and-idempotent-sort, as we could otherwise have different connected segments of the tuple interleaved with each other.
Finally, we have the following result, which states that the above map is indeed a sorting map.

nodes.title: Proposition: minimum sorting map is sorting map
nodes.statement: Let $(X, \preceq)$ be a partially ordered set. Then, the mapping $\varsigma_{\min}:\mathscr{T}(X) \to \mathscr{S}(X,\preceq)$ defined by sorting each connected segment separately and concatenating the results is a sorting map.

thesisProof.text: First, note that $\varsigma_{\min}(\bm{e}) = \bm{e}$, which is sorted by definition. Let $\bm{x} \in \mathscr{T}(X)$ with $\ell(\bm{x}) > 0$, and write \begin{align*} \mathcal{K}(\bm{x}) = \{K_1,\dots,K_\kappa\}, \end{align*} where the segments are ordered by first appearance. Since each $K_r$ is a distinct finite set, the map $\varsigma(K_r)$ is well-defined by Definition \ref{defn:sorting-finite-sets}, and so is the concatenation \begin{align*} \varsigma_{\min}(\bm{x}) = \bigoplus_{r=1}^{\kappa} \varsigma(K_r). \end{align*} Each block $\varsigma(K_r)$ is sorted by construction. Moreover, if $r < s$, then every element of $K_r$ is incomparable with every element of $K_s$ by Proposition \ref{prop:segments-partition-incomp}. Hence no element from the later block can be strictly smaller than an element from the earlier block. Therefore, the concatenation of the sorted blocks is again sorted, so $\varsigma_{\min}(\bm{x}) \in \mathscr{S}(X,\preceq)$. It remains to verify the permutation property. For each segment $K_r$, the tuple $\pi(K_r)$ produced in Definition \ref{defn:sorting-finite-sets} lists exactly the indices appearing in $K_r$, in the order used by $\varsigma(K_r)$. In particular, $\pi(K_r)$ is a bijection from $\{1,\dots,|K_r|\}$ onto the index set \begin{align*} I_r = \Pi_{\mathbb{N}}(K_r). \end{align*} Since the family $\mathcal{K}(\bm{x})$ is a partition of $\Gamma(\bm{x})$, the sets $I_1,\dots,I_\kappa$ form a partition of $\mathrm{domain}(\bm{x})$. Consequently, the concatenation \begin{align*} \bm{\pi} = \bigoplus_{r = 1}^{\kappa} \pi(K_r) \end{align*} has length $\ell(\bm{x})$ and image $\mathrm{domain}(\bm{x})$. Because the images of the blocks are pairwise disjoint, $\bm{\pi}:\mathrm{domain}(\bm{x}) \to \mathrm{domain}(\bm{x})$ is bijective. By construction, the tuple $\bm{x}\circ \bm{\pi}$ first lists the entries from $K_1$ in the order prescribed by $\varsigma(K_1)$, then the entries from $K_2$ in the order prescribed by $\varsigma(K_2)$, and so on. Hence \begin{align*} \bm{x}\circ\bm{\pi} = \bigoplus_{r=1}^{\kappa} \varsigma(K_r) = \varsigma_{\min}(\bm{x}), \end{align*} which proves that $\varsigma_{\min}$ is a sorting map.

However, it would not work in a well-defined way, c.f. Corollary cor:unique-and-idempotent-sort, as we could otherwise have different connected segments of the tuple interleaved with each other.
Finally, we have the following result, which states that the above map is indeed a sorting map.

We immediately have the following result, which states that the minimum sorting map is a well-defined sorting map for any partially ordered set, the sense that is satisfies the critera of the Corollary cor:unique-and-idempotent-sort.

Let us finally relate the above construction to the specific case in which a market is endowed with a partial order. For instance, many markets are endowed with a partial order based on price and time priority, where orders are first compared by price, and if they have the same price, then they are compared by time of arrival. However, in theory, it could occur that two orders with the same price arrive at the same time, in which case there is a tie in market. Since each $K_r$ is a distinct finite set, the map $\varsigma(K_r)$ is well-defined by Definition \ref{defn:sorting-finite-sets}, and so is the concatenation $ \varsigma_{\min}(\bm{x}) = \bigoplus_{r=1}^{\kappa} \varsigma(K_r). $ Each block $\varsigma(K_r)$ is sorted by construction. Moreover, if $r < s$, then every element of $K_r$ is incomparable with every element of $K_s$ by Proposition \ref{prop:segments-partition-incomp}. Hence no element from the later block can be strictly smaller than an element from the earlier block. Therefore, the concatenation of the sorted blocks is again sorted, so $\varsigma_{\min}(\bm{x}) \in \mathscr{S}(X,\preceq)$.

proofMoves.title: Unfold the definitions
proofMoves.text: It remains to verify the permutation property. For each segment $K_r$, the tuple $\pi(K_r)$ produced in Definition \ref{defn:sorting-finite-sets} lists exactly the indices appearing in $K_r$, in the order used by $\varsigma(K_r)$. Consequently, the concatenation $ \bm{\pi} = \bigoplus_{r = 1}^{\kappa} \pi(K_r) $ has length $\ell(\bm{x})$ and image $\mathrm{domain}(\bm{x})$. Because the images of the blocks are pairwise disjoint, $\bm{\pi}:\mathrm{domain}(\bm{x}) \to \mathrm{domain}(\bm{x})$ is bijective. By construction, the tuple $\bm{x}\circ \bm{\pi}$ first lists the entries from $K_1$ in the order prescribed by $\varsigma(K_1)$, then the entries from $K_2$ in the order prescribed by $\varsigma(K_2)$, and so on. Hence $ \bm{x}\circ\bm{\pi} = \bigoplus_{r=1}^{\kappa} \varsigma(K_r) = \varsigma_{\min}(\bm{x}), $ which proves that $\varsigma_{\min}$ is a sorting map.
