nodes.title: Tuple Space Properties
nodes.statement: Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space. Then, for every $\bm{x}, \bm{x}^\prime \in \mathscr{T}(X)$ it holds, that \begin{enumerate}[(i)] \item $\mathscr{d}_H(\bm{x}, \bm{x}^\prime) < 1$ implies $\ell(\bm{x}) = \ell(\bm{x}^\prime)$. \item $\mathscr{d}_H(\bm{x}, \bm{x}^\prime) < 1$ and $\ell(\bm{x}) > 0$ implies $\mathscr{d}_H(\bm{x},\bm{x}^\prime) = \max_{i\in\{1,\dots, \ell(\bm{x})\}} d(\bm{x}(i), \bm{x}^\prime(i))$. \end{enumerate} Moreover, it holds that \begin{enumerate}[(i)] \setcounter{enumi}{2} \item If $(X,d)$ is a complete metric space, then $(\mathscr{T}(X),\mathscr{d}_H)$ is a complete metric space. \item If $(X,d)$ is a separable metric space, then $(\mathscr{T}(X),\mathscr{d}_H)$ is a separable metric space. \item If $(X, \preceq, d)$ is a totally ordered separable metric space, then $(\mathscr{S}(X; \preceq),\mathscr{d}_H)$ is a separable metric subspace of $(\mathscr{T}(X),\mathscr{d}_H)$. \end{enumerate}

thesisProof.text: We show properties \eqref{eq:tuple-length} and \eqref{eq:tuple-collapse} in tandem. Note that the claims are trivial if one of the tuples is empty; the distance is either $0$ if both tuples are empty or $\infty$ otherwise. Therefore assume that $\bm{x},\bm{y}\in\mathscr{T}(X)$ are non-empty tuples. Then, by definition \begin{align*} \mathscr{d}_H(\bm{x},\bm{y}) = \left( \max_{(i,x) \in \Gamma(\bm{x})} \min_{(j,y) \in \Gamma(\bm{y})} |i-j| + d(x,y), \max_{(j,y) \in \Gamma(\bm{y})} \min_{(i,x) \in \Gamma(\bm{x})} |j-i| + d(y,x)\right) \end{align*} But note, \begin{align*} \mathscr{d}_H(\bm{x},\bm{y}) < 1, \end{align*} implies that \begin{align}\label{eq:bounded-by-one} \max_{(i,x) \in \Gamma(\bm{x})} \min_{(j,y) \in \Gamma(\bm{y})} |i-j| + d(x,y) < 1, \end{align} and \begin{align*} \max_{(j,y) \in \Gamma(\bm{y})} \min_{(i,x) \in \Gamma(\bm{x})} |j-i| + d(y,x) < 1. \end{align*} However, for two natural numbers $i,j\in \mathbb{N}$ it holds that $|i-j| < 1$ implies $i = j$. However, if $\ell(\bm{x}) \neq \ell(\bm{y})$, we can clearly find elements $i$ and $j$ such that \begin{align*} |i-j| + d(\bm{x}(i), \bm{y}(j)) \geq |i-j| \geq 1, \end{align*} and it follows that for $\ell(\bm{x}) \neq \ell(\bm{y})$ implies that $\mathscr{d}_H(\bm{x},\bm{y}) \geq 1$. By contraposition the claim follows. Moreover, we know that $|i-j| < 1$ implies $i = j$ for $i,j \in\mathbb{N}$. Therefore, \eqref{eq:bounded-by-one} implies that for the joint maximizer and minimizer it holds that $i = j$. Now, since the graph map is bijective on its range, I know that $(i,x)$ is uniquely determined by the element $\bm{x}(i)$. Hence, \begin{align*} &\max_{(i,x) \in \Gamma(\bm{x})} \min_{(j,y) \in \Gamma(\bm{y})} |i-j| + d(x,y) < 1 \implies \\ &\max_{(i,x) \in \Gamma(\bm{x})} \min_{(j,y) \in \Gamma(\bm{y})} |i-j| + d(x,y) = \max_{i \in \{1,\dots, n\}} d(\bm{x}(i),\bm{y}(i)) < 1, \end{align*} where $n = \ell(\bm{x}) = \ell(\bm{y})$. Similar arguments show that \begin{align*} &\max_{(j,y) \in \Gamma(\bm{y})} \min_{(i,x) \in \Gamma(\bm{x})} |j-i| + d(y,x) < 1 \implies\\ &\max_{(j,y) \in \Gamma(\bm{y})} \min_{(i,x) \in \Gamma(\bm{x})} |j-i| + d(y,x) = \max_{i \in \{1,\dots, n\}} d(\bm{x}(i),\bm{y}(i)) < 1, \end{align*} which proves the claims \eqref{eq:tuple-length} and \eqref{eq:tuple-collapse}. To prove \eqref{eq:tuple-complete}, let $(\bm{x}_i)_{i\in\mathbb{N}}$ be a Cauchy sequence in $\mathscr{T}(X)$. That is, for every $\varepsilon > 0$ there exists an $N\in\mathbb{N}$ such that \begin{align*} m,n\geq N \implies \mathscr{d}_H(\bm{x}_m, \bm{x}_n) < \varepsilon. \end{align*} Without loss of generality, assume that $\varepsilon < 1$ and let $N_0 \in \mathbb{N}$ be such that \begin{align*} m,n\geq N_0 \implies \mathscr{d}_H(\bm{x}_m, \bm{x}_n) < 1, \end{align*} and notice that by \eqref{eq:tuple-collapse} I have that $n \geq N_0$ implies $\ell(\bm{x}_n) = k \in \mathbb{N}_0$. Moreover, by \eqref{eq:tuple-length} it follows that \begin{align*} \mathscr{d}_H(\bm{x}_m, \bm{x}_n) < 1 \implies \mathscr{d}_H(\bm{x}_m, \bm{x}_n) = \max_{i \in \{1,\dots, k\}} d(\bm{x}_m(i),\bm{x}_n(i)). \end{align*} Now, clearly, the sequence $(\bm{x}_n)_{n = N_0}^\infty$ is Cauchy in $(X^k,d_\infty)$, which is complete and hence has a limit $\bm{x} \in (X^k, d_\infty)$. However $X^k \subset \mathscr{T}(X)$, and so $\bm{x} \in \mathscr{T}(X)$. By the local equality of the metrics, one has that $\bm{x}_n$ converges to $\bm{x} \in \mathscr{T}(X)$, as desired. For \eqref{eq:tuple-separable} and \eqref{eq:sorted-tuple-separable} I only need to show that $(\mathscr{T}(X), \mathscr{d}_H)$ is separable, provided $(X,d)$ is separable; if $(X, \prec, d)$ is a totally ordered metric space, then $\mathscr{S}(X;\prec) \subseteq \mathscr{T}(X)$ and if $\mathscr{T}(X)$ is separable, then $\mathscr{S}(X;\prec)$ will also be separable, as it is a subset of separable metric space. Now, clearly if $(X,d)$ is separable, then so is $(\mathscr{D}(X), d^\ast_H)$ by Theorem \ref{thm:distinct-properties}. By extension \begin{align*} \Gamma(\mathscr{T}(X)) \subset \mathscr{D}(X) \end{align*} so $(\Gamma(\mathscr{T}(X)),d^\ast_H)$ is separable, as it is a subset of a separable metric space. However, $(\Gamma(\mathscr{T}(X)),d^\ast_H)$ is isometric to $(\mathscr{T}(X),\mathscr{d}_H)$ under the map $\Gamma^{-1}$, which exists on $\Gamma(\mathscr{T}(X))$ as $\Gamma$ is injective. Therefore, it is a bijection between $\mathscr{T}(X)$ and $(\Gamma(\mathscr{T}(X)),d_H)$, from which the assertion follows.

proofMoves.text: We show properties \eqref{eq:tuple-length} and \eqref{eq:tuple-collapse} in tandem. Note that the claims are trivial if one of the tuples is empty; the distance is either $0$ if both tuples are empty or $\infty$ otherwise. Therefore assume that $\bm{x},\bm{y}\in\mathscr{T}(X)$ are non-empty tuples. Then, by definition $ \mathscr{d}_H(\bm{x},\bm{y}) = \left( \max_{(i,x) \in \Gamma(\bm{x})} \min_{(j,y) \in \Gamma(\bm{y})} |i-j| + d(x,y), \max_{(j,y) \in \Gamma(\bm{y})} \min_{(i,x) \in \Gamma(\bm{x})} |j-i| + d(y,x)\right) $ But note, $ \mathscr{d}_H(\bm{x},\bm{y}) < 1, $ implies that $ \max_{(i,x) \in \Gamma(\bm{x})} \min_{(j,y) \in \Gamma(\bm{y})} |i-j| + d(x,y) < 1, $ and $ \max_{(j,y) \in \Gamma(\bm{y})} \min_{(i,x) \in \Gamma(\bm{x})} |j-i| + d(y,x) < 1. $ However, for two natural numbers $i,j\in \mathbb{N}$ it holds that $|i-j| < 1$ implies $i = j$. However, if $\ell(\bm{x}) \neq \ell(\bm{y})$, we can clearly find elements $i$ and $j$ such that $ |i-j| + d(\bm{x}(i), \bm{y}(j)) \geq |i-j| \geq 1, $ and it follows that for $\ell(\bm{x}) \neq \ell(\bm{y})$ implies that $\mathscr{d}_H(\bm{x},\bm{y}) \geq 1$. By contraposition the claim follows. Moreover, we know that $|i-j| < 1$ implies $i = j$ for $i,j \in\mathbb{N}$. Therefore, \eqref{eq:bounded-by-one} implies that for the joint maximizer and minimizer it holds that $i = j$.

proofMoves.title: Construct the required object
proofMoves.text: Now, since the graph map is bijective on its range, I know that $(i,x)$ is uniquely determined by the element $\bm{x}(i)$. Hence, $ &\max_{(i,x) \in \Gamma(\bm{x})} \min_{(j,y) \in \Gamma(\bm{y})} |i-j| + d(x,y) < 1 \implies \\ &\max_{(i,x) \in \Gamma(\bm{x})} \min_{(j,y) \in \Gamma(\bm{y})} |i-j| + d(x,y) = \max_{i \in \{1,\dots, n\}} d(\bm{x}(i),\bm{y}(i)) < 1, $ where $n = \ell(\bm{x}) = \ell(\bm{y})$. Similar arguments show that $ &\max_{(j,y) \in \Gamma(\bm{y})} \min_{(i,x) \in \Gamma(\bm{x})} |j-i| + d(y,x) < 1 \implies\\ &\max_{(j,y) \in \Gamma(\bm{y})} \min_{(i,x) \in \Gamma(\bm{x})} |j-i| + d(y,x) = \max_{i \in \{1,\dots, n\}} d(\bm{x}(i),\bm{y}(i)) < 1, $ which proves the claims \eqref{eq:tuple-length} and \eqref{eq:tuple-collapse}. To prove \eqref{eq:tuple-complete}, let $(\bm{x}_i)_{i\in\mathbb{N}}$ be a Cauchy sequence in $\mathscr{T}(X)$. That is, for every $\varepsilon > 0$ there exists an $N\in\mathbb{N}$ such that $ m,n\geq N \implies \mathscr{d}_H(\bm{x}_m, \bm{x}_n) < \varepsilon. $ Without loss of generality, assume that $\varepsilon < 1$ and let $N_0 \in \mathbb{N}$ be such that $ m,n\geq N_0 \implies \mathscr{d}_H(\bm{x}_m, \bm{x}_n) < 1, $ and notice that by \eqref{eq:tuple-collapse} I have that $n \geq N_0$ implies $\ell(\bm{x}_n) = k \in \mathbb{N}_0$. Moreover, by \eqref{eq:tuple-length} it follows that $ \mathscr{d}_H(\bm{x}_m, \bm{x}_n) < 1 \implies \mathscr{d}_H(\bm{x}_m, \bm{x}_n) = \max_{i \in \{1,\dots, k\}} d(\bm{x}_m(i),\bm{x}_n(i)). $

proofMoves.title: Build the countability or density witness
proofMoves.text: Now, clearly, the sequence $(\bm{x}_n)_{n = N_0}^\infty$ is Cauchy in $(X^k,d_\infty)$, which is complete and hence has a limit $\bm{x} \in (X^k, d_\infty)$. However $X^k \subset \mathscr{T}(X)$, and so $\bm{x} \in \mathscr{T}(X)$. By the local equality of the metrics, one has that $\bm{x}_n$ converges to $\bm{x} \in \mathscr{T}(X)$, as desired. For \eqref{eq:tuple-separable} and \eqref{eq:sorted-tuple-separable} I only need to show that $(\mathscr{T}(X), \mathscr{d}_H)$ is separable, provided $(X,d)$ is separable; if $(X, \prec, d)$ is a totally ordered metric space, then $\mathscr{S}(X;\prec) \subseteq \mathscr{T}(X)$ and if $\mathscr{T}(X)$ is separable, then $\mathscr{S}(X;\prec)$ will also be separable, as it is a subset of separable metric space.

proofMoves.title: Build the countability or density witness
proofMoves.text: Now, clearly if $(X,d)$ is separable, then so is $(\mathscr{D}(X), d^\ast_H)$ by Theorem \ref{thm:distinct-properties}. By extension $ \Gamma(\mathscr{T}(X)) \subset \mathscr{D}(X) $ so $(\Gamma(\mathscr{T}(X)),d^\ast_H)$ is separable, as it is a subset of a separable metric space. However, $(\Gamma(\mathscr{T}(X)),d^\ast_H)$ is isometric to $(\mathscr{T}(X),\mathscr{d}_H)$ under the map $\Gamma^{-1}$, which exists on $\Gamma(\mathscr{T}(X))$ as $\Gamma$ is injective. Therefore, it is a bijection between $\mathscr{T}(X)$ and $(\Gamma(\mathscr{T}(X)),d_H)$, from which the assertion follows.

nodes.title: Corollary: tuple metrization
nodes.statement: Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space, and let $\mathscr{T}(X)$ be the associated tuple space. Define the mapping $\mathscr{d}_\infty : \mathscr{T}(X) \times \mathscr{T}(X) \to [0,\infty]$ by \begin{align*} \mathscr{d}_\infty(\bm{x},\bm{x}^\prime) = \begin{cases} 0 & \ell(\bm{x}) = \ell(\bm{x}^\prime) = 0\\ \max_{i \in \{1,\dots, \ell(\bm{x})\}} d(\bm{x}(i), \bm{x}^\prime(i)) & \ell(\bm{x}) = \ell(\bm{x}^\prime) > 0\\ \infty & \ell(\bm{x})\neq\ell(\bm{x}^\prime). \end{cases} \end{align*} Then, $(\mathscr{T}(X), \mathscr{d}_\infty)$ is a metric space. Moreover, if $(X,d)$ is separable, then $(\mathscr{T}(X), \mathscr{d}_\infty)$ is separable. Similarly, if $(X,d)$ is complete, then $(\mathscr{T}(X), \mathscr{d}_\infty)$ is complete.
proofBridge: cor:tuple-metrization d∞ metric on tuple space.

nodes.statement: Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space and let $\bar{d}:X\times X \to [0,1]$ be the metric defined by \begin{align*} \bar{d}(x,x^\prime)=\min(d(x,x^\prime), 1). \end{align*} Then, $(X,d)$ and $(X,\bar{d})$ are equivalent. nodes.title: The Standard Machinery
nodes.statement: Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space, and let $\mathscr{T}(X)$ be the associated tuple space. Let $\mathscr{d}_H:\mathscr{T}(X)\times \mathscr{T}(X) \to [0,\infty]$ be the Hausdorff tuple distance and $\mathscr{d}_\infty$ be the metric defined in Corollary \ref{cor:tuple-metrization}. For each $n \in \mathbb{N}_0$, let $X^n \subset\mathscr{T}(X)$ be the subset of tuples with length $n$ and let $d^n_\infty:X^n\times X^n \to [0,\infty]$ be the maximum product metric defined by $d^n_\infty(\bm{x}, \bm{x}^\prime) = \max_{i \in \{1,\dots, n\}} d(\bm{x}(i), \bm{x}^\prime(i))$. Let $E$ be a non-empty set and let $\rho : E \times E\to [0,\infty]$ be a metric on $E$, and $\Sigma \subseteq \wp(E)$ be a $\sigma$-algebra on $E$. Then, \begin{enumerate}[(i)] \item The identity mapping is a homeomorphism. \item Any mapping $f:\mathscr{T}(X) \to E$ is from $(\mathscr{T}(X),\mathscr{d}_H)$ continuous if, and only if, it is continuous from $(\mathscr{T}(X),\mathscr{d}_\infty)$. \item Any mapping $f:\mathscr{T}(X) \to E$ is continuous from $(\mathscr{T}(X), \mathscr{d}_H)$ if, and only if, each restricted map $f\restriction_{X^n}:X^n \to E$ is continuous from $(X^n, d^n_\infty)$. \item Any mapping $f:\mathscr{T}(X) \to E$ is $\mathcal{B}(\mathscr{T}(X),\mathscr{d}_H) / \Sigma$ measurable if, and only if, it is $\mathcal{B}(\mathscr{T}(X),\mathscr{d}_\infty) / \Sigma$ measurable. \item Any mapping $f:\mathscr{T}(X) \to E$ is $\mathcal{B}(\mathscr{T}(X))/\Sigma$ measurable if, and only if, for any $n \in \mathbb{N}_0$, the restricted map $f\restriction_{X^n}:X^n \to E$ is $\mathcal{B}(X^n, d^n_\infty)/\Sigma$-measurable. \end{enumerate}

thesisProof.text: For property \eqref{propert:identity-homeomorphic}, notice that \begin{align*} \min(\mathscr{d}_H(\bm{x}, \bm{x}^\prime),1) = \min(\mathscr{d}_\infty(\bm{x},\bm{x}^\prime), 1), \end{align*} which proves the claim, as the two spaces are consequently topologically equivalent. Next, we prove properties \eqref{property:continuous-iff} and \eqref{property:measurable-iff} in tandem. Notice that by construction, one has \begin{align*} \mathscr{T}(X) \cong \bigsqcup_{n\in\mathbb{N}_0} X^n, \end{align*} and in particular the spaces $(\mathscr{T}(X), \mathscr{d}_H)$ and $(\mathscr{T}(X), \mathscr{d}_\infty)$ are homeomorphic to the space $\left(\bigsqcup_{n\in\mathbb{N}_0} X^n, d_\infty\right)$ where $d_\infty$ is the disjoint union metric. By Propositions \ref{thm:pasting-lemma} and \ref{thm:pasting-lemma-measurable} the results now follow naturally, due to the mapping \begin{align*} \iota :\mathscr{T}(X) \to \bigsqcup_{n\in\mathbb{N}_0} X^n\\ \iota(\bm{x}) = (\bm{x}, \ell(\bm{x})) \end{align*} being a continuous bijection. Properties \eqref{property:continuous-iff-restricted} and \eqref{property:measurable-iff-restricted} follow naturally from the homeomorphic properties with the disjoint union and \eqref{property:continuous-iff} and \eqref{property:measurable-iff} respectively.

nodes.title: Sorting is Discontinuous
nodes.statement: Let $\mathscr{T}(\mathbb{R}^2)$ denote the space of tuples and let $\preceq$ be the lexicographic ordering on $\mathbb{R}^2$ defined by \begin{align*} (x,y) \preceq (x^\prime, y^\prime) \iff x < x^\prime \lor ((x =x^\prime) \land (y \leq y^\prime)). \end{align*} The order is total and, as a result, the sorting map is unique. Now, define the sequence \begin{align*} \bm{x}_n = i \mapsto \begin{cases} (0, 1) & i =1\\ \left(\frac{1}{n}, 0\right) &i =2 \end{cases} \end{align*} and notice that $\bm{x}_n \in \mathscr{S}(\mathbb{R}^2, \preceq)$ by construction. However, \begin{align*} \lim_{n \to \infty} \bm{x}_n = \bm{x}= i \mapsto \begin{cases} (0, 1) & i = 1 \\ (0, 0) & i = 2, \end{cases} \end{align*} but clearly $\bm{x}\notin\mathscr{S}(\mathbb{R}^2,\preceq)$. However, note that since $\varsigma$ is idempotent on $\mathscr{S}(\mathbb{R}^2, \preceq)$ it follows that \begin{align*} \bm{x} =\lim_{n\to\infty} \bm{x}_n =\lim_{n\to\infty} \varsigma(\bm{x}_n) \neq \varsigma(\lim_{n\to \infty}\bm{x}_n) = \varsigma(\bm{x}) =i \mapsto\begin{cases} (0,0) &i = 1\\ (0, 1) & i =2. \end{cases} \end{align*}

In the previous sections, we introduced a metric for the tuple space and showed the topological properties of the space, as well as the subspace of sorted tuples. It would be convenient if the subspace was complete in its own right. Unfortunately, that is not the case, as sorting is, generally, a discontinuous function.

Example exmp:sort-discont shows the problem; there are sequences which are sorted, but for which the limit is not sorted, even if the underlying order is total. Therefore, the space of sorted tuples is not a complete subspace in general.

While completeness is desirable, it is by no means required. However, in the stochastic setting, it is convenient if sorting is measurable, which we devote the following subsection to prove. First, we require the following Theorem, similar to the thm:pasting-lemma-measurable.

nodes.title: Theorem: measurable partition
nodes.statement: Let $(X,\mathcal{F})$ and $(Y, \mathcal{G})$ be measurable spaces. Let $(X_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ be a measurable partition of $X$. That is, for each $n\in \mathbb{N}$ one has $X_n \in \mathcal{F}$, and for $n,m \in\mathbb{N}$ with $n \neq m$ it holds that $X_n \cap X_m =\emptyset$, and \begin{align*} \bigcup_{n\in\mathbb{N}} X_n =X. \end{align*} Then, any function $f:X \to Y$ is $\mathcal{F}/\mathcal{G}$-measurable if and only if $f\restriction_{X_n} :X_n \to Y$ is $\mathcal{F}_n/\mathcal{G}$-measurable for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$, where $\mathcal{F}_n = \{ B \cap X_n \mid B \in \mathcal{F}\}$ is the trace $\sigma$-algebra.

thesisProof.text: First, note that if $f$ is measurable, then $f\restriction_{X_n}$ is immediately seen to be measurable by definition of the trace $\sigma$-algebra. Therefore, we will prove that if $f\restriction_{X_n}$ is measurable for each $n\in \mathbb{N}$, then $f$ is measurable. That is, we must show that \begin{align*} \forall n \in \mathbb{N}: f\restriction_{X_n}^{-1}(B) \in \mathcal{F}_n \implies f^{-1}(B) \in \mathcal{F}. \end{align*} But note that \begin{align*} f^{-1}(B) &= \{x \in X \mid f(x) \in B\}\\ &= \bigcup_{n\in \mathbb{N}}\{x \in X_n \mid f(x) \in B\}\\ &=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb{N}} f\restriction_{X_n}^{-1}(B) \\ &= \bigcup_{n\in\mathbb{N}} (U_n \cap X_n), \end{align*} where $U_n \in \mathcal{F}$ by the definition of the trace $\sigma$-algebra. Consequently, $f^{-1}(B) \in \mathcal{F}$, as $\mathcal{F}$ is closed under countable unions.

nodes.title: Permutation map

nodes.title: Proposition: permuting continuous
nodes.statement: Let $(X, d)$ be a metric space and let $(\mathscr{T}(X), \mathscr{d}_H)$ be the associated tuple Hausdorff distance. Moreover, let $\mathscr{P} \subseteq \mathscr{T}(\mathbb{N})$ be endowed with the tuple Hausdorff distance induced by the Euclidean distance on $\mathbb{N}$, which we denote by $\mathscr{d}_H^{\mathbb{N}}$. Then, the permutation map \begin{align*} (\bm{x}, \pi) \mapsto \bm{x}[\pi] \end{align*} is continuous, whenever $\mathscr{T}(X) \times \mathscr{P}$ is endowed with the product topology.

thesisProof.text: We must show that for any $(\bm{x}_0, \pi_0) \in \mathscr{T}(X) \times \mathscr{P}$ and $\varepsilon > 0$ there exists a $\delta > 0$ such that \begin{align*} \max(\mathscr{d}_H(\bm{x}, \bm{x}_0), \mathscr{d}_H^\mathbb{N}(\pi, \pi_0)) < \delta \implies \mathscr{d}_H(\bm{x}[\pi], \bm{x_0}[\pi_0]) < \varepsilon. \end{align*} However, by \nameref{thm:the-standard-machinery}, note that \begin{align*} \max(\mathscr{d}_H(\bm{x}, \bm{x}_0), \mathscr{d}_H^\mathbb{N}(\pi, \pi_0)) < 1 \implies \begin{cases} \ell(\bm{x}) = \ell(\bm{x}_0)\\ \pi = \pi_0 \\ \mathscr{d}_H(\bm{x},\bm{x}_0) = \max_{i \in \mathrm{domain}(\bm{x}_0)} d(\bm{x}(i), \bm{x}_0(i)). \end{cases} \end{align*} Now, if the bound above holds, and $\ell(\bm{x}_0) \neq \ell(\pi_0)$ the result is trivial, as $\bm{x}[\pi] = \bm{e} = \bm{x}_0[\pi_0]$. Therefore, assume without loss of generality, that $\ell(\bm{x}) = \ell(\pi)$ which, constrained to the bound above by $1$, implies that $\ell(\bm{x}) = \ell(\pi) =\ell(\bm{x}_0) = \ell(\pi_0)$. Moreover, if $\ell(\bm{x}_0) = 0$, the result is again trivial, so assuming $\ell(\bm{x}_0) >0$, notice that whenever $\delta < \min(1,\varepsilon)$ it holds that \begin{align*} \mathscr{d}_H(\bm{x}[\pi], \bm{x_0}[\pi_0]) = \mathscr{d}_H(\bm{x}[\pi_0], \bm{x_0}[\pi_0]) = \mathscr{d}_H(\bm{x}, \bm{x_0}) < \delta < \min(1,\varepsilon) < \varepsilon, \end{align*} as desired.

proofBridge: prop:permuting-continuous permutation map is continuous.

nodes.title: Proposition: permutations countable
nodes.statement: The set $\mathscr{P}$ is countable.

thesisProof.text: First, note that $\mathbb{N}$ is naturally countable. Moreover, for any $n \in \mathbb{N}_0$ the set $\mathbb{N}^n$ is countable, as a finite product of countable spaces are countable. Finally, \begin{align*} \mathscr{T}(\mathbb{N})=\bigcup_{n \in \mathbb{N}_0} \mathbb{N}^n \end{align*} is a countable union of countable sets and, hence, countable. Finally, as $\mathscr{P}\subset \mathscr{T}(\mathbb{N})$ is a subset of a countable set it is countable.

nodes.title: Proposition: measurable partition sorting
nodes.statement: Let $(X, \preceq, d)$ be a complete and separable metric space endowed with a Borel partial order. Let $\varphi:\mathscr{P}\to \mathbb{N}$ be a bijection. Then, the sets \begin{align*} \mathscr{U}_n = \mathscr{V}_{\varphi^{-1}(n)} \backslash\bigcup_{\substack{m \in \mathbb{N}:\\ m < n }} \mathscr{V}_{\varphi^{-1}(m)} \end{align*} form a measurable partition of $\mathscr{T}(X)$.

thesisProof.text:
Note, that by construction we have  egin{align*}  igcup_{n \in \mathbb{N}} \mathscr{U}_n =  igcup_{\pi \in \mathscr{P}} \mathscr{V}_\pi = \mathscr{T}(X), \end{align*} and $\mathscr{U}_n \cap \mathscr{U}_m = \emptyset$ for all $n,m\in \mathbb{N}: n 
eq m$. Therefore, it suffices to show, that each $\mathscr{U}_n$ is measurable. To this end, note that it suffices to show, that each $\mathscr{V}_\pi$ for $\pi \in \mathscr{P}$ is measurable. Notice that, by definition, we have  egin{align*} \mathscr{V}_\pi = \{ m{x} \in \mathscr{T}(X) \mid \ell( m{x}) = \ell(\pi) 	ext{ and }  m{x} \circ \pi \in \mathscr{S}(X, \preceq)\} \subseteq X^{\ell(\pi)}. \end{align*} Therefore, let $N = \ell(\pi)$ and note that by 
ameref{thm:the-standard-machinery}, it suffices to show that $\mathscr{V}_\pi$ is measurable in $X^N$ endowed with the maximum product metric and the associated Borel $\sigma$-algebra. However, as the space $(X,\preceq, d)$ is assumed to be complete and separable and the partial relation is Borel, one obtains that the set  egin{align*} A_{i,j} =\{ m{x}:\{1,\dots,N\} 	o X \mid  m{x}(\pi(j)) \prec  m{x}(\pi(i))\} \end{align*} is Borel, for each $i,j \in \{1,\dots,N\}$. Consequently, the complement, $A_{i,j}^{\mathtt{C}}$, is measurable. However, notice that  egin{align*} \mathscr{V}_{\pi} &= \{  m{x} \in \mathscr{T}(X) \mid N=\ell( m{x}) 	ext{ and }  m{x}\circ\pi \in \mathscr{S}(X,\preceq)\} \ &= \{ m{x} \in X^{N} \mid  orall i,j \in \{1,\dots, N\}: i \leq j \implies 
eg( m{x}(\pi(j)) \prec  m{x}(\pi(i)))\}\ &= igcap_{\substack{i,j\in \{1,\dots,N\}\i \leq j}} \{ m{x} \in X^{\ell(\pi)} \mid 
eg( m{x}(\pi(j)) \prec  m{x}(\pi(i)))\} \ &= igcap_{\substack{i,j \in \{1,\dots,N\}: \ i \leq j}} A_{i,j}^{\mathtt{C}} \end{align*} is hence a finite intersection of measurable sets and, hence, measurable.

nodes.title: Theorem: measurable sorting exists
nodes.statement: Let $(X, \preceq, d)$ be a partially ordered, complete, and separable metric space, for which the partial order is Borel. Let $(\mathscr{T}(X), \mathscr{d}_H)$ be the associated Hausdorff tuple space. Then there exists a Borel measurable sorting map $\varsigma:\mathscr{T}(X) \to \mathscr{S}(X,\preceq)$.

thesisProof.text: First, note that since $\mathscr{P}$ and $\mathbb{N}$ are equinumerous, there exists a bijection $\varphi:\mathscr{P} \to \mathbb{N}$. Consequently, the associated sorting map defined in Proposition \ref{prop:induced-sorting} is continuous when restricting to the sets $(\mathscr{U}_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ (as defined in Proposition \ref{prop:measurable-partition-sorting}) by Corollary \ref{cor:local-continuity-sorting}. However, as $(\mathscr{U}_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ forms a measurable partition, it follows by Theorem \ref{thm:measurable-partition} that the associated sorting map is measurable.

nodes.title: Theorem: minimal sorting measurable
nodes.statement: Let $(X, \preceq, d)$ be a partially ordered, complete, and separable metric space, for which the partial order is Borel. Let $(\mathscr{T}(X), \mathscr{d}_H)$ be the associated Hausdorff tuple space. Then, the minimal sorting map $\varsigma_{\mathrm{min}}:\mathscr{T}(X) \to \mathscr{S}(X,\preceq)$ is Borel measurable.

thesisProof.text:
By 
ameref{thm:the-standard-machinery}, it suffices to show that the restriction of $\varsigma_{\mathrm{min}}$ to each $X^n$ is Borel measurable when $X^n$ is endowed with the maximum product metric. The cases $n = 0$ and $n = 1$ are trivial, since $\varsigma_{\mathrm{min}}$ is then the identity. Fix therefore $n > 1$. For each $i,j \in \{1,\dots,n\}$ define  egin{align*} C_{i,j} &= \{ m{x} \in X^n \mid i \overset{ m{x}}{\leftrightsquigarrow} j\}\ &= \{ m{x} \in X^n \mid  m{x}(i) \preceq  m{x}(j) \lor  m{x}(j) \preceq  m{x}(i)\}. \end{align*} Each set $C_{i,j}$ is measurable because the order relation $\preceq \subseteq X 	imes X$ is Borel and the coordinate evaluation maps on $X^n$ are continuous. Next, define  egin{align*} \mathbf{C}_{i,j} = \{ m{x} \in X^n \mid i \overset{ m{x}}{\sim} j\}. \end{align*} By Proposition ef{prop:transitive-closure-finite}, two indices are connected if and only if they can be joined by a path of length at most $n-1$. Hence, with  egin{align*} \mathsf{path}(i,j) =  igcup_{k = 0}^{n-1} \{(i_0,\dots,i_k) \in \{1,\dots,n\}^{k+1} \mid i_0 = i,\ i_k = j\}, \end{align*} which is a finite set, we have  egin{align*} \mathbf{C}_{i,j} =  igcup_{(i_0,\dots,i_k) \in \mathsf{path}(i,j)}  igcap_{l=0}^{k-1} C_{i_l,i_{l+1}}. \end{align*} Therefore, each $\mathbf{C}_{i,j}$ is measurable. Let  egin{align*} \mathsf{part}(n) = \{\{I_1,\dots,I_m\} \mid \{I_1,\dots,I_m\} 	ext{ is a partition of } \{1,\dots,n\}\}. \end{align*} For $P \in \mathsf{part}(n)$ define  egin{align*} \mathsf{same}(P) &= \{(i,j) \in \{1,\dots,n\}^2 \mid \exists I \in P: i,j \in I\},\ \mathsf{diff}(P) &= \{(i,j) \in \{1,\dots,n\}^2 \mid  orall I \in P: 
eg(i \in I \land j \in I)\}, \end{align*} and  egin{align*} \mathscr{E}(P) =  igcap_{(i,j) \in \mathsf{same}(P)} \mathbf{C}_{i,j} \cap  igcap_{(i,j) \in \mathsf{diff}(P)} \mathbf{C}_{i,j}^{\mathtt{C}}. \end{align*} Thus $\mathscr{E}(P)$ is exactly the set of tuples whose connectivity partition of $\{1,\dots,n\}$ equals $P$. Since $\overset{ m{x}}{\sim}$ is an equivalence relation, the family $(\mathscr{E}(P))_{P \in \mathsf{part}(n)}$ is a finite measurable partition of $X^n$. Now, the diagonal $\Delta = \{(x,x) \mid x \in X\} \subseteq X 	imes X$ is Borel because $X$ is metric. Hence the strict order  egin{align*} \prec = \preceq \setminus \Delta \end{align*} is Borel as well. For $i,j \in \{1,\dots,n\}$ define  egin{align*} A_{i,j} = \{ m{x} \in X^n \mid  m{x}(j) \prec  m{x}(i)\}. \end{align*} Each $A_{i,j}$ is measurable. Fix a non-empty set $C \subseteq \{1,\dots,n\}$ and a permutation $\pi \in \Pi(C)$, where $\Pi(C)$ denotes the set of bijections from $\{1,\dots,|C|\}$ to $C$. Define  egin{align*} C^{(1)} &= C,\ C^{(r)} &= C \setminus \{\pi(1),\dots,\pi(r-1)\}, \qquad r > 1. \end{align*} For each $r \in \{1,\dots,|C|\}$ set  egin{align*} M_{C,\pi,r} =  igcap_{j \in C^{(r)}} A_{\pi(r),j}^{\mathtt{C}} \cap  igcap_{\substack{i \in C^{(r)}\ i < \pi(r)}}  igcup_{j \in C^{(r)}} A_{i,j}. \end{align*} The first intersection states that no remaining index is strictly smaller than $\pi(r)$, so $\pi(r)$ is minimal among the remaining indices. The second states that every remaining index smaller than $\pi(r)$ fails to be minimal, so among the minimal remaining indices the least one is exactly $\pi(r)$. Therefore  egin{align*} B_{C,\pi} =  igcap_{r=1}^{|C|} M_{C,\pi,r} \end{align*} is precisely the set of tuples for which the minimal sorting permutation on the block $C$ equals $\pi$. In particular, $B_{C,\pi}$ is measurable. Now fix a partition $P = \{C_1,\dots,C_m\} \in \mathsf{part}(n)$, ordered so that  egin{align*} \min C_1 < \dots < \min C_m, \end{align*} and choose permutations $\pi_k \in \Pi(C_k)$ for $k=1,\dots,m$. Define  egin{align*} \mathscr{E}(P,\pi_1,\dots,\pi_m) = \mathscr{E}(P) \cap  igcap_{k=1}^m B_{C_k,\pi_k}. \end{align*} As $P$ and the $\pi_k$ vary, these sets form a finite measurable partition of $X^n$. On each set $\mathscr{E}(P,\pi_1,\dots,\pi_m)$, both the connected segments and the minimal sorting permutation within each segment are fixed. Consequently, on this set the map $\varsigma_{\mathrm{min}}$ agrees with the fixed permutation map  egin{align*}  m{x} \mapsto  m{x}[\pi_1 \oplus \dots \oplus \pi_m]. \end{align*} By Proposition ef{prop:permuting-continuous}, this map is continuous, hence measurable. Therefore, by Theorem ef{thm:measurable-partition}, the restriction of $\varsigma_{\mathrm{min}}$ to $X^n$ is measurable. Since $n$ was arbitrary, another application of 
ameref{thm:the-standard-machinery} yields that $\varsigma_{\mathrm{min}}:\mathscr{T}(X) 	o \mathscr{S}(X,\preceq)$ is Borel measurable.

proofMoves.title: Reduce to a simpler target
proofMoves.text: By \nameref{thm:the-standard-machinery}, it suffices to show that the restriction of $\varsigma_{\mathrm{min}}$ to each $X^n$ is Borel measurable when $X^n$ is endowed with the maximum product metric. The cases $n = 0$ and $n = 1$ are trivial, since $\varsigma_{\mathrm{min}}$ is then the identity. Fix therefore $n > 1$. For each $i,j \in \{1,\dots,n\}$ define $ C_{i,j} &= \{\bm{x} \in X^n \mid i \overset{\bm{x}}{\leftrightsquigarrow} j\}\\ &= \{\bm{x} \in X^n \mid \bm{x}(i) \preceq \bm{x}(j) \lor \bm{x}(j) \preceq \bm{x}(i)\}. $ Each set $C_{i,j}$ is measurable because the order relation $\preceq \subseteq X \times X$ is Borel and the coordinate evaluation maps on $X^n$ are continuous.

proofMoves.title: Construct the required object
proofMoves.text: Next, define $ \mathbf{C}_{i,j} = \{\bm{x} \in X^n \mid i \overset{\bm{x}}{\sim} j\}. $ By Proposition \ref{prop:transitive-closure-finite}, two indices are connected if and only if they can be joined by a path of length at most $n-1$. Hence, with $ \mathsf{path}(i,j) = \bigcup_{k = 0}^{n-1} \{(i_0,\dots,i_k) \in \{1,\dots,n\}^{k+1} \mid i_0 = i,\ i_k = j\}, $ which is a finite set, we have $ \mathbf{C}_{i,j} = \bigcup_{(i_0,\dots,i_k) \in \mathsf{path}(i,j)} \bigcap_{l=0}^{k-1} C_{i_l,i_{l+1}}. $ Therefore, each $\mathbf{C}_{i,j}$ is measurable. Let $ \mathsf{part}(n) = \{\{I_1,\dots,I_m\} \mid \{I_1,\dots,I_m\} \text{ is a partition of } \{1,\dots,n\}\}. $ For $P \in \mathsf{part}(n)$ define $ \mathsf{same}(P) &= \{(i,j) \in \{1,\dots,n\}^2 \mid \exists I \in P: i,j \in I\},\\ \mathsf{diff}(P) &= \{(i,j) \in \{1,\dots,n\}^2 \mid \forall I \in P: \neg(i \in I \land j \in I)\}, $ and $ \mathscr{E}(P) = \bigcap_{(i,j) \in \mathsf{same}(P)} \mathbf{C}_{i,j} \cap \bigcap_{(i,j) \in \mathsf{diff}(P)} \mathbf{C}_{i,j}^{\mathtt{C}}. $ Thus $\mathscr{E}(P)$ is exactly the set of tuples whose connectivity partition of $\{1,\dots,n\}$ equals $P$. Since $\overset{\bm{x}}{\sim}$ is an equivalence relation, the family $(\mathscr{E}(P))_{P \in \mathsf{part}(n)}$ is a finite measurable partition of $X^n$.

proofMoves.title: Construct the required object
proofMoves.text: Now, the diagonal $\Delta = \{(x,x) \mid x \in X\} \subseteq X \times X$ is Borel because $X$ is metric. Hence the strict order $ \prec = \preceq \setminus \Delta $ is Borel as well. For $i,j \in \{1,\dots,n\}$ define $ A_{i,j} = \{\bm{x} \in X^n \mid \bm{x}(j) \prec \bm{x}(i)\}. $ Each $A_{i,j}$ is measurable. Fix a non-empty set $C \subseteq \{1,\dots,n\}$ and a permutation $\pi \in \Pi(C)$, where $\Pi(C)$ denotes the set of bijections from $\{1,\dots,|C|\}$ to $C$. Define $ C^{(1)} &= C,\\ C^{(r)} &= C \setminus \{\pi(1),\dots,\pi(r-1)\}, \qquad r > 1. $ For each $r \in \{1,\dots,|C|\}$ set $ M_{C,\pi,r} = \bigcap_{j \in C^{(r)}} A_{\pi(r),j}^{\mathtt{C}} \cap \bigcap_{\substack{i \in C^{(r)}\\ i < \pi(r)}} \bigcup_{j \in C^{(r)}} A_{i,j}. $ The first intersection states that no remaining index is strictly smaller than $\pi(r)$, so $\pi(r)$ is minimal among the remaining indices. The second states that every remaining index smaller than $\pi(r)$ fails to be minimal, so among the minimal remaining indices the least one is exactly $\pi(r)$. Therefore $ B_{C,\pi} = \bigcap_{r=1}^{|C|} M_{C,\pi,r} $ is precisely the set of tuples for which the minimal sorting permutation on the block $C$ equals $\pi$. In particular, $B_{C,\pi}$ is measurable.

proofMoves.title: Construct the required object
proofMoves.text: Now fix a partition $P = \{C_1,\dots,C_m\} \in \mathsf{part}(n)$, ordered so that $ \min C_1 < \dots < \min C_m, $ and choose permutations $\pi_k \in \Pi(C_k)$ for $k=1,\dots,m$. Define $ \mathscr{E}(P,\pi_1,\dots,\pi_m) = \mathscr{E}(P) \cap \bigcap_{k=1}^m B_{C_k,\pi_k}. $ As $P$ and the $\pi_k$ vary, these sets form a finite measurable partition of $X^n$. On each set $\mathscr{E}(P,\pi_1,\dots,\pi_m)$, both the connected segments and the minimal sorting permutation within each segment are fixed. Consequently, on this set the map $\varsigma_{\mathrm{min}}$ agrees with the fixed permutation map $ \bm{x} \mapsto \bm{x}[\pi_1 \oplus \dots \oplus \pi_m]. $ By Proposition \ref{prop:permuting-continuous}, this map is continuous, hence measurable. Therefore, by Theorem \ref{thm:measurable-partition}, the restriction of $\varsigma_{\mathrm{min}}$ to $X^n$ is measurable. Since $n$ was arbitrary, another application of \nameref{thm:the-standard-machinery} yields that $\varsigma_{\mathrm{min}}:\mathscr{T}(X) \to \mathscr{S}(X,\preceq)$ is Borel measurable.

nodes.title: Concatenation
nodes.statement: Let $X$ be a set, and let $\mathscr{T}(X)$ be the associated tuple space. The binary operation $\oplus: \mathscr{T}(X)\times \mathscr{T}(X) \to \mathscr{T}(X)$ given by \begin{align*} \bm{x} \oplus \bm{y}: \{1, \dots, \ell(\bm{x}) + \ell(\bm{y})\} &\to X \\ i &\mapsto \begin{cases} \bm{x}(i) & i \in \mathrm{domain}(\bm{x}) \\ \bm{y}(i - \ell(\bm{x})) & i \in \{j +\ell(\bm{x}) \mid j \in \mathrm{domain}(\bm{y})\}. \end{cases} \end{align*} is called the concatenation operator.

motivationContexts.text: So far, we have introduced tuples to represent markets. Moreover, we have shown how to sort a tuple, so that orders within the market are ranked by their execution priority. However, an important component is, of course, to endow the tuple space with operations that mimic the admissible operations within a market, so that our theory will allow for market interaction. In particular, we consider operations that coincide with adding orders to the market, cancelling orders from the market, and modifying orders within the market.
First, we consider the operation which allows us to add orders to the market. Of course, any market participant may submit multiple orders simultaneously.

Concatenation allows for appending one tuple onto another tuple to form a new tuple. In cases where the market does not admit an ordering, one can think of the concatenation map as adding orders into the market in an unsorted fashion; suppose m T(X) represents the current state of the market, and a collection of new orders, o T(X), is submitted to the market. If it is unordered, the new resulting market will be m o. See Figure fig:concat for a visual interpretation.
Of course, in many settings, the market admits an ordering. Therefore, we consider the following extended map on the sorted tuple space.

nodes.title: Sorted Tuple Space forms Commutative Monoid
nodes.statement: Let $(X, \preceq)$ be a totally ordered set. Then the restriction of $+$ from Definition \ref{defn:sorted-tuple-add} to $\mathscr{S}(X, \preceq)\times \mathscr{S}(X, \preceq)$ makes $(\mathscr{S}(X, \preceq), +)$ into a commutative monoid with the cancellation property.

thesisProof.text: We must show that for all $\bm{x},\bm{x}^\prime, \bm{x}^\ast \in \mathscr{S}(X, \preceq)$ that the operation satisfies \begin{enumerate}[(i)] \item Associativity: $(\bm{x} + \bm{x}^\prime) + \bm{x}^\ast = \bm{x} + (\bm{x}^\prime + \bm{x}^\ast)$. \label{property:associative} \item Identity Element: $\bm{x} + \bm{e} = \bm{x}$. \label{property:identity} \item Commutativity: $\bm{x} + \bm{x}^\prime = \bm{x}^\prime + \bm{x}$ \label{property:commutative} \item Right Cancellation: $\bm{x} + \bm{x}^\prime = \bm{x}^\ast + \bm{x}^\prime \text{ implies } \bm{x} = \bm{x}^\ast$ \label{property:right-cancel} \item Left Cancellation: $\bm{x}^\prime + \bm{x} = \bm{x}^\prime +\bm{x}^\ast, \text{ implies } \bm{x} = \bm{x}^\ast$ . \label{property:left-cancel} \end{enumerate} Clearly, \eqref{property:identity} is trivial; since $\bm{x}\oplus \bm{e} = \bm{x}$ and $\bm{x}$ is already sorted, idempotency of the sorting map on $\mathscr{S}(X,\preceq)$ yields $\bm{x} + \bm{e} = \bm{x}$. For \eqref{property:associative}, notice that both $(\bm{x} \oplus \bm{x}^\prime) \oplus \bm{x}^\ast$ and $\bm{x} \oplus (\bm{x}^\prime \oplus \bm{x}^\ast)$ contain exactly the same entries with the same multiplicities. Since sorting with respect to a total order is unique, both expressions sort to the same tuple. The same argument proves \eqref{property:commutative}. Now, from \eqref{property:commutative} it suffices to show \eqref{property:right-cancel}, as \eqref{property:left-cancel} then follows immediately. For each $a \in X$ and each tuple $\bm{z}\in \mathscr{T}(X)$ define the multiplicity \begin{align*} N_a(\bm{z}) = |\{i \in \mathrm{domain}(\bm{z}) \mid \bm{z}(i) = a\}|. \end{align*} Now, sorting does not change multiplicities, and concatenation adds them, i.e., for every $a \in X$ and $\bm{x},\bm{y} \in \mathscr{T}(X)$, \begin{align*} N_a(\bm{x}+\bm{y}) = N_a(\bm{x}) + N_a(\bm{y}). \end{align*} Therefore, if $\bm{x} + \bm{x}^\prime = \bm{x}^\ast + \bm{x}^\prime$, then for every $a \in X$, \begin{align*} N_a(\bm{x}) + N_a(\bm{x}^\prime) = N_a(\bm{x}+\bm{x}^\prime) = N_a(\bm{x}^\ast+\bm{x}^\prime) = N_a(\bm{x}^\ast) + N_a(\bm{x}^\prime), \end{align*} and hence $N_a(\bm{x}) = N_a(\bm{x}^\ast)$. Since both $\bm{x}$ and $\bm{x}^\ast$ are sorted in the same total order, equality of all multiplicities implies $\bm{x} = \bm{x}^\ast$. This proves right cancellation.

proofMoves.text: We must show that for all $\bm{x},\bm{x}^\prime, \bm{x}^\ast \in \mathscr{S}(X, \preceq)$ that the operation satisfies

proofMoves.title: Prove the equality
proofMoves.text: Item: Associativity: $(\bm{x} + \bm{x}^\prime) + \bm{x}^\ast = \bm{x} + (\bm{x}^\prime + \bm{x}^\ast)$.

proofMoves.title: Prove the equality
proofMoves.text: Item: Identity Element: $\bm{x} + \bm{e} = \bm{x}$.

proofMoves.title: Prove the equality
proofMoves.text: Item: Commutativity: $\bm{x} + \bm{x}^\prime = \bm{x}^\prime + \bm{x}$

proofMoves.title: Prove the equality
proofMoves.text: Item: Right Cancellation: $\bm{x} + \bm{x}^\prime = \bm{x}^\ast + \bm{x}^\prime \text{ implies } \bm{x} = \bm{x}^\ast$

proofMoves.title: Verify the order relation
proofMoves.text: Item: Left Cancellation: $\bm{x}^\prime + \bm{x} = \bm{x}^\prime +\bm{x}^\ast, \text{ implies } \bm{x} = \bm{x}^\ast$. Clearly, \eqref{property:identity} is trivial; since $\bm{x}\oplus \bm{e} = \bm{x}$ and $\bm{x}$ is already sorted, idempotency of the sorting map on $\mathscr{S}(X,\preceq)$ yields $\bm{x} + \bm{e} = \bm{x}$. For \eqref{property:associative}, notice that both $(\bm{x} \oplus \bm{x}^\prime) \oplus \bm{x}^\ast$ and $\bm{x} \oplus (\bm{x}^\prime \oplus \bm{x}^\ast)$ contain exactly the same entries with the same multiplicities. Since sorting with respect to a total order is unique, both expressions sort to the same tuple. The same argument proves \eqref{property:commutative}.

proofMoves.title: Reduce to a simpler target
proofMoves.text: Now, from \eqref{property:commutative} it suffices to show \eqref{property:right-cancel}, as \eqref{property:left-cancel} then follows immediately. For each $a \in X$ and each tuple $\bm{z}\in \mathscr{T}(X)$ define the multiplicity $ N_a(\bm{z}) = |\{i \in \mathrm{domain}(\bm{z}) \mid \bm{z}(i) = a\}|. $

proofMoves.title: Verify the order relation
proofMoves.text: Now, sorting does not change multiplicities, and concatenation adds them, i.e., for every $a \in X$ and $\bm{x},\bm{y} \in \mathscr{T}(X)$, $ N_a(\bm{x}+\bm{y}) = N_a(\bm{x}) + N_a(\bm{y}). $ Therefore, if $\bm{x} + \bm{x}^\prime = \bm{x}^\ast + \bm{x}^\prime$, then for every $a \in X$, $ N_a(\bm{x}) + N_a(\bm{x}^\prime) = N_a(\bm{x}+\bm{x}^\prime) = N_a(\bm{x}^\ast+\bm{x}^\prime) = N_a(\bm{x}^\ast) + N_a(\bm{x}^\prime), $ and hence $N_a(\bm{x}) = N_a(\bm{x}^\ast)$. Since both $\bm{x}$ and $\bm{x}^\ast$ are sorted in the same total order, equality of all multiplicities implies $\bm{x} = \bm{x}^\ast$. This proves right cancellation.

The pairing map allows us to re-index tuples: suppose that one or more elements of the graph of a tuple are to be dropped, then the remaining set does not constitute a tuple in general. In particular, if the tuple is not empty, and one or more points in the graph are omitted, then the remaining graph still defines a function. However, in general, it is no longer a tuple as the domain is not guaranteed to be of the form \1,, n\ for some n 1 or the empty set. Therefore, the domain must be changed back into the form \1,,n\ (or the empty set), which a pairing accomplishes in the following way.

nodes.title: Theorem: analytic properties actions
nodes.statement: Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space, and let \begin{enumerate}[-] \item $(\mathscr{T}(X), \mathscr{d}_H)$ be the tuple space over $X$ endowed with the tuple Hausdorff distance. \item $(\mathscr{F}(\mathbb{N}), d_H)$ be the set of finite subsets of the natural numbers, endowed with the Hausdorff distance induced by the Euclidean distance, and \item $(\mathscr{D}(X), d_H^\ast)$ be the set of distinct finite sets over $X$, endowed with the index-augmented Hausdorff distance, and \end{enumerate} When all product spaces are endowed with the product metrics, then \begin{enumerate}[(i)] \item $\oplus:\mathscr{T}(X) \times \mathscr{T}(X) \to \mathscr{T}(X)$ as defined in Definition \ref{defn:concat-tuple} is continuous, \item $\ominus:\mathscr{T}(X)\times \mathscr{F}(\mathbb{N})\to\mathscr{T}(X)$ as defined in Definition \ref{defn:cancel} is continuous, and \item $\circledast:\mathscr{T}(X) \times \mathscr{D}(X) \to \mathscr{T}(X)$ as defined in Definition \ref{defn:modification} is continuous. \end{enumerate}

thesisProof.text:
Let $\varepsilon > 0$ and fix $\delta \in (0,\min(1,\varepsilon))$. For \eqref{property:concat-continuous}, suppose that  egin{align*} \max(\mathscr{d}_H( m{x},  m{x}_0), \mathscr{d}_H( m{y},  m{y}_0)) < \delta. \end{align*} Since $\delta < 1$, 
ameref{thm:the-standard-machinery} implies  egin{align*} m \overset{def}{=} \ell( m{x}) = \ell( m{x}_0) \qquad 	ext{and} \qquad n \overset{def}{=} \ell( m{y}) = \ell( m{y}_0), \end{align*} and the tuple Hausdorff distance collapses to the maximum pointwise metric on each layer. If $m+n = 0$, then both outputs are empty tuples and there is nothing to show. Otherwise,  egin{align*} \mathscr{d}_H( m{x}\oplus m{y},  m{x}_0\oplus m{y}_0) = \max_{i \in \{1,\dots,m+n\}} d ig(( m{x}\oplus m{y})(i),( m{x}_0\oplus m{y}_0)(i) ig) < \delta < \varepsilon. \end{align*} Hence $\oplus$ is continuous. For \eqref{property:cancel-continuous}, suppose that  egin{align*} \max(\mathscr{d}_H( m{x},  m{x}_0), d_H(\eta,\eta_0)) < \delta. \end{align*} Again, $\delta < 1$ implies $\ell( m{x}) = \ell( m{x}_0)$ and  egin{align*} d_H(\eta,\eta_0) < 1 \implies \eta = \eta_0 \end{align*} because $(\mathbb{N},|\cdot|)$ is isolative. Let  egin{align*} I = \mathrm{domain}( m{x}_0)\setminus \eta_0. \end{align*} If $I = \emptyset$, then both $ m{x}\ominus\eta$ and $ m{x}_0\ominus\eta_0$ are empty tuples, so the distance is $0$. Otherwise, if  egin{align*} I = \{i_1 < \dots < i_k\}, \end{align*} then reindexing simply produces the tuples  egin{align*}  m{x}\ominus\eta &= r \mapsto  m{x}(i_r),\  m{x}_0\ominus\eta_0 &= r \mapsto  m{x}_0(i_r), \end{align*} and therefore  egin{align*} \mathscr{d}_H( m{x}\ominus\eta,  m{x}_0\ominus\eta_0) = \max_{r\in\{1,\dots,k\}} d( m{x}(i_r),  m{x}_0(i_r)) \leq \max_{i \in \mathrm{domain}( m{x}_0)} d( m{x}(i),  m{x}_0(i)) < \delta < \varepsilon. \end{align*} Hence $\ominus$ is continuous. Finally, consider \eqref{property:modification-continuous} and suppose that  egin{align*} \max(\mathscr{d}_H( m{x},  m{x}_0), d_H^\ast(\xi,\xi_0)) < \delta. \end{align*} Since $\delta < 1$, the tuple part gives $\ell( m{x}) = \ell( m{x}_0)$, and the indexed Hausdorff part implies that $\xi$ and $\xi_0$ have exactly the same set of indices. Denote this common finite index set by  egin{align*} D = \mathrm{domain}(\xi) = \mathrm{domain}(\xi_0). \end{align*} Moreover, for every $n \in D$ there are unique elements $\xi(n), \xi_0(n) \in X$ with  egin{align*} (n,\xi(n)) \in \xi \qquad 	ext{and} \qquad (n,\xi_0(n)) \in \xi_0, \end{align*} and they satisfy  egin{align*} d(\xi(n),\xi_0(n)) < \delta. \end{align*} Now let $m = \ell( m{x}_0) = \ell( m{x})$. For each $i \in \{1,\dots,m\}$ there are two cases. If $i 
otin D$, then  egin{align*} ( m{x}\circledast \xi)(i) =  m{x}(i) \qquad 	ext{and} \qquad ( m{x}_0\circledast \xi_0)(i) =  m{x}_0(i). \end{align*} If $i \in D$, then  egin{align*} ( m{x}\circledast \xi)(i) = \xi(i) \qquad 	ext{and} \qquad ( m{x}_0\circledast \xi_0)(i) = \xi_0(i). \end{align*} Hence, for every $i \in \{1,\dots,m\}$,  egin{align*} d ig(( m{x}\circledast \xi)(i), ( m{x}_0\circledast \xi_0)(i) ig) < \delta. \end{align*} By 
ameref{thm:the-standard-machinery}, the output tuples lie on the same length layer, so  egin{align*} \mathscr{d}_H( m{x}\circledast \xi,  m{x}_0\circledast \xi_0) = \max_{i\in\{1,\dots,m\}} d ig(( m{x}\circledast \xi)(i), ( m{x}_0\circledast \xi_0)(i) ig) < \delta < \varepsilon. \end{align*} Therefore, $\circledast$ is continuous.

proofMoves.title: Transfer continuity
proofMoves.text: Let $\varepsilon > 0$ and fix $\delta \in (0,\min(1,\varepsilon))$. For \eqref{property:concat-continuous}, suppose that $ \max(\mathscr{d}_H(\bm{x}, \bm{x}_0), \mathscr{d}_H(\bm{y}, \bm{y}_0)) < \delta. $ Since $\delta < 1$, \nameref{thm:the-standard-machinery} implies $ m \overset{def}{=} \ell(\bm{x}) = \ell(\bm{x}_0) \qquad \text{and} \qquad n \overset{def}{=} \ell(\bm{y}) = \ell(\bm{y}_0), $ and the tuple Hausdorff distance collapses to the maximum pointwise metric on each layer. If $m+n = 0$, then both outputs are empty tuples and there is nothing to show. Otherwise, $ \mathscr{d}_H(\bm{x}\oplus\bm{y}, \bm{x}_0\oplus\bm{y}_0) = \max_{i \in \{1,\dots,m+n\}} d\big((\bm{x}\oplus\bm{y})(i),(\bm{x}_0\oplus\bm{y}_0)(i)\big) < \delta < \varepsilon. $ Hence $\oplus$ is continuous. For \eqref{property:cancel-continuous}, suppose that $ \max(\mathscr{d}_H(\bm{x}, \bm{x}_0), d_H(\eta,\eta_0)) < \delta. $ Again, $\delta < 1$ implies $\ell(\bm{x}) = \ell(\bm{x}_0)$ and $ d_H(\eta,\eta_0) < 1 \implies \eta = \eta_0 $ because $(\mathbb{N},|\cdot|)$ is isolative. Let $ I = \mathrm{domain}(\bm{x}_0)\setminus \eta_0. $ If $I = \emptyset$, then both $\bm{x}\ominus\eta$ and $\bm{x}_0\ominus\eta_0$ are empty tuples, so the distance is $0$. Otherwise, if $ I = \{i_1 < \dots < i_k\}, $ then reindexing simply produces the tuples $ \bm{x}\ominus\eta &= r \mapsto \bm{x}(i_r),\\ \bm{x}_0\ominus\eta_0 &= r \mapsto \bm{x}_0(i_r), $ and therefore $ \mathscr{d}_H(\bm{x}\ominus\eta, \bm{x}_0\ominus\eta_0) = \max_{r\in\{1,\dots,k\}} d(\bm{x}(i_r), \bm{x}_0(i_r)) \leq \max_{i \in \mathrm{domain}(\bm{x}_0)} d(\bm{x}(i), \bm{x}_0(i)) < \delta < \varepsilon. $ Hence $\ominus$ is continuous.

proofMoves.title: Transfer continuity
proofMoves.text: Finally, consider \eqref{property:modification-continuous} and suppose that $ \max(\mathscr{d}_H(\bm{x}, \bm{x}_0), d_H^\ast(\xi,\xi_0)) < \delta. $ Since $\delta < 1$, the tuple part gives $\ell(\bm{x}) = \ell(\bm{x}_0)$, and the indexed Hausdorff part implies that $\xi$ and $\xi_0$ have exactly the same set of indices. Denote this common finite index set by $ D = \mathrm{domain}(\xi) = \mathrm{domain}(\xi_0). $ Moreover, for every $n \in D$ there are unique elements $\xi(n), \xi_0(n) \in X$ with $ (n,\xi(n)) \in \xi \qquad \text{and} \qquad (n,\xi_0(n)) \in \xi_0, $ and they satisfy $ d(\xi(n),\xi_0(n)) < \delta. $

proofMoves.title: Transfer continuity
proofMoves.text: Now let $m = \ell(\bm{x}_0) = \ell(\bm{x})$. For each $i \in \{1,\dots,m\}$ there are two cases. If $i \notin D$, then $ (\bm{x}\circledast \xi)(i) = \bm{x}(i) \qquad \text{and} \qquad (\bm{x}_0\circledast \xi_0)(i) = \bm{x}_0(i). $ If $i \in D$, then $ (\bm{x}\circledast \xi)(i) = \xi(i) \qquad \text{and} \qquad (\bm{x}_0\circledast \xi_0)(i) = \xi_0(i). $ Hence, for every $i \in \{1,\dots,m\}$, $ d\big((\bm{x}\circledast \xi)(i), (\bm{x}_0\circledast \xi_0)(i)\big) < \delta. $ By \nameref{thm:the-standard-machinery}, the output tuples lie on the same length layer, so $ \mathscr{d}_H(\bm{x}\circledast \xi, \bm{x}_0\circledast \xi_0) = \max_{i\in\{1,\dots,m\}} d\big((\bm{x}\circledast \xi)(i), (\bm{x}_0\circledast \xi_0)(i)\big) < \delta < \varepsilon. $ Therefore, $\circledast$ is continuous.

nodes.title: Corollary: sorted operations measurable
nodes.statement: Let $(X, \preceq, d)$ be a complete and separable metric space endowed with a Borel partial order. Let $\varsigma :\mathscr{T}(X) \to \mathscr{S}(X,\preceq)$ be an idempotent measurable sorting map. Then, the following hold when all relevant product spaces are endowed with the product Borel $\sigma$-algebra. \begin{enumerate}[-] \item $(\mathscr{T}(X), \mathscr{d}_H)$ be the tuple space over $X$ endowed with the tuple Hausdorff distance. \item $\mathscr{S}(X, \preceq) \subseteq \mathscr{T}(X)$ be the space of sorted tuples. \item $(\mathscr{F}(\mathbb{N}), d_H)$ be the set of finite subsets of the natural numbers, endowed with the Hausdorff distance induced by the Euclidean distance, and \item $(\mathscr{D}(X), d_H^\ast)$ be the set of distinct finite sets over $X$, endowed with the index-augmented Hausdorff distance, and \item $\varsigma:\mathscr{T}(X) \to \mathscr{S}(X,\preceq)$ be a measurable sorting map. \end{enumerate} Then, \begin{enumerate}[(i)] \item $+:\mathscr{T}(X) \times \mathscr{T}(X) \to \mathscr{S}(X, \preceq)$ as defined in Definition \ref{defn:sorted-tuple-add} is measurable, \item $-:\mathscr{T}(X)\times \mathscr{F}(\mathbb{N})\to\mathscr{S}(X,\preceq)$ as defined in Definition \ref{defn:sorted-cancel} is measurable, and \item $\ast:\mathscr{T}(X) \times \mathscr{D}(X) \to \mathscr{S}(X,\preceq)$ as defined in Definition \ref{defn:modification} is measurable. \end{enumerate}

nodes.title: Corollary: action metrization
nodes.statement: Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space. Let $A = \{\oplus, \ominus, \circledast\}$ be the set of operations defined in Definitions \ref{defn:concat-tuple}, \ref{defn:cancel}, and \ref{defn:modification}, respectively. Let \begin{align*} F_\alpha = \begin{cases} \mathscr{T}(X) & \alpha = \oplus\\ \mathscr{F}(\mathbb{N}) & \alpha = \ominus \\ \mathscr{D}(X) &\alpha = \circledast \end{cases},\quad\quad d_\alpha = \begin{cases} \mathscr{d}_H & \alpha = \oplus\\ d_H & \alpha = \ominus \\ d_H^\ast &\alpha = \circledast \end{cases},\quad\quad \end{align*} and let $\mathscr{A}(X) = \bigsqcup_{\alpha \in A} F_\alpha$ and let $\Delta : \mathscr{A}(X)\times \mathscr{A}(X) \to [0,\infty]$ defined by \begin{align*} \Delta((o,\alpha),(o^\prime,\alpha^\prime))=\begin{cases} d_\alpha(o,o^\prime)&\alpha = \alpha^\prime \\ \infty &\alpha \neq \alpha^\prime. \end{cases} \end{align*} Then $(\mathscr{A}(X), \Delta)$ is a metric space. Moreover, if $(X,d)$ is complete, then so is $(\mathscr{A}(X), \Delta)$. Likewise, if $(X,d)$ is separable, then so is $(\mathscr{A}(X), \Delta)$.

thesisProof.text: By Proposition \ref{prop:disjoint-union-metrization}, $\Delta$ is indeed a metric on the disjoint union $\mathscr{A}(X)$. If $(X,d)$ is complete, then $(\mathscr{T}(X),\mathscr{d}_H)$ is complete by Theorem \ref{thm:tuple-space-metrization}, $(\mathscr{D}(X), d_H^\ast)$ is complete by Proposition \ref{prop:index-augmented-hausdorff}, and $(\mathscr{F}(\mathbb{N}), d_H)$ is complete because $(\mathbb{N},|\cdot|)$ is isolative, hence Proposition \ref{prop:finite-hausdorff-isolative} makes $\mathscr{F}(\mathbb{N})$ isolative and Proposition \ref{prop:isolative-finite-sets-complete} then yields completeness. Therefore, Proposition \ref{prop:disjoint-union-metric-properties} implies that $(\mathscr{A}(X),\Delta)$ is complete. If $(X,d)$ is separable, then $(\mathscr{T}(X),\mathscr{d}_H)$ is separable by Theorem \ref{thm:tuple-space-metrization}, $(\mathscr{D}(X), d_H^\ast)$ is separable by Proposition \ref{prop:index-augmented-hausdorff}, and $(\mathscr{F}(\mathbb{N}), d_H)$ is separable by Proposition \ref{prop:finite-separable}, since $(\mathbb{N},|\cdot|)$ is countable and hence separable. Another application of Proposition \ref{prop:disjoint-union-metric-properties} then yields that $(\mathscr{A}(X),\Delta)$ is separable.

nodes.statement: Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space and let $(\mathscr{A}(X), \Delta)$ denote the action space endowed with the metric as in Corollary \ref{cor:action-metrization}. nodes.title: Theorem: composite application continuous
nodes.statement: Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space, $(\mathscr{T}(X), \mathscr{d}_H)$ be the associated tuple Hausdorff space, and let $(\mathscr{C}(X), \Delta_H)$ be the space of composite actions with the metric as defined in Theorem \ref{thm:composite-action-metric}. Then, the extended application map $\lhd :\mathscr{T}(X) \times \mathscr{C}(X)\to\mathscr{T}(X)$ is defined by $\bm{x} \lhd \bm{c} = \bm{x}$ if $\bm{c} = \bm{e}$, otherwise define $\bm{x}_0 = \bm{x}$ and define recursively \begin{align} \bm{x}_i = \bm{x}_{i-1} \lhd \bm{c}(i) \end{align} for $i \in \{1,\dots, \ell(\bm{c})\}$, and subsequently define $\bm{x} \lhd \bm{c} = \bm{x}_{\ell(\bm{c})}$, where the application operation, $\lhd$, in \eqref{eq:recursive-application-composite} is the application map defined in Definition \ref{defn:actions}. Then, $\lhd :\mathscr{T}(X) \times \mathscr{C}(X) \to \mathscr{T}(X)$ is continuous.

thesisProof.text: For each $n \in \mathbb{N}_0$, let \begin{align*} \mathscr{C}_n(X) = \{\bm{c} \in \mathscr{C}(X) \mid \ell(\bm{c}) = n\}. \end{align*} By \nameref{thm:the-standard-machinery}, each layer $\mathscr{C}_n(X)$ is homeomorphic to the finite product $\mathscr{A}(X)^n$ endowed with the maximum product metric. Define recursively continuous maps \begin{align*} F_n : \mathscr{T}(X) \times \mathscr{A}(X)^n \to \mathscr{T}(X) \end{align*} by \begin{align*} F_0(\bm{x}) &= \bm{x},\\ F_n(\bm{x}, a_1,\dots,a_n) &= F_{n-1}(\bm{x}, a_1,\dots,a_{n-1}) \lhd a_n \end{align*} for $n \geq 1$. The map $F_0$ is continuous, and if $F_{n-1}$ is continuous, then $F_n$ is continuous by Proposition \ref{prop:application-continuous}. Hence $F_n$ is continuous for every $n$. Under the identification of $\mathscr{C}_n(X)$ with $\mathscr{A}(X)^n$, the restriction of the extended application map \begin{align*} \lhd : \mathscr{T}(X)\times \mathscr{C}(X) \to \mathscr{T}(X) \end{align*} to $\mathscr{T}(X)\times \mathscr{C}_n(X)$ is exactly $F_n$. Therefore, the restriction to each fixed-length layer is continuous. Finally, the composite-action space is the disjoint union of its length layers, \begin{align*} \mathscr{C}(X) = \bigsqcup_{n\in\mathbb{N}_0} \mathscr{C}_n(X), \end{align*} and the tuple metric is topologically equivalent to the corresponding disjoint-union metric by \nameref{thm:the-standard-machinery}. The continuity of the global map therefore follows from the pasting lemma for disjoint unions.

nodes.title: Proposition: characteristic functions tuple
nodes.statement: Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space, $(\mathscr{T}(X),\mathscr{d}_H)$ the Hausdorff tuple space, and let $(\mathscr{F}(\mathbb{N}), d_H)$ be the set of finite subsets of $\mathbb{N}$. For any family $(\chi_i)_{i\in\mathbb{N}}$ of functions such that $\chi_i:X \to \{0,1\}$ is a $\mathcal{B}(X)/\wp(\{0,1\})$ measurable function for each $i \in \mathbb{N}$, the mapping $\chi : \mathscr{T}(X) \to \mathscr{F}(\mathbb{N})$ defined by \begin{align*} \chi(\bm{x}) = \{ i \in \mathrm{domain}(\bm{x}) \mid \chi_i(\bm{x}(i)) = 1\} \end{align*} is $\mathcal{B}(\mathscr{T}(X))/\mathcal{B}(\mathscr{F}(\mathbb{N}))$ measurable.

thesisProof.text: First, note that by \nameref{thm:the-standard-machinery}, the fact that $\mathscr{T}(X)$ is homeomorphic to $\bigsqcup_{n \in \mathbb{N}_0} X^n$, and Theorem \ref{thm:pasting-lemma-measurable}, it suffices to show, that it holds for any fixed product space endowed with the product Borel $\sigma$-algebra induced by the maximum distance. Therefore, let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ be fixed; the case $n = 0$ is trivial, and therefore omitted. Now, we must show that for any $B \in \mathcal{B}(\mathscr{F}(\mathbb{N}))$ \begin{align*} \chi^{-1}(\{\eta \cap \{1,\dots, n\} \mid \eta \in B\}) \in \mathcal{B}(X^n). \end{align*} However, by Proposition \ref{prop:countable-finite-sets}, note that $B \subseteq\mathscr{F}(\mathbb{N})$ is always countable. As $\sigma$-algebras are closed under countable unions, and \begin{align*} \chi^{-1}(\{\eta \cap \{1,\dots, n\} \mid \eta \in B\}) =\bigcup_{\eta \in B}\chi^{-1}(\{\eta \cap \{1,\dots, n\}\}), \end{align*} it suffices to show that \begin{align*} \chi^{-1}(\{\eta\cap \{1,\dots, n\}\}) \in \mathcal{B}(X^n) \end{align*} for all $\eta \in \mathscr{F}(\mathbb{N})$. Now, for any $\eta \in \mathscr{F}(\mathbb{N})$ define \begin{align*} E_i^\eta = \{\bm{x}:\{1,\dots,n\} \to X \mid \chi_i(\bm{x}(i)) = \mathbbm{1}_\eta(i)\}, \end{align*} for all $i \in \{1,\dots, n\}$. Note that if $i \in \eta$, then $E^\eta_i$ contains all the $n$-tuples where $\chi_i(\bm{x}(i)) =1$. Now, clearly $E_i^\eta$ is measurable for all $i \in \{1,\dots,n\}$, since each $\chi_i$ is measurable. However, as $\sigma$-algebras are closed under finite intersections, it follows that \begin{align*} \bigcap_{i=1}^n E_i^\eta \in \mathcal{B}(X^n). \end{align*} However, by construction, we have that \begin{align*} \chi^{-1}(\{\eta\cap \{1,\dots, n\}\}) = \bigcap_{i=1}^n E_i^\eta, \end{align*} which proves the claim, as the choice of $n \in \mathbb{N}$ was arbitrary.

nodes.title: Proposition: tuple projection continuous
nodes.statement: Let $(X_\alpha, d_\alpha)_{\alpha\in A}$ be a finite non-empty family of metric spaces, $X = \prod_{\alpha\in A} X_\alpha$ and let $d: X \times X \to [0,\infty]$ be the maximum product metric on $X$. Let $(\mathscr{T}(X_\alpha), \mathscr{d}_{H,\alpha})_{\alpha \in A}$ be the associated Hausdorff tuple spaces, and let $(\mathscr{T}(X), \mathscr{d}_H)$ be the tuple space associated to $(X,d)$. Then, \begin{enumerate} \item the projection $\bm{P}_\alpha :\mathscr{T}(X) \to \mathscr{T}(X_\alpha)$ is continuous for every $\alpha \in A$. \item the tuple decomposition $\bm{P}:\mathscr{T}(X) \to \prod_{\alpha \in A}\mathscr{T}(X_\alpha)$ is continuous, whenever $\prod_{\alpha \in A}\mathscr{T}(X_\alpha)$ is endowed with the product topology. \item The mapping $\bm{P}$ is injective, and hence invertible on its image. \end{enumerate}

thesisProof.text: First, we must show, that for every $\varepsilon > 0$ and $\bm{x}_0 \in \mathscr{T}(X)$ there exists a $\delta >0$ such that \begin{align*} \mathscr{d}_H(\bm{x},\bm{x}_0) < \delta \implies \mathscr{d}_{H,\alpha}(\bm{P}_\alpha\bm{x}, \bm{P}_\alpha\bm{x}_0) < \varepsilon, \end{align*} but one easily verifies that \begin{align*} \mathscr{d}_{H,\alpha}(\bm{P}_\alpha\bm{x}, \bm{P}_\alpha\bm{x}_0) \leq \mathscr{d}_H(\bm{x},\bm{x}_0), \end{align*} and so for a given $\varepsilon > 0$ one can choose $\delta = \varepsilon$. Note that the second assertion follows trivially from the first, as one leverages the maximum metric to generate the product topology. It remains to show that $\bm{P}$ is injective. Let $\bm{x}, \bm{x}^\prime \in \mathscr{T}(X)$ and assume that \begin{align*} \bm{P}(\bm{x}) = \bm{P}(\bm{x}^\prime). \end{align*} Then $\bm{P}_\alpha \bm{x} = \bm{P}_\alpha \bm{x}^\prime$ for every $\alpha \in A$. Since $A$ is non-empty, fix $\alpha_0 \in A$. The equality $\bm{P}_{\alpha_0}\bm{x} = \bm{P}_{\alpha_0}\bm{x}^\prime$ implies that \begin{align*} \mathrm{domain}(\bm{x}) = \mathrm{domain}(\bm{P}_{\alpha_0}\bm{x}) = \mathrm{domain}(\bm{P}_{\alpha_0}\bm{x}^\prime) = \mathrm{domain}(\bm{x}^\prime). \end{align*} Now let $i \in \mathrm{domain}(\bm{x}) = \mathrm{domain}(\bm{x}^\prime)$. nodes.title: Proposition: minimal sorting measurable
nodes.statement: For $\preceq \in \{\leq, \geq\}$, where $\{\leq, \geq\}$ are the typical relations on $\mathbb{R}$, the $\preceq$-minimal permutation map is a Borel measurable map between $\mathscr{T}(\mathbb{R})$ and the set of finite permutations, $\mathscr{P}$, where both are endowed with the tuple Hausdorff distance induced by the Euclidean distance.

thesisProof.text:
We must show, that for any $B\in \mathcal{B}(\mathscr{P})$, it holds that  egin{align*} (\pi^\preceq)^{-1}(B) \in \mathcal{B}(\mathscr{T}(\mathbb{R})). \end{align*} First, notice that $\mathcal{B}(\mathscr{P})$ is equal to the power set, $\wp(\mathscr{P})$, as each singleton $\{\pi\}\in \mathcal{B}(\mathscr{P})$ and each subset $B \subseteq \mathscr{P}$ is countable and may hence be written by  egin{align*} B =  igcup_{\pi \in B} \{\pi\}. \end{align*} In particular, by Proposition ef{prop:permutations-countable}, the set $\mathscr{P}$ is countable. By extension, $B \subseteq \mathscr{P}$ is countable and, as $\sigma$-algebras are closed under countable unions, it suffices to prove that  egin{align*} (\pi^\preceq)^{-1}(\{\pi\}) \in \mathcal{B}(\mathscr{T}(\mathbb{R})), \end{align*} for any $\pi \in \mathscr{P}$. Let $\mathscr{W}_\pi$ be the set defined by  egin{align*} \mathscr{W}_\pi = (\pi^\preceq)^{-1}(\{\pi\}) =\{ m{x} \in \mathscr{T}(\mathbb{R}) \mid \pi^\preceq( m{x}) = \pi\}. \end{align*} Now, notice that since $\ell(\pi)$ is fixed, one immediately has  egin{align*} \mathscr{W}_\pi = \{ m{x} \in \mathbb{R}^{\ell(\pi)} \mid \pi^\preceq( m{x}) = \pi\} \subseteq \mathbb{R}^{\ell(\pi)}. \end{align*} Now, naturally, any set that is Borel in $\mathbb{R}^n$ for some $n \in \mathbb{N}$ will also be Borel in $\mathscr{T}(\mathbb{R})$ due to 
ameref{thm:the-standard-machinery}. To this end, let $n = \ell(\pi)$ and define  egin{align*} D_{k-1}^\pi =\{\pi(j) \mid j \in \{k, \dots, n\}\}, \end{align*} and, by extension, the sets  egin{align*} A^\pi_k = igcap_{j \in D_{k-1}^\pi} \{ m{x}\in \mathbb{R}^n \mid  m{x}(\pi(k))\preceq m{x}(j)\}, \end{align*} which is measurable because, for each fixed $j$, the set $\{ m{x}\in \mathbb{R}^n \mid  m{x}(\pi(k))\preceq m{x}(j)\}$ is Borel. Moreover, define  egin{align*} B^{\pi}_k =  igcap_{\substack{j \in D^\pi_{k-1}\j < \pi(k)}} \{ m{x}\in \mathbb{R}^n \mid  m{x}(\pi(k)) 
eq  m{x}(j)\}, \end{align*} which is measurable as the diagonal is closed in $\mathbb{R}^2$, and finite intersections of measurable sets are measurable. However, notice that  egin{align*} \mathscr{W}_\pi = igcap_{k = 1}^n (A^\pi_k \cap B^\pi_k); \end{align*} to see why, note that $A^\pi_k$ contains all the tuples, where $\pi(k)$ attains the $k^{\mathrm{th}}$ minimizer for the tuples. The set $B^\pi_k$, on the other hand, breaks ties preferring the minimum index first. To see why, note that $j \in D_{k-1}^\pi = \{\pi(k), \dots, \pi(n)\}$, we may write $j = \pi(m)$ for $k < m$. Consequently, we may write  egin{align*} B_k^\pi =  igcap_{\substack{m \in \{k+1, \dots, n\}\ \pi(m) < \pi(k)}}\{ m{x}\in \mathbb{R}^n \mid  m{x}(\pi(k))
eq  m{x}(\pi(m)) \}, \end{align*} which can be interpreted as follows: the set  egin{align*} \{ m{x}\in \mathbb{R}^n \mid  m{x}(\pi(k))
eq  m{x}(\pi(m))\}, \end{align*} simply says that, under the permutation, $ m{x}(\pi(k))$ and $ m{x}(\pi(m))$ are not equal. Under the intersection condition, $B^\pi_k$ enforces the tie-breaking rule that smaller original indices are chosen first. In other words, if there were an $m \in \{k+1, \dots, n\}$ such that $ m{x}(\pi(k)) =  m{x}(\pi(m))$ but $\pi(m) < \pi(k)$, then $\pi^\preceq( m{x})$ would have selected $\pi(m)$ before $\pi(k)$, a contradiction. Now, clearly, $A_k^\pi$ and $B_k^\pi$ are Borel sets for each $k \in \{1,\dots, n\}$. Hence, $\mathscr{W}_\pi$ is a finite intersection of Borel sets and hence Borel.

nodes.title: Lemma: cumulative summation continuous
nodes.statement: Let $(\mathscr{T}([0,\infty)), \mathscr{d}_H)$ denote the tuple Hausdorff space over the the positive reals and define the cumulative summation function by \begin{align*} &\bm{\Sigma} : \mathscr{T}([0,\infty)) \to \mathscr{T}([0,\infty))\\ &\bm{\Sigma}(\bm{x}) = i \mapsto \sum_{j=1}^i \bm{x}(j), \end{align*} where $i \in \mathrm{domain}(\bm{x})$. Then, $\bm{\Sigma}$ is continuous.

thesisProof.text: Note that for each $n \in \mathbb{N}$ the linear transformation $S_n:\mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^n$ defined by the matrix \begin{align*} (S_n)_{i,j} = \begin{cases} 1 & j \leq i\\ 0 & j > i \end{cases}, \end{align*} is naturally continuous. However, $\bm{\Sigma} \restriction_{\mathbb{R}^n} = S_n$ and so, by \nameref{thm:the-standard-machinery}, the result follows.

nodes.title: Lemma: increasing decreasing measurable
nodes.statement: For any $n \in \mathbb{N}$, the sets \begin{align*} I_n = \{x\in \mathbb{R}^n \mid x_1 \leq \dots \leq x_n\}, \end{align*} and \begin{align*} D_n =\{x\in \mathbb{R}^n \mid x_1 \geq \dots \geq x_n\} \end{align*} are Borel measurable sets in $\mathbb{R}^n$.

thesisProof.text: Without loss of generality, assume that $n \geq 2$, as otherwise the statement is tautological. First, notice that the functions \begin{align*} \Delta_{i,j} :\mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}, \end{align*} defined by \begin{align*} \Delta_{i,j}(x) = x_i - x_j \end{align*} are Borel measurable, as the difference is continuous. Now, notice that \begin{align*} I_n = \bigcap_{i =2}^n \Delta_{i, i-1}^{-1}([0,\infty)), \end{align*} which is a finite intersection of measurable sets and hence measurable. Likewise, \begin{align*} D_n = \bigcap_{i=2}^n \Delta_{i, i-1}^{-1}((-\infty,0]) \end{align*} is a finite intersection of measurable sets and hence measurable.

nodes.title: Lemma: bounded sets measurable
nodes.statement: For any $n,m \in \mathbb{N}$ and $(i,j) \in \{1,\dots, n\}\times \{1,\dots, m\}$ the sets \begin{align*} L^{i,j}_{n,m} = \{(x,y) \in I_n\times D_m \mid x_i \leq y_j\} \end{align*} and \begin{align*} G^{i,j}_{n,m} = \{(x,y) \in I_n\times D_m \mid x_i > y_j\}, \end{align*} where $I_n$ and $D_m$ are defined as in Lemma \ref{lem:increasing-decreasing-measurable}, are Borel measurable sets in $\mathbb{R}^n \times \mathbb{R}^m$.

thesisProof.text: Similarly to the proof of Lemma \ref{lem:increasing-decreasing-measurable}, define \begin{align*} \Delta_{i,j}(x,y) = y_j - x_i, \end{align*} which for each $i \in \{1,\dots, n\}$ and $j \in \{1,\dots,m\}$ is a continuous function and hence Borel measurable. But now, notice that \begin{align*} L_{n,m}^{i,j} = \Delta_{i,j}^{-1}([0,\infty)) \cap (I_n\times D_m), \end{align*} and likewise \begin{align*} G_{n,m}^{i,j} = \Delta_{i,j}^{-1}((-\infty,0)) \cap (I_n \times D_m). \end{align*} are measurable, as $(I_n \times D_m) \in \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^n)\otimes\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^m) =\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^n \times \mathbb{R}^m)$ and each $\Delta_{i,j}$ is continuous and hence measurable. Finally, the intersection between measurable sets is also measurable as desired.

nodes.statement: Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space, and let $\mathcal{M}(X)$ denote the family of finite measures on $(X,\mathcal{B}(X))$. Let $\rho:\mathcal{M}(X) \times \mathcal{M}(X) \to [0,\infty]$ be the function defined by \begin{align*} \rho(\mu, \eta) = \inf \{ \varepsilon > 0 \mid \forall B \in \mathcal{B}(X): \mu(B) \leq \eta(B^\varepsilon) + \varepsilon \mathrm{~and~}\eta(B) \leq \mu(B^\varepsilon) + \varepsilon\}. \end{align*} Then, $(\mathcal{M}(X), \rho)$ is a metric space, and $\rho$ is called the Prokhorov metric. Moreover, \begin{enumerate}[(i)] \item A sequence $(\mu_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}} \subseteq \mathcal{M}(X)$ converges weakly to $\mu \in \mathcal{M}(X) $ if, and only if, $\lim_{n \to \infty}\rho(\mu_n,\mu) = 0$. \item If $(X,d)$ is a complete and separable metric space, then so is $(\mathcal{M}(X), \rho)$. \item If $(X,d)$ is a complete and separable metric space, then so is $(\mathcal{N}(X), \rho)$. \end{enumerate}

nodes.title: Atomic Decomposition of Finite Integer Measures
nodes.statement: Let $(X,\Sigma)$ be a standard Borel space, then every $\xi \in \mathcal{N}(X)$ has the representation \begin{align*} \xi = \sum_{k \leq \kappa} \beta_k \delta_{x_k} \end{align*} where $\kappa \in \mathbb{N}_0$, $(\beta_k)_{k = 1}^\kappa \subset \mathbb{N}$, $(x_k)_{k = 1}^\kappa \subseteq X$ are distinct, and $\delta_x$ is the Dirac measure concentrated in $x$. For $\kappa \leq 1$ the representation is unique, otherwise the representation is unique up to permutations of $\{1, \dots, \kappa\}$.

nodes.title: Lemma: helpful point process
nodes.statement: Let $(X, \Sigma)$ be a standard Borel space and let $(\mathcal{N}(X), \rho)$ be the associated space of finite integer-valued measures endowed with the Prokhorov metric. Then, for all $\xi, \eta \in \mathcal{N}(X)$ and $\varepsilon \in (0,1)$ with $\rho(\xi, \eta) < \varepsilon$ we have \begin{enumerate}[(i)] \item $\xi(B) \leq \eta(B^\varepsilon)$ \item $\eta(B) \leq \xi(B^\varepsilon)$ \item $\xi(X) = \eta(X)$ \end{enumerate}

thesisProof.text: \textbf{Proof of \eqref{eq:lem-helpful-point-process-1} and \eqref{eq:lem-helpful-point-process-2}:} It suffices to show \eqref{eq:lem-helpful-point-process-1}, as \eqref{eq:lem-helpful-point-process-2} is analogous. Let $\varepsilon \in (0,1)$ satisfy $\rho(\xi,\eta)<\varepsilon$. By the definition of the Prokhorov metric, there exists $\delta \in (0,\varepsilon)$ such that \begin{align*} \xi(B) \leq \eta(B^\delta) + \delta \end{align*} for every $B \in \mathcal{B}(X)$. Since $B^\delta \subseteq B^\varepsilon$, it follows that \begin{align*} \xi(B) \leq \eta(B^\varepsilon) + \delta. \end{align*} Now $\xi(B)$ and $\eta(B^\varepsilon)$ are integers and $\delta < 1$, so the above inequality implies \begin{align*} \xi(B) \leq \eta(B^\varepsilon), \end{align*} which proves \eqref{eq:lem-helpful-point-process-1}. \textbf{Proof of \eqref{eq:lem-helpful-point-process-3}:} Apply \eqref{eq:lem-helpful-point-process-1} and \eqref{eq:lem-helpful-point-process-2} with $B=X$. Since $X^\varepsilon = X$, we obtain \begin{align*} \xi(X) \leq \eta(X) \quad \text{and} \quad \eta(X) \leq \xi(X), \end{align*} which implies that $\xi(X) = \eta(X)$.

nodes.title: Lemma: disintegration lemma
nodes.statement: Let $(X,d)$ be a complete and separable metric space, and let $(\mathcal{N}(X), \rho)$ be the associated Prokhorov space of finite integer valued measures on $(X, \mathcal{B}(X))$. Let $\xi \in \mathcal{N}(X)$ be a non-zero measure with atomic decomposition \begin{align*} \xi = \sum_{k\leq \kappa} \beta_k \delta_{x_k}. \end{align*} Let \begin{align*} \gamma = \begin{cases} 1 & \kappa = 1,\\ \min\left(\frac{1}{2} \min_{\substack{k, k^\prime \leq \kappa \\ k \neq k^\prime}} d(x_k, x_{k^\prime}), 1 \right) & \kappa \geq 2, \end{cases} \end{align*} and $0 < \varepsilon < \gamma$. Then, let $\eta \in \mathcal{N}(X)$ be another non-zero measure with atomic decomposition \begin{align*} \eta = \sum_{l\leq \lambda} \alpha_l \delta_{y_l}. \end{align*} Then if $\rho(\xi, \eta) < \varepsilon$ we have \begin{enumerate}[(i)] \item For every $k \in \{1,\dots,\kappa\}$ there exists $L_k \subset \{1,\dots ,\lambda\}$ such that $\beta_k = \sum_{l \in L_k} \alpha_l$. \item For every $k, k^\prime \in \{1,\dots, \kappa\}:k\neq k^\prime$ it holds that $L_k \cap L_{k^\prime} = \emptyset$. \item For every $k \in \{1,\dots, \kappa\}$ and $l \in L_k$ it holds that $\max_{l \in L_k} d(x_k, y_l) < \varepsilon$. \end{enumerate}

thesisProof.text:
First, note that since $(X,d)$ is a complete and separable metric space, the Borel $\sigma$-algebra contains all singletons as well as all open balls $B_\varepsilon(x) = \{x^\prime \in X \mid d(x,x^\prime) < \varepsilon\}$. Now, we will prove the properties simultaneously; let $k \in \{1,\dots, \kappa\}$ be arbitrary, and note that  egin{align*} \{x_k\} \in \mathcal{B}(X). \end{align*} and  egin{align*} \{x_k\}^\varepsilon = B_\varepsilon(x_k) \in \mathcal{B}(X). \end{align*} Now, recall that $ho(\xi, \eta) < \varepsilon < 1$ implies that  egin{align*} \xi(B) \leq \eta(B^\varepsilon), \end{align*} by Lemma ef{lem:helpful-point-process}. In particular, the above yields the bound  egin{align*} \xi(\{x_k\}) =  eta_k \leq \eta(B_\varepsilon(x_k)), \end{align*} for all $k \leq \kappa$ by definition of the Prokhorov metric. In addition, since $\varepsilon < \gamma$ it moreover holds that  egin{align*} \eta(B_\varepsilon(x_k)) \leq \xi((B_{\varepsilon}(x_k))^{\varepsilon}) = \xi(B_{2\varepsilon}(x_k)) =  eta_k, \end{align*} and hence  egin{align*}  eta_k = \eta(B_\varepsilon(x_k)). \end{align*} Consequently,  egin{align*}  eta_k = \sum_{l \leq \lambda}\alpha_l \delta_{y_l}(B_\varepsilon(x_k)), \end{align*} and hence, we may define  egin{align*} L_k = \{l \in \{1,\dots \lambda\} \mid \delta_{y_l}(B_\varepsilon(x_k)) = 1 \}. \end{align*} Note that by construction,  egin{align*} \delta_{y_l}(B_\varepsilon(x_k)) = 1 \iff d(y_l, x_k) < \varepsilon, \end{align*} as desired. otin L_{k^\prime}$ for $k^\prime

motivationContexts.text: We remark, that Lemma lem:helpful-point-process is reminiscent of the property for tuples, where two tuples with a distance less than 1 from one another, must have the same length. In particular, the following Corollary follows naturally.

Lemma lem:helpful-point-process and its Corollary show, that whenever two finite integer valued measures have a Prokhorov distance less than 1, then the sum of multiplicities of each atom must coincide. Of course, we can leverage the same strategy to ensure the same holds true in a sufficiently small ball around each atom, if chosen carefully.
The implication of Lemma lem:disintegration-lemma allows us to separate each point and its multiplicity; we visualize the idea in Figure fig:visualize.

nodes.title: Permutative equality
nodes.statement: Let $X$ be a set. Let $\overset{\pi}{\sim} \subseteq \mathscr{T}(X)\times \mathscr{T}(X)$ be the relation defined by \begin{align*} \bm{x} \overset{\pi}{\sim} \bm{x}^\prime \iff \ell(\bm{x}) =\ell(\bm{x}^\prime) \land \exists \pi \in \mathscr{P}_{\ell(\bm{x})} : \bm{x} = \bm{x}^\prime\circ\pi. \end{align*} For any two elements $\bm{x} \overset{\pi}{\sim} \bm{x}^\prime$, we say that $\bm{x}$ and $\bm{x}^{\prime}$ are equal up to a permutation, and we call the property permutative equality.
proofBridge: defn:permutative-equality permutative equality.

motivationContexts.text: The implication of Lemma lem:disintegration-lemma allows us to separate each point and its multiplicity; we visualize the idea in Figure fig:visualize.

So far, we have shown some results relating to finite integer-valued measures. We now proceed by identifying the similarities with the tuple space. However, there is currently an inherent problem; if one recalls the mapping eq:prelim-pp, it is easy to notice, that there are more than one tuple that produces the same integer-valued measure. Therefore, we first require a way to combine all tuples that produce the same integer-valued measure.

The relation, \pi allows us to disregard the specific ordering in which the points are presented in the tuple, ultimately implying that the only remaining data is the image as well as the multiplicity of each element in the image, which, by construction, leads to a strong correspondence with the atomic decomposition of an integer-valued measure.
Using permutative equality, we can separate all the tuples that are the same up to a permutation.

lean.informal: permutatively equal tuples have the same length.

nodes.title: Permutative equality is an equivalence relation
nodes.statement: For any set $X$, the permutative equality relation, $\overset{\pi}{\sim} \subseteq \mathscr{T}(X)\times \mathscr{T}(X)$, is an equivalence relation.

thesisProof.text: For any $\bm{x},\bm{x}^\prime, \bm{x}^\ast \in \mathscr{T}(X)$ we must show, that \begin{enumerate} \item $\bm{x} \overset{\pi}{\sim} \bm{x}$. \label{property:permutation-reflexive} \item $\bm{x} \overset{\pi}{\sim} \bm{x}^\prime$ if and only if $\bm{x}^\prime\overset{\pi}{\sim} \bm{x}$.\label{property:permutation-symmetry} \item If $\bm{x}\overset{\pi}{\sim} \bm{x}^\prime $ and $\bm{x}^\prime \overset{\pi}{\sim} \bm{x}^\ast$, then $\bm{x} \overset{\pi}{\sim} \bm{x}^\ast$. \label{property:permutation-transitivity} \end{enumerate} For \eqref{property:permutation-reflexive}, notice that for any $\bm{x} \in \mathscr{T}(X)$ the mapping $\pi:\mathrm{domain}(\bm{x}) \to \mathrm{domain}(\bm{x})$ defined by $\pi(i) = i$ is a permutation, from which the result follows. For \eqref{property:permutation-symmetry}, notice that if $\bm{x} \overset{\pi}{\sim} \bm{x}^\prime$, then there exists a $\pi \in \mathscr{P}_{\ell(\bm{x})}$ such that $\bm{x} = \bm{x}^\prime \circ \pi$. However, as $\pi$ is bijective, and hence invertible, it follows that $\bm{x} \circ \pi^{-1} = \bm{x}^\prime \circ \pi \circ \pi^{-1} = \bm{x}^\prime$. Moreover, it is clear that $\pi^{-1} \in \mathscr{P}_{\ell(\bm{x})} = \mathscr{P}_{\ell(\bm{x}^\prime)}$ as $\ell(\bm{x}) = \ell(\bm{x}^\prime)$ by assumption. Hence, the relation is symmetric. Finally, notice that if $\bm{x}\overset{\pi}{\sim} \bm{x}^\prime $ and $\bm{x}^\prime \overset{\pi}{\sim} \bm{x}^\ast$, then we immediately have $\ell(\bm{x}) =\ell(\bm{x}^\prime) =\ell(\bm{x}^\ast)$. Moreover, there exists $\pi, \pi^\ast \in \mathscr{P}_{\ell(\bm{x})}$ such that \begin{align*} \bm{x} = \bm{x}^\prime \circ \pi \quad \text{and}\quad \bm{x}^\prime = \bm{x}^\ast \circ \pi^\prime. \end{align*} However, then clearly \begin{align*} \bm{x} = \bm{x}^\ast \circ \pi^{\prime} \circ \pi, \end{align*} and moreover $\pi^{\prime}\circ \pi \in \mathscr{P}_{\ell(\bm{x})}$ as desired. Hence, the relation is transitive.

proofBridge: prop:perm-equal-equiv permutative equality reflexive.
prop:perm-equal-equiv permutative equality symmetric.
prop:perm-equal-equiv permutative equality transitive.

nodes.title: Definition: permuted tuple quotient space
nodes.statement: For any set $X$, and tuple $\bm{x} \in \mathscr{T}(X)$ we define \begin{align*} \bm{x}^\pi = \{\bm{x}^\prime \in \mathscr{T}(X) \mid \bm{x} \overset{\pi}{\sim} \bm{x}^\prime\}, \end{align*} as the equivalence class induced by $\bm{x}$; any $\bm{x}^\prime \in \bm{x}^\pi$ is said to be equal to $\bm{x}$ up to a permutation. Moreover, we define \begin{align*} \mathscr{T}^\pi(X) = \{\bm{x}^\pi \mid \bm{x} \in \mathscr{T}(X)\} \end{align*} as the quotient space, and call it the space of permuted tuples.

nodes.title: Definition: permuted tuple hausdorff distance
nodes.statement: Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space and let $(\mathscr{T}(X), \mathscr{d}_H)$ be the associated tuple Hausdorff space. Define the mapping $\mathscr{d}_\pi : \mathscr{T}^\pi(X) \times \mathscr{T}^\pi(X) \to [0,\infty]$ by \begin{align*} \mathscr{d}_\pi(\bm{x}^\pi, \bm{y}^\pi) = \max\begin{cases} \max_{\pi \in \mathscr{P}_{\ell(\bm{x})}} \min_{ \pi ^\prime \in \mathscr{P}_{\ell(\bm{y})}} \mathscr{d}_H(\bm{x}\circ \pi , \bm{y} \circ \pi^\prime) \\ \max_{ \pi ^\prime \in \mathscr{P}_{\ell(\bm{y})}} \min_{\pi \in \mathscr{P}_{\ell(\bm{x})}} \mathscr{d}_H(\bm{x}\circ \pi , \bm{y} \circ \pi^\prime) \end{cases} \end{align*} We call $\mathscr{d}_\pi$ the permuted tuple Hausdorff distance.
