nodes.title: Theorem: permuted tuple hausdorff metric complete separable
nodes.statement: Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space and let $(\mathscr{T}(X), \mathscr{d}_H)$ be the associated tuple Hausdorff space. Then, $(\mathscr{T}^\pi(X), \mathscr{d}_\pi)$ is a metric space. Moreover, if \begin{enumerate} \item $(X,d)$ is separable, then $(\mathscr{T}^\pi(X), \mathscr{d}_\pi)$ is separable, and \item $(X,d)$ is complete, then $(\mathscr{T}^\pi(X), \mathscr{d}_\pi)$ is complete. \end{enumerate}

thesisProof.text: For $\bm{x}^\pi \in \mathscr{T}^\pi(X)$ define \begin{align*} \mathcal{O}(\bm{x}) = \{\bm{x}\circ \pi \mid \pi \in \mathscr{P}_{\ell(\bm{x})}\} \subseteq \mathscr{T}(X). \end{align*} This set is finite. Moreover, $\mathcal{O}(\bm{x}) = \mathcal{O}(\bm{y})$ if and only if $\bm{x} \overset{\pi}{\sim} \bm{y}$. Hence the map \begin{align*} \Psi:\mathscr{T}^\pi(X) \to \mathscr{F}(\mathscr{T}(X)), \qquad \Psi(\bm{x}^\pi)=\mathcal{O}(\bm{x}), \end{align*} is well defined and injective. By definition, $\mathscr{d}_\pi(\bm{x}^\pi,\bm{y}^\pi)$ is exactly the Hausdorff distance between the two finite subsets $\mathcal{O}(\bm{x})$ and $\mathcal{O}(\bm{y})$ of $(\mathscr{T}(X),\mathscr{d}_H)$. Therefore, $\Psi$ is an isometric embedding. Since the Hausdorff distance on finite non-empty subsets is a metric, it follows that $\mathscr{d}_\pi$ is a metric on $\mathscr{T}^\pi(X)$. It is also useful to notice that \begin{align*} \mathscr{d}_\pi(\bm{x}^\pi,\bm{y}^\pi) = \min_{\pi \in \mathscr{P}_{\ell(\bm{x})}} \min_{\pi' \in \mathscr{P}_{\ell(\bm{y})}} \mathscr{d}_H(\bm{x}\circ \pi,\bm{y}\circ \pi'), \end{align*} because the permutation action is by isometries on $(\mathscr{T}(X),\mathscr{d}_H)$, so the inner minima do not depend on the chosen representative within each composition. If $(X,d)$ is separable, then $(\mathscr{T}(X),\mathscr{d}_H)$ is separable by the results of the former chapters. Hence the quotient $\mathscr{T}^\pi(X)$ is separable, since the image of any countable dense subset of $\mathscr{T}(X)$ under the quotient map is countable and dense in $\mathscr{T}^\pi(X)$. If $(X,d)$ is complete, then $(\mathscr{T}(X),\mathscr{d}_H)$ is complete. Let $(\bm{x}_n^\pi)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ be a Cauchy sequence in $(\mathscr{T}^\pi(X),\mathscr{d}_\pi)$. Choose a subsequence $(\bm{x}_{n_k}^\pi)_{k\in\mathbb{N}}$ such that \begin{align*} \mathscr{d}_\pi(\bm{x}_{n_k}^\pi,\bm{x}_{n_{k+1}}^\pi) < 2^{-k} \end{align*} for every $k$. Choose a representative $\bm{y}_1 \in \bm{x}_{n_1}^\pi$. Recursively, having chosen $\bm{y}_k \in \bm{x}_{n_k}^\pi$, choose $\bm{y}_{k+1} \in \bm{x}_{n_{k+1}}^\pi$ such that \begin{align*} \mathscr{d}_H(\bm{y}_k,\bm{y}_{k+1}) = \mathscr{d}_\pi(\bm{x}_{n_k}^\pi,\bm{x}_{n_{k+1}}^\pi). \end{align*} Such a choice is possible by the finite minimum above. Then \begin{align*} \sum_{k=1}^\infty \mathscr{d}_H(\bm{y}_k,\bm{y}_{k+1}) \leq \sum_{k=1}^\infty 2^{-k} < \infty, \end{align*} so $(\bm{y}_k)$ is Cauchy in $(\mathscr{T}(X),\mathscr{d}_H)$ and therefore converges to some $\bm{y}\in\mathscr{T}(X)$. By continuity of the quotient map, $\bm{x}_{n_k}^\pi = \bm{y}_k^\pi \to \bm{y}^\pi$. Since the original sequence $(\bm{x}_n^\pi)$ is Cauchy and has a convergent subsequence, it converges to the same limit $\bm{y}^\pi$. Hence $(\mathscr{T}^\pi(X),\mathscr{d}_\pi)$ is complete.

One can interpret eq:special-case-permuted-hausdorff as a game, where the first player, corresponding to the tuple x must try to choose a permutation to get as far away from y as possible. proofMoves.title: Proof move 6

proofMoves.title: Control the finite data

nodes.title: Proposition: tuple induced measure continuous
nodes.statement: Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space, $(\mathscr{T}(X), \mathscr{d}_H)$ be the associated tuple Hausdorff space, and $(\mathcal{N}(X), \rho)$ be the space of integer-valued measures endowed with the Prokhorov distance. Then the mapping $\mathfrak{m} :\mathscr{T}(X) \to \mathcal{N}(X)$ defined by \begin{align*} \mathfrak{m}(\bm{x}) = B \mapsto \sum_{i \in \mathrm{domain}(\bm{x})} \delta_{\bm{x}(i)}(B) \end{align*} is continuous.

thesisProof.text: We must show that for every $\varepsilon > 0$ and $\bm{x}_0$ there exists a $\delta > 0 $ such that \begin{align*} \mathscr{d}_H(\bm{x}, \bm{x}_0) < \delta \implies \rho(\mathfrak{m}(\bm{x}), \mathfrak{m}(\bm{x}_0)) < \varepsilon. \end{align*} Choose $\delta < \min(\varepsilon,1)$. First, recall that by \nameref{thm:the-standard-machinery} we have that \begin{align*} \mathscr{d}_H(\bm{x}, \bm{x}_0) < \delta < 1 \end{align*} implies that $\ell(\bm{x}) = \ell(\bm{x}_0)$. Now, if $\bm{x}_0$ is the empty tuple, then $\bm{x}$ is also the empty tuple, and therefore \begin{align*} \rho(\mathfrak{m}(\bm{x}),\mathfrak{m}(\bm{x}_0)) = 0 < \varepsilon. \end{align*} Assume therefore that $\bm{x}_0 \neq \bm{e}$. Then, we additionally have \begin{align*} \mathscr{d}_H(\bm{x},\bm{x}_0) = \max_{i \in \mathrm{domain}(\bm{x}_0)} d(\bm{x}(i), \bm{x}_0(i)) < \delta < 1, \end{align*} Consequently, for any Borel set $B$ and every index $i \in \mathrm{domain}(\bm{x}_0)$, \begin{align*} \bm{x}_0(i)\in B \implies \bm{x}(i)\in B^\delta. \end{align*} Therefore, \begin{align*} \mathfrak{m}(\bm{x}_0)(B) \leq \mathfrak{m}(\bm{x})(B^\delta). \end{align*} By symmetry, \begin{align*} \mathfrak{m}(\bm{x})(B) \leq \mathfrak{m}(\bm{x}_0)(B^\delta). \end{align*} Hence, by the definition of the Prokhorov metric, \begin{align*} \rho(\mathfrak{m}(\bm{x}), \mathfrak{m}(\bm{x}_0)) \leq \delta < \varepsilon, \end{align*} as desired.

nodes.title: Proposition: tuple measure surjective
nodes.statement: Let $X$ be a metric space, $\mathscr{T}(X)$ be the associated tuple space, and $\mathcal{N}(X)$ be the space of integer-valued measures on $X$. Then, the mapping $\mathfrak{m}:\mathscr{T}(X) \to \mathcal{N}(X)$ is surjective.

thesisProof.text: By Theorem \ref{thm:sufficient-decomposition} any measure $\xi \in \mathcal{N}(X)$ admits the decomposition \begin{align*} \xi =\sum_{k \leq \kappa } \beta_k\delta_{x_k}, \end{align*} with $(\beta_k)_{k \leq \kappa}\subseteq \mathbb{N}$ and $(x_k)_{k\leq \kappa} \subseteq X$. Note, that the representation is unique, up to a permutation of $\{k \in \mathbb{N} \mid k \leq \kappa\}$. Therefore, choose an arbitrary enumeration and define the tuple \begin{align*} \bm{x}(i) = \begin{cases} x_1 & i \in \{1,\dots, \beta_1\} \\ x_2 & i \in \{ \beta_1 + 1, \dots, \beta_1 +\beta_2\}\\ ~\vdots &~~~\vdots \\ x_\kappa & i \in \{\sum_{k = 1}^{\kappa-1} \beta_k+1, \sum_{k \leq \kappa}\beta_k\}, \end{cases} \end{align*} which, by construction, satisfies that for every measurable $B$, it holds that \begin{align*} \xi(B) =\sum_{i \in \mathrm{domain}(\bm{x})} \delta_{\bm{x}(i)}(B) =\mathfrak{m}(\bm{x})(B), \end{align*} as desired.

proofMoves.title: Unfold the definitions
proofMoves.text: By Theorem \ref{thm:sufficient-decomposition} any measure $\xi \in \mathcal{N}(X)$ admits the decomposition $ \xi =\sum_{k \leq \kappa } \beta_k\delta_{x_k}, $ with $(\beta_k)_{k \leq \kappa}\subseteq \mathbb{N}$ and $(x_k)_{k\leq \kappa} \subseteq X$. Note, that the representation is unique, up to a permutation of $\{k \in \mathbb{N} \mid k \leq \kappa\}$. Therefore, choose an arbitrary enumeration and define the tuple $ \bm{x}(i) = \begin{cases} x_1 & i \in \{1,\dots, \beta_1\} \\ x_2 & i \in \{ \beta_1 + 1, \dots, \beta_1 +\beta_2\}\\ ~\vdots &~~~\vdots \\ x_\kappa & i \in \{\sum_{k = 1}^{\kappa-1} \beta_k+1, \sum_{k \leq \kappa}\beta_k\}, \end{cases} $ which, by construction, satisfies that for every measurable $B$, it holds that $ \xi(B) =\sum_{i \in \mathrm{domain}(\bm{x})} \delta_{\bm{x}(i)}(B) =\mathfrak{m}(\bm{x})(B), $ as desired.

nodes.title: Proposition: permuted tuple measure map bijective
nodes.statement: Let $X$ be a metric space, $\mathscr{T}(X)$ be the associated tuple space, and $\mathcal{N}(X)$ be the space of integer-valued measures on $X$. Then, the mapping $\mathfrak{m}^\pi:\mathscr{T}^\pi(X) \to \mathcal{N}(X)$ defined by \begin{align*} \mathfrak{m}^\pi(\bm{x}^\pi) = \mathfrak{m}(\bm{x}) \end{align*} is bijective.

thesisProof.text: First, note that $\mathfrak{m}^\pi$ is well defined, as every $\bm{x}^\prime \in \bm{x}^\pi$ satisfies $\mathfrak{m}(\bm{x}^\prime) = \mathfrak{m}(\bm{x})$. By Proposition \ref{prop:tuple-measure-surjective}, the mapping is surjective. It therefore remains to prove injectivity. Let $\bm{x}^\pi, \bm{y}^\pi \in \mathscr{T}^\pi(X)$ satisfy \begin{align*} \mathfrak{m}^\pi(\bm{x}^\pi)=\mathfrak{m}^\pi(\bm{y}^\pi). \end{align*} Choose representatives $\bm{x}\in \bm{x}^\pi$ and $\bm{y}\in \bm{y}^\pi$. Then $\mathfrak{m}(\bm{x})=\mathfrak{m}(\bm{y})$. In particular, \begin{align*} \ell(\bm{x}) = \mathfrak{m}(\bm{x})(X) = \mathfrak{m}(\bm{y})(X) = \ell(\bm{y}). \end{align*} For each $a \in X$, define \begin{align*} I_a = \{i \in \mathrm{domain}(\bm{x}) \mid \bm{x}(i)=a\}, \qquad J_a = \{j \in \mathrm{domain}(\bm{y}) \mid \bm{y}(j)=a\}. \end{align*} Equality of the induced measures implies $|I_a| = |J_a|$ for every $a \in X$. Since only finitely many of these sets are non-empty, we may choose bijections \begin{align*} \pi_a : I_a \to J_a \end{align*} for each such $a \in X$. The union of these bijections defines a permutation \begin{align*} \pi:\mathrm{domain}(\bm{x}) \to \mathrm{domain}(\bm{y}), \end{align*} and by construction $\bm{y}(\pi(i))=\bm{x}(i)$ for every $i$. Hence \begin{align*} \bm{x} = \bm{y}\circ \pi, \end{align*} so $\bm{x} \overset{\pi}{\sim} \bm{y}$ and therefore $\bm{x}^\pi = \bm{y}^\pi$. Thus $\mathfrak{m}^\pi$ is injective.

nodes.title: Proposition: inverse permuted tuple measure continuous
nodes.statement: Let $(X,d)$ be a complete and separable metric space, $(\mathscr{T}(X), \mathscr{d}_H)$ be the associated tuple Hausdorff space, and $(\mathcal{N}(X), \rho)$ be the space of integer-valued measures endowed with the Prokhorov distance. Then the mapping $(\mathfrak{m}^\pi)^{-1} :\mathcal{N}(X)\to\mathscr{T}^\pi(X)$ is continuous.

thesisProof.text: We must show, that for every $\varepsilon > 0$ and $\xi_0 \in \mathcal{N}(X)$ there exists a $\delta > 0$ such that \begin{align*} \rho(\xi, \xi_0) < \delta \implies \mathscr{d}_\pi((\mathfrak{m}^\pi)^{-1}(\xi), (\mathfrak{m}^\pi)^{-1}(\xi_0)) < \varepsilon. \end{align*} If $\xi_0 = 0$, choose $\delta < \min(\varepsilon,1)$. If $\rho(\xi,\xi_0)<\delta$, then Lemma \ref{lem:helpful-point-process} gives \begin{align*} \xi(X)=\xi_0(X)=0, \end{align*} so $\xi=0$ and the conclusion is immediate. Therefore, assume that $\xi_0 \neq 0$. By Theorem \ref{thm:sufficient-decomposition}, $\xi_0$ admits the decomposition \begin{align*} \xi_0 = \sum_{k \leq \kappa} \beta_k \delta_{x_k}, \end{align*} with $(\beta_k)_{k \leq \kappa} \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ and distinct $(x_k)_{k \leq \kappa} \subseteq X$. Define \begin{align*} N_0 = 0, \qquad N_k = \sum_{r=1}^k \beta_r \quad \text{for } k \in \{1,\dots,\kappa\}, \end{align*} and let $\bm{x}_0 \in \mathscr{T}(X)$ be the tuple defined by \begin{align*} \bm{x}_0(i) = x_k \quad \text{whenever } N_{k-1} < i \leq N_k. \end{align*} Then $\mathfrak{m}(\bm{x}_0)=\xi_0$, so $(\mathfrak{m}^\pi)^{-1}(\xi_0)=\bm{x}_0^\pi$. Define \begin{align*} \gamma = \begin{cases} 1 & \kappa = 1,\\ \min\left(\frac{1}{2} \min_{\substack{k,j \leq \kappa \\ k \neq j}} d(x_k, x_j), 1\right) & \kappa \geq 2. \end{cases} \end{align*} and choose $\delta < \min(\varepsilon,\gamma)$. Let $\xi \in \mathcal{N}(X)$ satisfy $\rho(\xi,\xi_0)<\delta$. By Theorem \ref{thm:sufficient-decomposition}, $\xi$ admits the decomposition \begin{align*} \xi = \sum_{l \leq \lambda} \alpha_l \delta_{y_l}, \end{align*} with $(\alpha_l)_{l \leq \lambda} \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ and distinct $(y_l)_{l \leq \lambda} \subseteq X$. By Lemma \ref{lem:disintegration-lemma}, for each $k \in \{1,\dots,\kappa\}$ there exists a disjoint set $L_k \subseteq \{1,\dots,\lambda\}$ such that \begin{align*} \beta_k = \sum_{l\in L_k} \alpha_l \qquad \text{and} \qquad d(x_k,y_l) < \delta \quad \forall l \in L_k. \end{align*} Choose an enumeration $L_k = \{l_{k,1},\dots,l_{k,m_k}\}$ for each $k$, and define partial sums \begin{align*} M_{k,0} = 0, \qquad M_{k,r} = \sum_{s=1}^r \alpha_{l_{k,s}} \quad \text{for } r \in \{1,\dots,m_k\}. \end{align*} Define a tuple $\bm{x} \in \mathscr{T}(X)$ by declaring that, on the $k$-th block $N_{k-1} < i \leq N_k$, one has \begin{align*} \bm{x}(i) = y_{l_{k,r}} \quad \text{whenever } N_{k-1}+M_{k,r-1} < i \leq N_{k-1}+M_{k,r}. \end{align*} Since $\sum_{l\in L_k} \alpha_l = \beta_k$, this indeed fills the entire $k$-th block. By construction, $\mathfrak{m}(\bm{x})=\xi$, so $(\mathfrak{m}^\pi)^{-1}(\xi)=\bm{x}^\pi$. Finally, for every index $i$ in the $k$-th block we have $\bm{x}_0(i)=x_k$ and $\bm{x}(i)=y_l$ for some $l\in L_k$, hence \begin{align*} d(\bm{x}(i),\bm{x}_0(i)) < \delta. \end{align*} Therefore, \begin{align*} \mathscr{d}_H(\bm{x},\bm{x}_0) < \delta < \varepsilon, \end{align*} and consequently \begin{align*} \mathscr{d}_\pi((\mathfrak{m}^\pi)^{-1}(\xi),(\mathfrak{m}^\pi)^{-1}(\xi_0)) = \mathscr{d}_\pi(\bm{x}^\pi,\bm{x}_0^\pi) \leq \mathscr{d}_H(\bm{x},\bm{x}_0) < \varepsilon. \end{align*} This proves continuity.

motivationContexts.text: We omit the proof of the Corollary, as it corresponds to the discussion immediately preceding it. However, the above allows us to extend the mapping from T(X) to T^(X).

The proposition tells us, that finite-integer measures correspond in a one-to-one fashion with permuted tuples. Of course, the mapping m^ is continuous, whenever m is continuous, so the interesting case is when the inverse is continuous.

At a high-level, Theorem thm:integer-measures-tuples-homeomorphic tells us that we can sample a tuple, by first sampling from a point-process. However, in practice we are not interested in sampling an equivalence class of tuples, but rather a single tuple. Fortunately, this is not a problem; the set x^ T^(X) is finite, and so we can simply pick one at random. In order to justify such an approach, we first require the auxilarry result.

Lemma lem:measurable-enumeration tells us that we can measurably pick a tuple from the equivalence class of tuples associated to a point-process. However, this tuple is fixed; given a point-process, we can only pick one tuple. However, we can do better; we can pick a tuple uniformly at random from the equivalence class of tuples associated to a point-process.

proofMoves.title: Unfold the definitions
proofMoves.text: We must show, that for every $\varepsilon > 0$ and $\xi_0 \in \mathcal{N}(X)$ there exists a $\delta > 0$ such that $ \rho(\xi, \xi_0) < \delta \implies \mathscr{d}_\pi((\mathfrak{m}^\pi)^{-1}(\xi), (\mathfrak{m}^\pi)^{-1}(\xi_0)) < \varepsilon. $ If $\xi_0 = 0$, choose $\delta < \min(\varepsilon,1)$. If $\rho(\xi,\xi_0)<\delta$, then Lemma \ref{lem:helpful-point-process} gives $ \xi(X)=\xi_0(X)=0, $ so $\xi=0$ and the conclusion is immediate. Therefore, assume that $\xi_0 \neq 0$. By Theorem \ref{thm:sufficient-decomposition}, $\xi_0$ admits the decomposition $ \xi_0 = \sum_{k \leq \kappa} \beta_k \delta_{x_k}, $ with $(\beta_k)_{k \leq \kappa} \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ and distinct $(x_k)_{k \leq \kappa} \subseteq X$. Define $ N_0 = 0, \qquad N_k = \sum_{r=1}^k \beta_r \quad \text{for } k \in \{1,\dots,\kappa\}, $ and let $\bm{x}_0 \in \mathscr{T}(X)$ be the tuple defined by $ \bm{x}_0(i) = x_k \quad \text{whenever } N_{k-1} < i \leq N_k. $ Then $\mathfrak{m}(\bm{x}_0)=\xi_0$, so $(\mathfrak{m}^\pi)^{-1}(\xi_0)=\bm{x}_0^\pi$. Define $ \gamma = \begin{cases} 1 & \kappa = 1,\\ \min\left(\frac{1}{2} \min_{\substack{k,j \leq \kappa \\ k \neq j}} d(x_k, x_j), 1\right) & \kappa \geq 2. \end{cases} $ and choose $\delta < \min(\varepsilon,\gamma)$. Let $\xi \in \mathcal{N}(X)$ satisfy $\rho(\xi,\xi_0)<\delta$. By Theorem \ref{thm:sufficient-decomposition}, $\xi$ admits the decomposition $ \xi = \sum_{l \leq \lambda} \alpha_l \delta_{y_l}, $ with $(\alpha_l)_{l \leq \lambda} \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ and distinct $(y_l)_{l \leq \lambda} \subseteq X$. By Lemma \ref{lem:disintegration-lemma}, for each $k \in \{1,\dots,\kappa\}$ there exists a disjoint set $L_k \subseteq \{1,\dots,\lambda\}$ such that $ \beta_k = \sum_{l\in L_k} \alpha_l \qquad \text{and} \qquad d(x_k,y_l) < \delta \quad \forall l \in L_k. $ Choose an enumeration $L_k = \{l_{k,1},\dots,l_{k,m_k}\}$ for each $k$, and define partial sums $ M_{k,0} = 0, \qquad M_{k,r} = \sum_{s=1}^r \alpha_{l_{k,s}} \quad \text{for } r \in \{1,\dots,m_k\}. $ Define a tuple $\bm{x} \in \mathscr{T}(X)$ by declaring that, on the $k$-th block $N_{k-1} < i \leq N_k$, one has $ \bm{x}(i) = y_{l_{k,r}} \quad \text{whenever } N_{k-1}+M_{k,r-1} < i \leq N_{k-1}+M_{k,r}. $ Since $\sum_{l\in L_k} \alpha_l = \beta_k$, this indeed fills the entire $k$-th block. By construction, $\mathfrak{m}(\bm{x})=\xi$, so $(\mathfrak{m}^\pi)^{-1}(\xi)=\bm{x}^\pi$.

proofMoves.title: Verify the order relation
proofMoves.text: Finally, for every index $i$ in the $k$-th block we have $\bm{x}_0(i)=x_k$ and $\bm{x}(i)=y_l$ for some $l\in L_k$, hence $ d(\bm{x}(i),\bm{x}_0(i)) < \delta. $ Therefore, $ \mathscr{d}_H(\bm{x},\bm{x}_0) < \delta < \varepsilon, $ and consequently $ \mathscr{d}_\pi((\mathfrak{m}^\pi)^{-1}(\xi),(\mathfrak{m}^\pi)^{-1}(\xi_0)) = \mathscr{d}_\pi(\bm{x}^\pi,\bm{x}_0^\pi) \leq \mathscr{d}_H(\bm{x},\bm{x}_0) < \varepsilon. $ This proves continuity.

nodes.title: Theorem: point process tuple
nodes.statement: Let $(\Omega, \mathcal{F},\mathbb{P})$ be a probability space, $(X,d)$ be a complete and separable metric space. Let $\xi :\Omega \to \mathcal{N}(X)$ be a point process. Let $\tau:\mathcal{N}(X) \to \mathscr{T}(X)$ be a measurable enumeration of the points of $\xi$. Define the mapping $\mathbb{Q} :\Omega \times \mathcal{B}(\mathscr{T}(X)) \to [0,1]$ by \begin{align*} \mathbb{Q}(\omega, B) = \frac{1}{n(\omega)!} \sum_{\pi \in \mathscr{P}_{n(\omega)}} \mathbbm{1}_B(\tau(\xi(\omega))\circ \pi), \end{align*} where $n(\omega) = \xi(\omega)(X)$ is the total number of points in the point-process $\xi(\omega)$. Then, $\mathbb{Q}$ is a Markov kernel from $(\Omega, \mathcal{F})$ to $(\mathscr{T}(X), \mathcal{B}(\mathscr{T}(X)))$.

thesisProof.text: We must show that \begin{enumerate} \item $B \mapsto \mathbb{Q}(\omega, B)$ is a probability measure for all $\omega \in \Omega$, and \item $\omega \mapsto \mathbb{Q}(\omega, B)$ is a $\mathcal{F}/\mathcal{B}([0,1])$ measurable random variable. \end{enumerate} For fixed $\omega$, let $n=n(\omega)$. Then \begin{align*} \mathbb{Q}(\omega,\cdot) = \frac{1}{n!}\sum_{\pi \in \mathscr{P}_n} \delta_{\tau(\xi(\omega))\circ \pi}, \end{align*} which is a finite convex combination of Dirac probability measures, hence a probability measure. It remains to prove measurability in $\omega$. For $n \in \mathbb{N}_0$, define \begin{align*} A_n = \{\omega \in \Omega \mid n(\omega)=n\} = \{\omega \in \Omega \mid \xi(\omega)(X)=n\}. \end{align*} Since $\omega \mapsto \xi(\omega)(X)$ is measurable, each $A_n \in \mathcal{F}$. Now let $B \in \mathcal{B}(\mathscr{T}(X))$ be fixed. By measurability of $\tau \circ \xi$ and continuity of the permutation maps for fixed $\pi \in \mathscr{P}_n$, the map \begin{align*} \omega \mapsto \mathbbm{1}_{A_n}(\omega)\mathbbm{1}_{B}(\tau(\xi(\omega))\circ \pi) \end{align*} is measurable for every $n$ and every $\pi \in \mathscr{P}_n$. Therefore, \begin{align*} \omega \mapsto \frac{1}{n!}\sum_{\pi \in \mathscr{P}_n}\mathbbm{1}_{A_n}(\omega)\mathbbm{1}_{B}(\tau(\xi(\omega))\circ \pi) \end{align*} is measurable for each $n$. Finally, \begin{align*} \mathbb{Q}(\omega,B) = \sum_{n=0}^\infty \frac{1}{n!}\sum_{\pi \in \mathscr{P}_n}\mathbbm{1}_{A_n}(\omega)\mathbbm{1}_{B}(\tau(\xi(\omega))\circ \pi), \end{align*} and this is measurable because the sum is countable and, for each fixed $\omega$, exactly one term in $n$ is non-zero. Hence $\omega \mapsto \mathbb{Q}(\omega,B)$ is measurable, as desired.

nodes.title: Functionals and Operators
nodes.statement: Let $X$ be a non-empty set and let $\mathbb{K}$ be a field, then any mapping $\varphi: X \to \mathbb{K}$ is called a $\mathbb{K}$-functional, or simply a functional. Similarly, let $V$ be a vector space over some field $\mathbb{K}$. Then, any mapping $\varphi:X \to V$ is called a $V$-operator or simply an operator.
proofBridge: defn:functional-and-operator functionals and operators.

motivationContexts.text: On the other hand, one may have a function which, in some sense, is simple or natural to work with, but is not bijective. In what follows, we will construct a weaker version of the transport of structure. We remark that there are distinct differences and that, in some cases, one will lose some information or granularity of the original set X. Moreover, we focus on copying a Hilbert space structure, but the method will, mutatis mutandis, apply in general to other algebraic or analytic structures.
First, we will extend the definitions of functionals and operators slightly, from their original definitions in functional analysis.

Now, the goal is to leverage the vector space structure on some vector space V, to define some that structure resembles a vector space structure on an arbitrary set X. In order to do so, I require the existence of an operator that satisfies something that resembles linearity.

Recall, that a classical linear operator is any operator that preserves linear combinations. However, in the case above, X is a priori not a vector space. Therefore, it is not possible for it to preserve linear combinations. Instead, the requirement is that linear combinations in the image of the operator, (X) V, must have a non-empty pre-image, so that it is possible to identify at least one point which could be considered as a representative for the linear combination in X. We visualize the idea in Figure fig:weakly-linear-operator.

nodes.title: Kernel of a Function
nodes.statement: Let $X$ and $Y$ be non-empty sets and $\varphi : X \to Y$ a function. nodes.title: Proposition: function kernel quotient injective extension
nodes.statement: Let $X$ and $Y$ be non-empty sets and $\varphi : X \to Y$ a function. Then, $\varphi$ extends to a well-defined injective mapping $\Phi : X_\varphi \to Y$ such that $\Phi([x]_{\overset{\varphi}{\sim}}) = \varphi(x)$ for all $x_\varphi \in X_\varphi$.

thesisProof.text: First, we show that $\Phi$ is well defined. If $[x]_{\overset{\varphi}{\sim}} = [x']_{\overset{\varphi}{\sim}}$, then $x \overset{\varphi}{\sim} x'$, hence $\varphi(x)=\varphi(x')$. Therefore the value $\Phi([x]_{\overset{\varphi}{\sim}})$ does not depend on the chosen representative. We now show injectivity. We must show that \begin{align*} \Phi(x_\varphi) = \Phi(x^\prime_\varphi) \implies x_\varphi = x^\prime_\varphi, \end{align*} Let $x_\varphi, x^\prime_\varphi \in X_\varphi$ be arbitrary. By the definition of $\Phi$, we have that $\Phi(x_\varphi) = \Phi(x^\prime_\varphi)$ implies that $\varphi(x) = \varphi(x^\prime)$, which implies that $x \overset{\varphi}{\sim} x^\prime$, and hence $x_\varphi = x^\prime_\varphi$, as desired.

nodes.title: Weak Transport of Structure
nodes.statement: Let $X$ be a non-empty set, $V$ a vector space over some field $\mathbb{K}$, and $\varphi : X \to V$ a weakly linear operator. thesisProof.text: By Proposition \ref{prop:phi-subspace}, the image $\varphi(X)$ is a subspace of $V$. By the preceding proposition, $\Phi:X_\varphi \to \varphi(X)$ is a bijection. The displayed formulas therefore define the pullback of addition and scalar multiplication on the vector space $\varphi(X)$ along the bijection $\Phi$. Consequently, all vector-space axioms on $X_\varphi$ follow immediately from the corresponding axioms on $\varphi(X)$.

nodes.title: Proposition: weak linear kernel inner product space
nodes.statement: Let $X$ be a non-empty set, $(V, \langle \cdot,\cdot\rangle)$ be a real inner product space, and $\varphi : X \to V$ be a weakly linear operator. Define $\llangle \cdot, \cdot \rrangle : X_\varphi \times X_\varphi \to \mathbb{R}$ by \begin{align*} \llangle \vphantom{.}x_\varphi, x^\prime_\varphi \rrangle = \langle \varphi(x), \varphi(x^\prime)\rangle, \end{align*} for $x_\varphi, x^\prime_\varphi \in X_\varphi$. Then, $(X_\varphi, \llangle \cdot, \cdot \rrangle)$ is an inner product space.

thesisProof.text: The claim is follows simply from the fact, that the mapping $\varphi$ extends uniquely to the mapping $\Phi$ which is an injective map on $X_\varphi$ such that \begin{align*} \llangle \vphantom{.}x_\varphi, x^\prime_\varphi \rrangle = \langle \vphantom{.}\Phi(x_\varphi), \Phi(x^\prime_\varphi) \rangle = \langle \varphi(x), \varphi(x^\prime)\rangle. \end{align*} However, since $(V, \langle \cdot, \cdot \rangle)$ is an inner product space over $\mathbb{R}$ the claim follows trivially.

nodes.title: Proposition: kernel space separable
nodes.statement: Let $X$ be a non-empty set, $(V, \langle \cdot,\cdot\rangle)$ a separable inner product space, and $\varphi: X \to V$ a weakly linear operator. Then, $(X_\varphi, \llangle \cdot, \cdot \rrangle)$ is a separable inner product space.

thesisProof.text: Since $V$ is separable, every subset of $V$ endowed with the subspace topology is separable. In particular, $\varphi(X) \subseteq V$ is separable. By Proposition \ref{prop:phi-subspace}, the image $\varphi(X)$ is a subspace of $V$, and by the preceding proposition the map $\Phi:X_\varphi \to \varphi(X)$ is bijective. Moreover, for $x_\varphi, y_\varphi \in X_\varphi$, the transported inner product satisfies \begin{align*} \llangle x_\varphi, y_\varphi \rrangle = \langle \Phi(x_\varphi), \Phi(y_\varphi)\rangle. \end{align*} Hence $\Phi$ is an isometric linear isomorphism between $(X_\varphi,\llangle \cdot,\cdot \rrangle)$ and the separable inner product space $\varphi(X)$. Therefore $(X_\varphi,\llangle \cdot,\cdot \rrangle)$ is separable.

nodes.title: Theorem: closed convex cone closure projection
nodes.statement: Let $(\mathcal{H}, \langle \cdot, \cdot \rangle)$ be a real separable Hilbert space and let $C \subset \mathcal{H}$ be a convex cone. Then, \begin{enumerate}[(i)] \item The closure of $C$, denoted by $\overline{C}$, is a convex cone, and a complete subset of $\mathcal{H}$. \item If $C$ is a closed convex cone, then the metric projection $P:\mathcal{H} \to C$ defined by \begin{align*} P(v) = \argmin_{c \in C} ||v - c||, \end{align*} is well defined. \item If $C$ is a closed convex cone, then the metric projection $P:\mathcal{H} \to C$ satisfies \begin{enumerate} \item $P$ is idempotent. That is, $P \circ P = P$. \item For all $\alpha \geq 0$ and $v \in \mathcal{H}$ the relation $P(\alpha v) = \alpha P(v)$ holds. \end{enumerate} \end{enumerate}

nodes.title: Theorem: grothendieck vector space from convex cone
nodes.statement: Let $X$ be a non-empty set, $V$ a real vector space, and $\varphi :X \to V$ a weakly convex operator. Define the relation $\sim$ on $X_\varphi \times X_\varphi$ by \begin{align*} (x_\varphi, z_\varphi) \sim (x^\prime_\varphi, z^\prime_\varphi) \iff x_\varphi + z^\prime_\varphi = x^\prime_\varphi + z_\varphi, \end{align*} and let $\mathscr{V}(X, \varphi)$ denote the quotient space $X_\varphi \times X_\varphi / \sim $. Define the binary operations by $+:\mathscr{V}(X,\varphi) \times \mathscr{V}(X,\varphi) \to \mathscr{V}(X,\varphi)$ and $\cdot : \mathbb{R} \times \mathscr{V}(X, \varphi) \to \mathscr{V}(X,\varphi)$ by \begin{align*} [(x_\varphi,z_\varphi)] + [(x^\prime_\varphi, z^\prime_\varphi)] = [(x_\varphi + x^\prime_\varphi, z_\varphi + z^\prime_\varphi)], \end{align*} and \begin{align*} \alpha [(x_\varphi,z_\varphi)] = \begin{cases} [(\alpha x_\varphi, \alpha z_\varphi)] & \alpha \geq 0,\\ [(|\alpha| z_\varphi, |\alpha| x_\varphi)] & \alpha < 0. \end{cases} \end{align*} Then $(\mathscr{V}(X,\varphi), +, \cdot)$ is a real vector space.

thesisProof.text: For simplicity, we will write $x$ instead of $x_\varphi$ and $z$ instead of $z_\varphi$. First, we must verify that $\sim$ is indeed an equivalence relation. We must show that for all $(x,z),(x^\prime,z^\prime), (x^\ast, z^\ast) \in X_\varphi \times X_\varphi$ it holds that \begin{enumerate} \item $(x,z) \sim (x,z)$. \item $(x,z) \sim (x^\prime, z^\prime)$ if and only if $(x^\prime, z^\prime)\sim (x,z)$. \item $(x, z) \sim (x^\prime, z^\prime)$ and $(x^\prime, z^\prime) \sim (x^\ast, z^\ast)$ implies $(x, z) \sim (x^\ast, z^\ast)$. \end{enumerate} First, notice that for all $x,z \in X_\varphi$ it holds that \begin{align*} x+z = x+z, \end{align*} and so $(x,z) \sim (x,z)$. Thus $\sim$ is reflexive. Next, suppose that $(x,z) \sim (x^\prime, z^\prime)$. Then, by definition, \begin{align*} x + z^\prime = x^\prime + z. \end{align*} By symmetry of equality, this gives \begin{align*} x^\prime + z = x + z^\prime. \end{align*} Therefore $(x^\prime,z^\prime)\sim (x,z)$. The converse follows analogously, and hence $\sim$ is symmetric. For the third criterion, we first note that $X_\varphi$ is cancellative. Indeed, the convex cone structure on $X_\varphi$ is obtained by transporting the cone structure of $\varphi(X)\subseteq V$ along the bijection \begin{align*} \Phi:X_\varphi \to \varphi(X)\subseteq V. \end{align*} Thus, for all $a,c \in X_\varphi$, the transported addition satisfies \begin{align*} \Phi(a+c)=\Phi(a)+\Phi(c). \end{align*} Now suppose that $a+c=b+c$ in $X_\varphi$. Applying $\Phi$ yields \begin{align*} \Phi(a+c)=\Phi(b+c). \end{align*} Using the compatibility of $\Phi$ with the transported addition, we obtain \begin{align*} \Phi(a)+\Phi(c)=\Phi(b)+\Phi(c). \end{align*} Since $V$ is a vector space, addition in $V$ is cancellative, and hence \begin{align*} \Phi(a)=\Phi(b). \end{align*} By injectivity of $\Phi$, it follows that \begin{align*} a=b. \end{align*} Therefore $X_\varphi$ is cancellative. Now suppose that $(x, z) \sim (x^\prime, z^\prime)$ and $(x^\prime, z^\prime) \sim (x^\ast, z^\ast)$. Then \begin{align}\label{eq:non-prime-and-prime} x + z^\prime = x^\prime + z, \end{align} and \begin{align}\label{eq:prime-and-ast} x^\prime + z^\ast = x^\ast + z^\prime. \end{align} Using associativity and commutativity of addition in $X_\varphi$, together with equations \eqref{eq:non-prime-and-prime} and \eqref{eq:prime-and-ast}, we have \begin{align*} (x+z^\ast)+z^\prime &= (x+z^\prime)+z^\ast \\ &= (x^\prime+z)+z^\ast \\ &= z+(x^\prime+z^\ast) \\ &= z+(x^\ast+z^\prime) \\ &= (x^\ast+z)+z^\prime. \end{align*} Since $X_\varphi$ is cancellative, we may cancel the common term $z^\prime$, obtaining \begin{align*} x+z^\ast = x^\ast+z. \end{align*} Therefore $(x,z)\sim (x^\ast,z^\ast)$, from which it follows that $\sim$ is transitive. Hence $\sim$ is an equivalence relation on $X_\varphi \times X_\varphi$. Next, we prove that $\mathscr{V}(X,\varphi)$ is a vector space. First, let us prove that addition and scalar multiplication are well-defined; for addition, suppose that $(x,y) \sim (x^\prime, y^\prime)$ and $(z,w) \sim (z^\prime, w^\prime)$. We will show that the choice of representatives from the equivalence classes are irrelevant. That is, we will show that \begin{align*} [(x + z, y + w)] = [(x^\prime + z^\prime, y^\prime + w^\prime)]. \end{align*} By definition of $\sim$, we have \begin{align*} x+y^\prime = x^\prime+y \end{align*} and \begin{align*} z+w^\prime = z^\prime+w. \end{align*} We must show that \begin{align*} (x+z,y+w)\sim(x^\prime+z^\prime,y^\prime+w^\prime). \end{align*} By definition of $\sim$, this is equivalent to showing that \begin{align*} (x+z)+(y^\prime+w^\prime) = (x^\prime+z^\prime)+(y+w). \end{align*} Using associativity and commutativity of addition in $X_\varphi$, we obtain \begin{align*} (x+z)+(y^\prime+w^\prime) &= (x+y^\prime)+(z+w^\prime) \\ &= (x^\prime+y)+(z^\prime+w) \\ &= (x^\prime+z^\prime)+(y+w). \end{align*} Therefore \begin{align*} (x+z,y+w)\sim(x^\prime+z^\prime,y^\prime+w^\prime). \end{align*} Hence \begin{align*} [(x+z,y+w)] = [(x^\prime+z^\prime,y^\prime+w^\prime)]. \end{align*} Thus addition is independent of the representatives chosen. Next, we show that scalar multiplication is well-defined. Suppose that \begin{align*} (x,z)\sim(x^\prime,z^\prime). \end{align*} Then, by definition of $\sim$, we have \begin{align*} x+z^\prime=x^\prime+z. \end{align*} Let $\alpha\in\mathbb{R}$. We must show that \begin{align*} \alpha[(x,z)]=\alpha[(x^\prime,z^\prime)]. \end{align*} First, suppose that $\alpha\geq 0$. Then \begin{align*} \alpha[(x,z)] = [(\alpha x,\alpha z)] \end{align*} and \begin{align*} \alpha[(x^\prime,z^\prime)] = [(\alpha x^\prime,\alpha z^\prime)]. \end{align*} Thus, it suffices to show that \begin{align*} (\alpha x,\alpha z)\sim(\alpha x^\prime,\alpha z^\prime). \end{align*} By definition of $\sim$, this is equivalent to showing that \begin{align*} \alpha x+\alpha z^\prime = \alpha x^\prime+\alpha z. \end{align*} Using compatibility of the transported cone structure with non-negative scalar multiplication, we have \begin{align*} \alpha x+\alpha z^\prime &= \alpha(x+z^\prime) \\ &= \alpha(x^\prime+z) \\ &= \alpha x^\prime+\alpha z. \end{align*} Therefore \begin{align*} (\alpha x,\alpha z) \sim (\alpha x^\prime,\alpha z^\prime), \end{align*} and hence \begin{align*} [(\alpha x,\alpha z)] = [(\alpha x^\prime,\alpha z^\prime)]. \end{align*} So scalar multiplication is independent of representatives when $\alpha\geq 0$. Now suppose that $\alpha<0$. Let \begin{align*} \beta=|\alpha|. \end{align*} Then $\beta>0$, and \begin{align*} \alpha[(x,z)] = [(\beta z,\beta x)] \end{align*} while \begin{align*} \alpha[(x^\prime,z^\prime)] = [(\beta z^\prime,\beta x^\prime)]. \end{align*} Thus, it suffices to show that \begin{align*} (\beta z,\beta x)\sim(\beta z^\prime,\beta x^\prime). \end{align*} By definition of $\sim$, this is equivalent to showing that \begin{align*} \beta z+\beta x^\prime = \beta z^\prime+\beta x. \end{align*} Since $(x,z)\sim(x^\prime,z^\prime)$, we have \begin{align*} x+z^\prime=x^\prime+z. \end{align*} Multiplying by $\beta$ and using compatibility with non-negative scalar multiplication gives \begin{align*} \beta x+\beta z^\prime &= \beta(x+z^\prime) \\ &= \beta(x^\prime+z) \\ &= \beta x^\prime+\beta z. \end{align*} Using commutativity of addition in $X_\varphi$, this gives \begin{align*} \beta z^\prime+\beta x = \beta z+\beta x^\prime. \end{align*} By symmetry of equality, \begin{align*} \beta z+\beta x^\prime = \beta z^\prime+\beta x. \end{align*} Therefore \begin{align*} (\beta z,\beta x)\sim(\beta z^\prime,\beta x^\prime). \end{align*} Since $\beta=|\alpha|$, this means that \begin{align*} (|\alpha|z,|\alpha|x)\sim(|\alpha|z^\prime,|\alpha|x^\prime), \end{align*} and hence \begin{align*} [(\left|\alpha\right|z,\left|\alpha\right|x)] = [(\left|\alpha\right|z^\prime,\left|\alpha\right|x^\prime)]. \end{align*} So scalar multiplication is independent of representatives when $\alpha<0$. We now proceed to show that $(\mathscr{V}, +, \cdot)$ is a real vector space. To do so, we define the auxillary map $T:\mathscr{V}(X, \varphi) \to \mathrm{span}~\varphi(X)$ by \begin{align*} T([(x,z)]) := \Phi(x) - \Phi(z). \end{align*} First, let us verify that $T$ is well-defined. Note that \begin{align*} [(x,z)] &= \{ (x^\prime, z^\prime) \in X_\varphi \times X_\varphi \mid x + z^\prime = z + x^\prime\}\\ &=\{ (x^\prime, z^\prime) \in X_\varphi \times X_\varphi \mid \Phi(x) + \Phi(z^\prime) = \Phi(z) + \Phi(x^\prime)\}\\ &=\{ (x^\prime, z^\prime) \in X_\varphi \times X_\varphi \mid \Phi(x) - \Phi(z) = \Phi(x^\prime) - \Phi(z^\prime)\}. \end{align*} Hence, $T$ is well-defined; its value is uniquely defined on each equivalence class as $\Phi(x) - \Phi(z) = \Phi(x^\prime) - \Phi(z^\prime)$ for all $(x,z)$ and $(x^\prime, z^\prime)$ such that $(x,z) \sim (x^\prime, z^\prime)$ and clearly $\Phi(x) - \Phi(z) \in \mathrm{span}~\varphi(X)$ by construction. Now, we claim that $T$ is a bijection. Injectivity follows from the property that if \begin{align*} T([(x,z)]) = \Phi(x) - \Phi(z) = \Phi(x^\prime) - \Phi(z^\prime) = T([(x^\prime, z^\prime)]) \end{align*} then $(x,z) \sim (x^\prime, z^\prime)$ and so $[(x,z)] = [(x^\prime,z^\prime)]$. For surjectivity, let $v \in \mathrm{span}\,\varphi(X)$ and write \begin{align*} v = \sum_{i=1}^n \alpha_i \varphi(u_i), \end{align*} for $(u_i)_{i=1}^n \subseteq X$ and $(\alpha_i)_{i=1}^n \subseteq \mathbb{R}$. Define \begin{align*} \alpha^+_i =\max(\alpha_i, 0), \quad \alpha^-_i =-\min(\alpha_i, 0), \end{align*} and set \begin{align*} v^+ = \sum_{i=1}^n \alpha^+_i \varphi(u_i), \quad v^- = \sum_{i=1}^n \alpha^-_i \varphi(u_i). \end{align*} Since $\varphi(X)$ is a convex cone and $\Phi : X_\varphi \to \varphi(X)$ is bijective, there exist $x,z \in X_\varphi$ such that $\Phi(x)=v^+$ and $\Phi(z)=v^-$. By construction, \begin{align*} T([(x,z)]) = v^+ - v^- = v, \end{align*} so $T$ is surjective. Now, we claim, the following relationships: \begin{align*} T([(x,z)] + [(x^\prime, z^\prime)]) = T([(x,z)]) + T([(x^\prime, z^\prime)]) \end{align*} and \begin{align*} T(\alpha [(x, z)]) = \alpha T([(x,z)]). \end{align*} Indeed, \begin{align*} T([(x,z)] + [(x^\prime, z^\prime)]) &= T([(x + x^\prime, z + z^\prime)])\\ &= \Phi(x + x^\prime) - \Phi(z + z^\prime) \\ &= \Phi(\Phi^{-1}(\Phi(x) + \Phi(x^\prime))) - \Phi(\Phi^{-1}(\Phi(z) + \Phi(z^\prime)))\\ &= \Phi(x) - \Phi(z) + \Phi(x^\prime) - \Phi(z^\prime)\\ &= T([(x,z)]) + T([(x^\prime, z^\prime)]), \end{align*} and \begin{align*} T(\alpha [(x, z)]) = \begin{cases} T([(\alpha x, \alpha z)]) & \alpha \geq 0,\\ T([(|\alpha| z, |\alpha| x)]) & \alpha < 0. \end{cases} \end{align*} For the case $\alpha \geq 0$ notice that \begin{align*} T([(\alpha x, \alpha z)]) &= \Phi(\alpha x) - \Phi(\alpha z)\\ &= \alpha \Phi(x) - \alpha \Phi(z) \\ &= \alpha T([(x,z)]). \end{align*} Likewise, the case $\alpha < 0$ yields \begin{align*} T([(|\alpha| z, |\alpha| x)]) &= \Phi(|\alpha| z) - \Phi(|\alpha| x)\\ &=|\alpha| \Phi(z) - |\alpha| \Phi(x)\\ &=-\alpha \Phi(z) + \alpha \Phi(x)\\ &=\alpha T([(x,z)]), \end{align*} by commutativity in $\mathrm{span}~\varphi(X)$. However, as $\mathrm{span} ~\varphi(X)$ is naturally a vector space, the claim follows through bijection of $T$ and the fact that the algebraic structure is preserved by $T$.

motivationContexts.text: While the former doesn't immediately tell us how to construct the analogous theory for convex cones, we rely on the following Theorem for working within an appropriate convex cone.

The theorem justifies the following approach to some extent; to model elements within a convex cone, one approach is to model them within the underlying Hilbert space first, and subsequently project onto the convex cone. We remark that there may be elements within the convex cone that are closer to the original element.

proofMoves.text: First, let us prove that addition and scalar multiplication are well-defined; for addition, suppose that $(x,y) \sim (x^\prime, y^\prime)$ and $(z,w) \sim (z^\prime, w^\prime)$. We will show that the choice of representatives from the equivalence classes are irrelevant. That is, we will show that $ [(x + z, y + w)] = [(x^\prime + z^\prime, y^\prime + w^\prime)]. $ By definition of $\sim$, we have $ x+y^\prime = x^\prime+y $ and $ z+w^\prime = z^\prime+w. $ We must show that $ (x+z,y+w)\sim(x^\prime+z^\prime,y^\prime+w^\prime). $ By definition of $\sim$, this is equivalent to showing that $ (x+z)+(y^\prime+w^\prime) = (x^\prime+z^\prime)+(y+w). $ Using associativity and commutativity of addition in $X_\varphi$, we obtain $ (x+z)+(y^\prime+w^\prime) &= (x+y^\prime)+(z+w^\prime) \\ &= (x^\prime+y)+(z^\prime+w) \\ &= (x^\prime+z^\prime)+(y+w). $ Therefore $ (x+z,y+w)\sim(x^\prime+z^\prime,y^\prime+w^\prime). $ Hence $ [(x+z,y+w)] = [(x^\prime+z^\prime,y^\prime+w^\prime)]. $ Thus addition is independent of the representatives chosen. Next, we show that scalar multiplication is well-defined. Suppose that $ (x,z)\sim(x^\prime,z^\prime). $ Then, by definition of $\sim$, we have $ x+z^\prime=x^\prime+z. $ Let $\alpha\in\mathbb{R}$. We must show that $ \alpha[(x,z)]=\alpha[(x^\prime,z^\prime)]. $ First, suppose that $\alpha\geq 0$. Then $ \alpha[(x,z)] = [(\alpha x,\alpha z)] $ and $ \alpha[(x^\prime,z^\prime)] = [(\alpha x^\prime,\alpha z^\prime)]. $ Thus, it suffices to show that $ (\alpha x,\alpha z)\sim(\alpha x^\prime,\alpha z^\prime). $ By definition of $\sim$, this is equivalent to showing that $ \alpha x+\alpha z^\prime = \alpha x^\prime+\alpha z. $ Using compatibility of the transported cone structure with non-negative scalar multiplication, we have $ \alpha x+\alpha z^\prime &= \alpha(x+z^\prime) \\ &= \alpha(x^\prime+z) \\ &= \alpha x^\prime+\alpha z. $ Therefore $ (\alpha x,\alpha z) \sim (\alpha x^\prime,\alpha z^\prime), $ and hence $ [(\alpha x,\alpha z)] = [(\alpha x^\prime,\alpha z^\prime)]. $ So scalar multiplication is independent of representatives when $\alpha\geq 0$. Now suppose that $\alpha<0$. Let $ \beta=|\alpha|. $ Then $\beta>0$, and $ \alpha[(x,z)] = [(\beta z,\beta x)] $ while $ \alpha[(x^\prime,z^\prime)] = [(\beta z^\prime,\beta x^\prime)]. $ Thus, it suffices to show that $ (\beta z,\beta x)\sim(\beta z^\prime,\beta x^\prime). $ By definition of $\sim$, this is equivalent to showing that $ \beta z+\beta x^\prime = \beta z^\prime+\beta x. $ Since $(x,z)\sim(x^\prime,z^\prime)$, we have $ x+z^\prime=x^\prime+z. $ Multiplying by $\beta$ and using compatibility with non-negative scalar multiplication gives $ \beta x+\beta z^\prime &= \beta(x+z^\prime) \\ &= \beta(x^\prime+z) \\ &= \beta x^\prime+\beta z. $ Using commutativity of addition in $X_\varphi$, this gives $ \beta z^\prime+\beta x = \beta z+\beta x^\prime. $ By symmetry of equality, $ \beta z+\beta x^\prime = \beta z^\prime+\beta x. $ Therefore $ (\beta z,\beta x)\sim(\beta z^\prime,\beta x^\prime). $ Since $\beta=|\alpha|$, this means that $ (|\alpha|z,|\alpha|x)\sim(|\alpha|z^\prime,|\alpha|x^\prime), $ and hence $ [(\left|\alpha\right|z,\left|\alpha\right|x)] = [(\left|\alpha\right|z^\prime,\left|\alpha\right|x^\prime)]. $ So scalar multiplication is independent of representatives when $\alpha<0$. We now proceed to show that $(\mathscr{V}, +, \cdot)$ is a real vector space. To do so, we define the auxillary map $T:\mathscr{V}(X, \varphi) \to \mathrm{span}~\varphi(X)$ by $ T([(x,z)]):= \Phi(x) - \Phi(z). $ First, let us verify that $T$ is well-defined. Note that $ [(x,z)] &= \{ (x^\prime, z^\prime) \in X_\varphi \times X_\varphi \mid x + z^\prime = z + x^\prime\}\\ &=\{ (x^\prime, z^\prime) \in X_\varphi \times X_\varphi \mid \Phi(x) + \Phi(z^\prime) = \Phi(z) + \Phi(x^\prime)\}\\ &=\{ (x^\prime, z^\prime) \in X_\varphi \times X_\varphi \mid \Phi(x) - \Phi(z) = \Phi(x^\prime) - \Phi(z^\prime)\}. $ Hence, $T$ is well-defined; its value is uniquely defined on each equivalence class as $\Phi(x) - \Phi(z) = \Phi(x^\prime) - \Phi(z^\prime)$ for all $(x,z)$ and $(x^\prime, z^\prime)$ such that $(x,z) \sim (x^\prime, z^\prime)$ and clearly $\Phi(x) - \Phi(z) \in \mathrm{span}~\varphi(X)$ by construction. Now, we claim that $T$ is a bijection. Injectivity follows from the property that if $ T([(x,z)]) = \Phi(x) - \Phi(z) = \Phi(x^\prime) - \Phi(z^\prime) = T([(x^\prime, z^\prime)]) $ then $(x,z) \sim (x^\prime, z^\prime)$ and so $[(x,z)] = [(x^\prime,z^\prime)]$. For surjectivity, let $v \in \mathrm{span}\,\varphi(X)$ and write $ v = \sum_{i=1}^n \alpha_i \varphi(u_i), $ for $(u_i)_{i=1}^n \subseteq X$ and $(\alpha_i)_{i=1}^n \subseteq \mathbb{R}$. Define $ \alpha^+_i =\max(\alpha_i, 0), \quad \alpha^-_i =-\min(\alpha_i, 0), $ and set $ v^+ = \sum_{i=1}^n \alpha^+_i \varphi(u_i), \quad v^- = \sum_{i=1}^n \alpha^-_i \varphi(u_i). $ Since $\varphi(X)$ is a convex cone and $\Phi: X_\varphi \to \varphi(X)$ is bijective, there exist $x,z \in X_\varphi$ such that $\Phi(x)=v^+$ and $\Phi(z)=v^-$. By construction, $ T([(x,z)]) = v^+ - v^- = v, $ so $T$ is surjective. Now, we claim, the following relationships: $ T([(x,z)] + [(x^\prime, z^\prime)]) = T([(x,z)]) + T([(x^\prime, z^\prime)]) $ and $ T(\alpha [(x, z)]) = \alpha T([(x,z)]). $ Indeed, $ T([(x,z)] + [(x^\prime, z^\prime)]) &= T([(x + x^\prime, z + z^\prime)])\\ &= \Phi(x + x^\prime) - \Phi(z + z^\prime) \\ &= \Phi(\Phi^{-1}(\Phi(x) + \Phi(x^\prime))) - \Phi(\Phi^{-1}(\Phi(z) + \Phi(z^\prime)))\\ &= \Phi(x) - \Phi(z) + \Phi(x^\prime) - \Phi(z^\prime)\\ &= T([(x,z)]) + T([(x^\prime, z^\prime)]), $ and $ T(\alpha [(x, z)]) = \begin{cases} T([(\alpha x, \alpha z)]) & \alpha \geq 0,\\ T([(|\alpha| z, |\alpha| x)]) & \alpha < 0. \end{cases} $ For the case $\alpha \geq 0$ notice that $ T([(\alpha x, \alpha z)]) &= \Phi(\alpha x) - \Phi(\alpha z)\\ &= \alpha \Phi(x) - \alpha \Phi(z) \\ &= \alpha T([(x,z)]). $ Likewise, the case $\alpha < 0$ yields $ T([(|\alpha| z, |\alpha| x)]) &= \Phi(|\alpha| z) - \Phi(|\alpha| x)\\ &=|\alpha| \Phi(z) - |\alpha| \Phi(x)\\ &=-\alpha \Phi(z) + \alpha \Phi(x)\\ &=\alpha T([(x,z)]), $ by commutativity in $\mathrm{span}~\varphi(X)$. However, as $\mathrm{span} ~\varphi(X)$ is naturally a vector space, the claim follows through bijection of $T$ and the fact that the algebraic structure is preserved by $T$.

motivation.summary: Once the order book is allowed to move randomly, finite market states must become objects that probability can see. This is where stochastic point-process language enters the story. The financial-market picture is that the theorem justifies the following approach to some extent; to model elements within a convex cone, one approach is to model them within the underlying Hilbert space first, and subsequently project onto the convex cone.

motivationContexts.text: Although the proof is long and fairly technical, the main idea of Theorem thm:grothendieck-vector-space-from-convex-cone is simple. As in the weakly linear case, a weakly convex operator need not preserve all information from the original set X; distinct elements may become indistinguishable after applying , and this loss of information is encoded through equivalence classes. The recovery of a vector space from the convex cone X_ then follows the usual Grothendieck construction: one considers pairs of cone elements, with the first component representing positive contributions and the second representing negative contributions, just as in the construction of Z from N.

Central to proof of Theorem thm:grothendieck-vector-space-from-convex-cone was the operator T as defined in Corollary thm:grothendieck-vectorization-is-span as it allowed us to carry the vector space structure from V onto V(X, ). The next corollary is likewise straightforward.

Corollary cor:grothendieck-vectorization-inner-product-space justifies, to a large extent, that one can work within a convex cone with little-to-no problems, provided one utilizes a metric projection to ultimately return to the closure of the cone.

nodes.title: Corollary: grothendieck vectorization inner product space
nodes.statement: Let $X$ be a set, $(V, \langle \cdot, \cdot \rangle)$ be a real inner product space, and $\varphi : X \to V$ a weakly convex operator. Let $T:\mathscr{V}(X,\varphi) \to \mathrm{span}~\varphi(X)$ be the linear isomorphism \begin{align*} T([(x_\varphi,z_\varphi)]) = \Phi(x_\varphi) - \Phi(z_\varphi). \end{align*} Endow $\mathscr{V}(X,\varphi)$ with the bilinear form $\llangle \cdot, \cdot \rrangle :\mathscr{V}(X,\varphi) \times \mathscr{V}(X,\varphi) \to \mathbb{R}$ defined by by \begin{align*} \llangle [(x_\varphi,z_\varphi)], [(x^\prime_\varphi, z^\prime_\varphi)] \rrangle &= \langle T([(x_\varphi,z_\varphi)]), T([(x^\prime_\varphi, z^\prime_\varphi)])\rangle \\ &= \langle \Phi(x_\varphi) - \Phi(z_\varphi), \Phi(x^\prime_\varphi) - \Phi(z^\prime_\varphi) \rangle. \end{align*} Then $(\mathscr{V}(X,\varphi), \llangle \cdot, \cdot \rrangle)$ is an inner product space and moreover, $T$ is an isometric linear isomorphism. Moreover, \begin{enumerate} \item The completion of $\mathscr{V}(X,\varphi)$ and the completion of $\mathrm{span}~\varphi(X)$ are isometrically isomorphic. \item The operator $T$ extends to a linear isometric isomorphism between the completion of $\mathscr{V}(X,\varphi)$ and the completion of ${\mathrm{span}~\varphi(X)}$. \item The convex cone $X_\varphi$ can be identified in the completion. Moreover, the closure of the convex cone $X_\varphi$ is isometrically identifiable in the completion of $\mathscr{V}(X,\varphi)$. \item There is a unique metric projection from the completion of $\mathscr{V}(X,\varphi)$ to the closure of $X_\varphi$. \end{enumerate}

motivationContexts.text: There are several approaches to the problem. However, to describe the market, it is desirable to distinguish between buy and sell orders. For our purposes, we shall leverage the disjoint union.

Disjoint unions allow us to consider several potentially unrelated sets as a whole, while retaining information about which set the element originally came from. Heuristically, from a financial market perspective, we typically have two types of orders: buy orders and sell orders. Although they are seemingly different, we would like to consider them as a common instance of an order in the market without forgetting which type of order they originally were.

Using disjoint unions, one can restrict the admissible actions over a range of scenarios as seen from Examples exmp:adm-static,exmp:agent-adm-static, exmp:adm-dyn, and exmp:agent-adm-dyn. However, as is shown in Examples exmp:agent-adm-static and exmp:agent-adm-dyn, choosing the sets on which one takes the set product and disjoint union depends highly on the application.
Proposition prop:disjoint-isomorphism states that if the sets are a priori disjoint, then one is, more or less, indifferent between the typical union and the disjoint union.

nodes.statement: Let $X$ be a non-empty set. The set \begin{align} \mathscr{T}(X) = \bigcup_{n\in\mathbb{N}_0} X^n, \end{align} where $X^0$ is the singleton containing the empty function, is called the space of tuples over $X$ and the elements $\bm{x} \in \mathscr{T}(X)$ either $X$-tuples or simply tuples.

motivationContexts.text: In the previous sections, we showed how disjoint unions can encode market information into its elements and how one can metricize the set of finite sets to produce complete and separable spaces, provided the underlying set is complete and separable. In this section, we combine the results and propose a structure to represent markets. It is worth remarking that the market could be represented by a distinct finite set or a finite set, but these sets are, generally, cumbersome to work within, as most operations carried out during trading or on exchanges can be described algorithmically. Therefore, it is convenient to enumerate each order within the market.

Note, that the construction of the market is independent from the orders at the present stage. Therefore, the forthcoming theory is presented for arbitrary non-empty sets, but one should, in general, think of the sets as being disjoint unions containing the relevant information.

The intuition behind introducing tuples is that we can collect all the orders within a market into a tuple, which defines the market uniquely up to permutations of the domain. Now, it is often convenient to specify the length of the tuple.

Let mT(X) be a tuple representing the market; each entry of the tuple, m(i) where i \1, ,(m)\, corresponds to an order in the set X, which can be thought of as a representative for the admissible orders, as seen in the former section.

motivationContexts.text: A somewhat natural question is whether or not a sorting permutation exists in the first place. Fortunately, the result is positive.
Now, we will require at least one function that sorts any potential market in the order of execution; one can think of such a function as the execution rule for the market or exchange.
Of course, Theorem thm:permutation-exists immediately guarantees that at least one such rule exists.

It is worth noticing that the problem is, as shown, not whether an execution rule exists for a market with a partial order, but rather that there may be several similar rules, from which one has to choose. However, if the market already specifies how all orders are compared explicitly, one does not need to choose the rule in any way, as seen from the following Corollary.

lean.signature:
theorem exists_sortingPermutation [Preorder X] (σ : SortingRule X) (x : Tuple X) :
    ∃ π : SortingPermutations x, σ.sort x = permute x π.1 := by
lean.informal: the output of a sorting rule is a permuted copy of the input tuple.

motivationContexts.text: Now, some markets are wholly unambiguous when deciding which orders to execute, while others allow for ambiguity. For instance, many exchanges, leverage so-called price-time priority, where orders are ranked first based on their price and subsequently by the time at which they arrived at the exchange. However, while improbable, one could, in principle, encounter a situation where two orders with the same price are submitted to (or arrive at) the exchange simultaneously, making the price-time priority ambiguous. In practice, the likelihood that such an event occurs is negligible, and the exchange will likely assign them a rank at random or based on whichever order enters their system first.

First, we will consider how one can extend a ranking on specific categories of order, such as buy/sell orders or the specific product one intends to trade, to the aggregate disjoint union representative.
Proposition prop:disjoint-partial-order is quite natural; it states that partial orders on, say, buy and sell orders respectively can be combined to a partial order on the market.
We shall often require a far stronger type of ordering, namely a total ordering, and so, we have the following Proposition.

Proposition prop:disjoint-total-order and Corollary cor:strict-disjoint-total-order allow us to define total orders, which will later be convenient for settling the market. However, one should note that the ordering on the market is generally not total; if one, e.g., includes agents in the market, then the market should not favour specific agents over others. Nonetheless, we have the following result due to (szpilrajn1930extension).

While ranking specific agents above others is indeed a severe problem, the shortcoming can be rectified once we consider the stochastic setting, as one can specify models such that the probability of equal orders from different agents is 0. Hence, while unsatisfying from a theoretical point of view, it is not crucial for practical purposes.

Proposition prop:disjoint-total-order and Corollary cor:strict-disjoint-total-order allow us to define total orders, which will later be convenient for settling the market. However, one should note that the ordering on the market is generally not total; if one, e.g., includes agents in the market, then the market should not favour specific agents over others. Nonetheless, we have the following result due to (szpilrajn1930extension).

While ranking specific agents above others is indeed a severe problem, the shortcoming can be rectified once we consider the stochastic setting, as one can specify models such that the probability of equal orders from different agents is 0. Hence, while unsatisfying from a theoretical point of view, it is not crucial for practical purposes.

nodes.title: Proposition: disjoint union metrization (1)
nodes.statement: Proposition: disjoint union metrization

motivationContexts.text: In this subsection, we introduce a topology for the set of potential orders. The results presented herein are also relevant for the further theoretical constructions. Now, the disjoint union can be endowed with a metric, provided the underlying sets, (X_)_ A are metric spaces.
Of course, we have yet to show that the disjoint union metric is in fact a metric.

Returning to Example exmp:adm-static, the definition, and in particular eq:disjoint-metric, says that if we compare either two buy orders or two sell orders, we can utilize the appropriate metric between them. However, the distance between a buy and a sell order is infinite, which can be interpreted as the two being incomparable. The adverse effect is that for certain representations of dynamic markets, such as seen in Examples exmp:adm-dyn and exmp:agent-adm-dyn, two orders that are submitted arbitrarily close in time, but not precisely at the same time, are incomparable; this phenomenon occurs only when time appears as an index set in the disjoint union.

In addition, the metrization of disjoint unions allows us to present a version of the so-called pasting lemma. The property is also known as the “Characteristic Property of Disjoint Union Spaces” in (lee2010introduction).

motivationContexts.text: The important part here is, that the Hausdorff distance alone cannot be complete, because it does not restrict the cardinality. However, if one includes information about the cardinality, then the metric may become complete. In particular, eq:cauchy-but-not fails to be a Cauchy sequence in the metric that discriminates on cardinality, as its cardinality increases.

implying that the topologies coincide. We will henceforth refer to the result as the standard machinery for tuples.

nodes.title: Proposition: separation continuous
nodes.statement: Let $(X_\alpha, d_\alpha)_{\alpha\in A}$ be a countable family of metric spaces and let $X = \bigsqcup_{\alpha\in A} X_\alpha$ be endowed with the disjoint union metric, $d:X\times X \to [0,\infty]$. Moreover, let $(\mathscr{T}(X_\alpha), \mathscr{d}_{H,\alpha})$ be the Hausdorff tuple space induced by $(X_\alpha, d_\alpha)$ and $(\mathscr{T}(X),\mathscr{d}_H)$ be the tuple Hausdorff space induced by $d$. Then, \begin{enumerate}[(i)] \item For each $\alpha \in A$, the $\alpha$-separation operator $\bm{\Pi}_\alpha : \mathscr{T}(X) \to \mathscr{T}(X_\alpha)$ is continuous. \item The separation operator $\bm{\Pi}:\mathscr{T}(X) \to \prod_{\alpha \in A} \mathscr{T}(X_\alpha)$ is continuous, whenever $\prod_{\alpha \in A} \mathscr{T}(X_\alpha)$ is endowed with the maximum product metric. \end{enumerate}

proofMoves.title: Construct the required object
proofMoves.text: To prove \eqref{prop:separation-1}, we must show that for any $\bm{x}_0 \in \mathscr{T}(X)$ and $\varepsilon >0$ there exists a $\delta > 0 $ such that $ \mathscr{d}_H(\bm{x}, \bm{x}_0) < \delta \implies \mathscr{d}_{H,\alpha}(\bm{\Pi}_\alpha \bm{x}, \bm{\Pi}_\alpha \bm{x}_0) < \varepsilon. $ We claim, that one can choose $\delta < \min(1, \varepsilon)$; assume without loss of generality that $\bm{x}_0 \neq \bm{e}$ - in which case the proof would be trivial - and note that there are two cases:

proofMoves.title: Construct the required object
proofMoves.text: First, if $\forall i \in \mathrm{domain}(\bm{x}_0):\bm{x}_0(i) \notin X_\alpha \times \{\alpha\}$, then clearly choosing $\delta$ as above yields the desired result, as $\bm{x} \in B_{\delta}(\bm{x}_0)$ clearly must have $\forall i \in \mathrm{domain}(\bm{x}):\bm{x}(i) \notin X_\alpha \times \{\alpha\}$, and hence $\bm{\Pi}_\alpha \bm{x}_0 = \bm{e} = \bm{\Pi}_\alpha \bm{x}$, as neither tuple has entries in $X_\alpha \times \{\alpha\}$ and hence selecting the sub-tuple with components only from $X_\alpha$ must be empty. The second case is whenever there exists a $I \subseteq \mathrm{domain}(\bm{x}_0)$ such that $\forall i \in I: \bm{x}_0(i) \in X_\alpha \times \{\alpha\}.$

proofMoves.title: Prove the equality
proofMoves.text: Now, choose $\bm{x} \in B_\delta (\bm{x}_0)$ and note that immediately one has $\forall i \in I: \bm{x}(i) \in X_\alpha \times \{\alpha\}$, but then $ \varepsilon > \delta > \mathscr{d}_H(\bm{x}, \bm{x}_0) &= \max_{i \in \mathrm{domain}(\bm{x}_0)} d(\bm{x}(i), \bm{x}_0(i)) \\ &\geq \max_{i \in I} d(\bm{x}(i), \bm{x}_0(i)) \\ &=\max_{i \in I} d_\alpha(\bm{P}_1 \bm{x}(i), \bm{P}_1 \bm{x}_0(i))\\ &= \max_{j \in \{1, \dots, |I|\}} d_\alpha(\bm{P}_1\left(\bm{x}[I]\right)(j), \bm{P}_1 \left(\bm{x}_0[I]\right)(j))\\ &= \mathscr{d}_{H,\alpha}(\bm{\Pi}_\alpha \bm{x}, \bm{\Pi}_\alpha\bm{x}_0) $ as desired, since $I = \{i \in \mathrm{domain}(\bm{x}_0) \mid \bm{x}_0(i) \in X_\alpha\times \{\alpha\}\} = \{i \in \mathrm{domain}(\bm{x}_0) \mid \bm{x}(i) \in X_\alpha\times \{\alpha\}\}$. For the second property, we once again let $\bm{x}_0 \in \mathscr{T}(X)$ and $\varepsilon > 0$ be given.

proofMoves.title: Unfold the definitions
proofMoves.text: Now, for the given $\bm{x}_0$ define $ A(\bm{x}_0) = \{\alpha \in A \mid \exists i \in \mathrm{domain}(\bm{x}_0): \bm{x}_0(i) \in X_\alpha \times \{\alpha\}\}, $ and note that by setting $\delta = \min(1, \varepsilon)$ one has that for $\bm{x}\in B_\delta(\bm{x}_0)$ $ A(\bm{x}) = A(\bm{x}_0). $ Moreover, note that $|A(\bm{x}_0)| < \infty$ since $\bm{x}_0$ is a tuple. It now follows that $ \varepsilon > \delta > \mathscr{d}_H(\bm{x}, \bm{x}_0) &= \max_{i \in \mathrm{domain}(\bm{x}_0)} d(\bm{x}(i), \bm{x}_0(i)) \\ &= \max_{\alpha \in A(\bm{x}_0)} \max_{\substack{i \in \mathrm{domain}(\bm{x}_0)\\ \bm{x}_0(i) \in X_\alpha \times \{\alpha\}}} d_\alpha(\bm{P}_{\mathrm{element}}(\bm{x}(i)), \bm{P}_{\mathrm{element}}(\bm{x}_0(i)))\\ &= \max_{\alpha \in A(\bm{x}_0)} \mathscr{d}_{H,\alpha}(\bm{\Pi}_\alpha \bm{x}, \bm{\Pi}_\alpha\bm{x}_0) \\ &= \max_{\alpha \in A} \mathscr{d}_{H,\alpha}(\bm{\Pi}_\alpha \bm{x}, \bm{\Pi}_\alpha\bm{x}_0), $ where the latter is by definition the maximum metric over $A$, the index set over which the disjoint union is taken, as the projections $\bm{\Pi}_\alpha \bm{x} = \bm{\Pi}_{\alpha} \bm{x}_0 = \bm{e}$ for all $\alpha \in A: \alpha\notin A(\bm{x}_0)$.

proofMoves.title: Prove the equality
proofMoves.text: Finally, since $ \bm{\Pi} \bm{x} = (\bm{\Pi}_\alpha \bm{x})_{\alpha \in A}, $ the result follows.

motivationContexts.text: So far, we have shown some results relating to finite integer-valued measures. We now proceed by identifying the similarities with the tuple space. However, there is currently an inherent problem; if one recalls the mapping eq:prelim-pp, it is easy to notice, that there are more than one tuple that produces the same integer-valued measure. Therefore, we first require a way to combine all tuples that produce the same integer-valued measure.

The relation, \pi allows us to disregard the specific ordering in which the points are presented in the tuple, ultimately implying that the only remaining data is the image as well as the multiplicity of each element in the image, which, by construction, leads to a strong correspondence with the atomic decomposition of an integer-valued measure.
Using permutative equality, we can separate all the tuples that are the same up to a permutation.

motivationContexts.text: While the former doesn't immediately tell us how to construct the analogous theory for convex cones, we rely on the following Theorem for working within an appropriate convex cone.

The theorem justifies the following approach to some extent; to model elements within a convex cone, one approach is to model them within the underlying Hilbert space first, and subsequently project onto the convex cone. We remark that there may be elements within the convex cone that are closer to the original element.

nodes.title: Corollary: pseudometric metric relation
nodes.statement: Let $X$ be a set and let $d,\rho:X \times X \to [0,\infty]$ be a metric and a pseudometric on $X$, respectively. Then: \begin{enumerate}[(i)] \item $(X,d)$ is a pseudometric space; \item $(X,\rho)$ is a metric space if and only if $\rho(x,x^\prime) = 0$ implies $x = x^\prime$ for all $x,x^\prime \in X$. \end{enumerate}

motivationContexts.text: Sometimes it is useful to relax the first axiom while keeping the symmetry and triangle inequality.

A pseudometric behaves like a metric except that distinct points are allowed to have distance zero. This is useful when one only cares about objects up to an equivalence that ignores certain distinctions.
Open balls are the metric version of local neighborhoods, so Proposition eq:topology-extended-pseudometric shows that every pseudometric comes with a canonical topology.
